title: The argument in the graph
text:
The argument in the graph


Part I · Week 1 of 8 · climate data




One dataset, three charts, three different stories, all of them defensible. So a chart is a claim, and someone chose which claim to make.




01Question02Claim03Evidence04Encoding05Annotationthis week: the first two steps, and why the other three exist






THE LECTURE



Tuesday · 15:30



There is no critique yet, so the lecture opens on three charts from the gallery, each rebuilt in R and changed once to say something new. Then: the grammar of graphics as a way of thinking rather than as syntax; perception as the reason design principles are findings and not taste; integrity; how we will argue about charts all term; and showing uncertainty, which every chart you hand in has to do.
Gallery. Van Langren’s twelve estimates of one distance, from 1644, rebuilt with the answer we know now and drawn on a map. The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, from Russell’s hand-drawn plate to 67,074 stars. Twenty years of news headlines turning negative, and the 47 outlets behind the average. And the Datasaurus dozen.
Open the slides



The slides open in their own tab, so you can keep them beside this page. Day, time and room for every session are on the schedule.




THE WORK GROUP




Thursday · R basics



Objects, vectors, tables, functions and help. Then the verbs that get a table into shape, joined with the pipe: filter(), select(), mutate(), group_by() and summarise(), and pivot_longer() for wide against long. Before the first work group walks through the install.




Thursday · the grammar



Tuesday’s eight slots, as code. One chart of the De Bilt temperature record, built one slot at a time, from data and mapping to theme, so you can see what each line of a ggplot call does.



Open the work group



THE DATA

On Tuesday, HadCRUT5: the global surface temperature record, 1850 to 2025, 176 annual means with a 95% interval on every one of them. The lecture’s three competing stories all come out of this one file.
On Thursday, KNMI De Bilt: one Dutch weather station, 1901 to now, exactly as the institute publishes it: thirteen lines of notes before the data, temperatures in tenths of a degree, and the twelve months side by side as columns.
Before you plot anything: what is one row, what kind of variable does each column hold, and what can the file not tell you? Finding your way around an unfamiliar dataset is one of the things this course teaches.



PORTFOLIO

Nothing is handed in this week. The first portfolio entry comes out of week 2’s work group, and every entry from then on carries the rule from Tuesday’s lecture: a claim written as a sentence, and a note on what the chart cannot tell you.



READINGS




Book · chapters 1 and 2 · read before Tuesday



Where the R starts. Thursday’s work group builds a first ggplot one slot at a time, and these two chapters get you ready for it.

Healy, K. (2018). Data visualization: A practical introduction. Princeton University Press. https://socviz.co

Open socviz.co




Book · two chapters and a section · read before Tuesday



Introduction and Visualizing data: mapping data onto aesthetics: Tuesday’s grammar of graphics, as a way of thinking rather than as syntax. Then the short no-3d section, which is the reason behind Tuesday’s slide on what follows from the ranking of channels.

Wilke, C. O. (2019). Fundamentals of data visualization. O’Reilly. https://clauswilke.com/dataviz

Open the book




Read before Tuesday, not between Tuesday and Thursday. The lecture is self-contained preparation for the build, so the reading is worth most before you hear it.

title: DSVAR
section: Rebuilt in R, with the correct answer
text:
Rebuilt in R, with the correct answer



langren |>
  ggplot(aes(Longitude,
             reorder(Name, Longitude))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 16.5,
             colour = "grey40") +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = 16.5, xmax = Longitude),
                 colour = "#2a8558", alpha = .4) +
  geom_point(colour = "#2a8558", size = 3) +
  labs(x = "Degrees east of Toledo", y = NULL,
       title = "All twelve put Rome too far east")













The same twelve rows. One layer, geom_vline(), adds the distance we know now. They disagree becomes they are all wrong, by 1.2 to 13.6 degrees.

title: DSVAR
text:
Twelve Romes










The same numbers as places on the ground, which is what a ship’s navigator needed. Only 2 of the twelve put Rome in Italy, 3 in the Adriatic and 7 in the Balkans.

title: DSVAR
section: A few hundred stars, by hand (1914)
text:
A few hundred stars, by hand (1914)





Henry Norris Russell’s plate. Each dot is one star whose distance had been measured, a few hundred stars here, a few thousand in later versions.
Across the top: spectral class, B to M. It is the star’s colour, and it gives its surface temperature: hot and blue on the left, cool and red on the right
Down the side: absolute magnitude, how bright the star really is once its distance is taken out. Smaller numbers are brighter, so the brightest stars are at the top
The dots stand in columns because a class is a category. Most fall on one diagonal band, from hot and bright to cool and faint. A few cool stars sit far above it, much brighter than their colour would suggest
The two ruled lines are Russell’s own, drawn along the band



Figure from H. N. Russell (1914), Relations between the spectra and other characteristics of the stars, Nature, 93, 252. Public domain in the US; in copyright in the EU until 2028; shown at reduced size for criticism and review.

title: DSVAR
text:
Rebuilt in R, with 67,074 stars



ggplot(stars, aes(ci, absmag, colour = ci)) +
  geom_point(size = .3, alpha = .4) +
  scale_colour_gradientn(
    colours = c("#3f66ff", "#8fb0ff", "#f4f1e8",
                "#ffd23f", "#ff8a1a", "#ff3b1f"),
    values = scales::rescale(
      c(-.3, 0, .4, .65, 1.1, 1.6)),
    limits = c(-.3, 1.6),
    oob = scales::squish, guide = "none") +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  annotate("label", colour = "white", fill = "#0b0e14",
    linewidth = 0, hjust = 0,
    x = c(1.75, 1.85, .2, -.25), y = c(8, -2.5, 2.4, 15.6),
    label = c("main sequence", "giants",
              "subgiants", "white dwarfs")) +
  labs(x = "Colour index (blue to red)",
       y = "Absolute magnitude") +
  theme_dsvar(dark = TRUE) +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#0b0e14"))













One row per star within 250 parsecs, from a modern catalogue; colour index replaced Russell’s spectral class.

title: DSVAR
section: At the same colour, two kinds of star
text:
At the same colour, two kinds of star













The same stars, another question. Cut them into strips by spectral class and ask: how bright are the stars of one colour?
One ridge per class, its height showing where the class’s stars are most common
The K stars come in two humps: dwarfs and giants about 100 times brighter, with little in between

title: DSVAR
text:
Headlines turning negative (2022)





One point per year, 2000 to 2019: the average tone of that year’s headlines across 47 US news outlets, from 23 million headlines
Sentiment was scored by a language model, from −1, negative, to +1, positive
The light band shows how uncertain each yearly average is
Top left, the change from 2000 to 2019, printed as −314 per cent
Shared widely as evidence that the news has turned negative



Rozado, D., Hughes, R., & Halberstadt, J. (2022). Longitudinal analysis of sentiment and emotion in news media headlines using automated labelling with Transformer language models. PLOS ONE, 17(10), e0276367. CC BY 4.0.

title: DSVAR
text:
Rebuilt in R



yearly |>
  ggplot(aes(year, mean)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = mean - ci,
                  ymax = mean + ci),
              fill = "#2a8558", alpha = .15) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2a8558", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Tone, −1 to +1",
       title = "Headlines grew more negative")













From the authors’ own data: 655 rows, one per outlet and year, averaged into the twenty points of the line.

title: DSVAR
text:
One change: draw every outlet



yearly |>
  ggplot(aes(year, mean)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(data = outlets, colour = "grey70",
    aes(y = sentiment, group = outlet)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = mean - ci,
                  ymax = mean + ci),
              fill = "#2a8558", alpha = .15) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2a8558", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Tone, −1 to +1",
       title = "Outlets differ more than years do")













One layer added: each grey line is one outlet. The fall in the average is real, and small next to how far outlets differ from each other. In 2019 alone they run from -0.57 to 0.33.

title: DSVAR
section: Not a chart menu, and not a ggplot manual
text:
Not a chart menu, and not a ggplot manual

A chart menu tells you which picture goes with which data. It cannot tell you why one of them is a better argument than another
A manual teaches syntax. Syntax you can look up, and increasingly you can ask for using AI
What neither gives you is the ability to judge: the thing that lets you say this chart is making a claim its data does not support


The course teaches you what a chart is being asked to do.

The same numbers, thirteen pictures










Matejka, J., & Fitzmaurice, G. (2017). Same stats, different graphs. CHI ’17. Original dinosaur by Alberto Cairo.

title: DSVAR
text:
Derived principle 1

  









  The summary is not the data


A mean, an sd and a correlation are a lossy compression, and Anscombe and the Datasaurus show exactly how much they throw away
The compression is not neutral. It preserves some structures and destroys others, and it never tells you which it just did
Plot before you model, and plot the residuals after. If you only ever do one of those, do the first

title: DSVAR
section: Two jobs, two sets of rules
text:
Two jobs, two sets of rules



A chart for finding


Made for one reader: you
Fast, ugly, disposable. Twenty of them in an afternoon
Succeeds if it shows you something you did not know
Hertzsprung and Russell’s was one, before anyone else saw it



A chart for arguing


Made for a reader who was not there
Slow, designed, defended. One of them in an afternoon
Succeeds if a sceptical reader believes the claim and can check it
Van Langren’s was one: it was drawn to win a royal grant

title: DSVAR
section: The code is the method section
text:
The code is the method section


climate |>
  filter(year >= 1850) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, anomaly)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi),
              alpha = .18) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .85) +
  theme_dsvar()


This is why the course is in R and not in a tool where you drag things
Every decision in that block is explicit, inspectable and reproducible
A chart you cannot regenerate is a claim you cannot defend

title: DSVAR
text:
Eight slots







Slot
The decision it holds




01
data
which table


02
mapping
which column to which channel


03
geom
what you can actually see


04
stat
what gets computed first


05
scale
how a value becomes a position, a size, a colour


06
coord
the space it is drawn in


07
facet
whether to split it


08
theme
everything carrying no data






Leland Wilkinson (1999) argued that every statistical graphic is one setting of a small number of slots like these
Hadley Wickham (2010) turned that into ggplot2, which is why the R you write on Thursday looks the way it does
You are not learning a library. You are learning a decomposition



Wilkinson, L. (1999). The Grammar of Graphics. Springer. · Wickham, H. (2010). A layered grammar of graphics. Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics, 19(1), 3–28.

title: DSVAR
section: Why this beats a chart menu
text:
Why this beats a chart menu



A chart menu says


“Use a bar chart for categories, a line chart for time, a pie for parts of a whole”
Useful once. Then you meet data that is none of those, and you are stuck
It cannot tell you what a bar chart and a line chart have in common



The grammar says


Decide eight things, in order
A bar chart and a line chart differ in one slot. So do an honest chart and a dishonest one
Which means you can reason about a chart you have never seen before



Every chart you have ever seen is one setting of eight dials.

HadCRUT5, the Met Office and University of East Anglia record of global surface temperature: one row per year, 1850 to 2025, each year’s average given as its difference from the 1961–1990 average, in °C
A new file: 176 rows, four columns. A year, a global temperature anomaly, and the two ends of a 95% interval
Nothing in this table says what it should look like. Not one thing
You will have this open again in week 5, when change over time gets a week of its own. Today it is only something to turn the dials on

title: DSVAR
section: 02 · mapping — axes, and still no chart
text:
02 · mapping — axes, and still no chart



ggplot(climate, aes(year, anomaly))










aes() says which column goes to which channel: year to horizontal position, anomaly to vertical position
Position is only two channels. colour, fill, size, shape and linetype take a column too, and group says which rows belong to one line
The two we set gave us axes, ranges, gridlines and breaks: a whole coordinate system
And not a single mark. There is nothing here that is the data


The most important empty panel in the course.

title: DSVAR
section: 03 · geom — now you can see it
text:
03 · geom — now you can see it



ggplot(climate, aes(year, anomaly)) +
  geom_point(size = .9, alpha = .8)










The geom is the mark: what actually gets drawn at each mapped position
176 observations, 176 points. One to one
This is the first thing on the page that is the data, rather than furniture around it

title: DSVAR
section: 03 · geom — one slot, a different claim
text:
03 · geom — one slot, a different claim



ggplot(climate, aes(year, anomaly)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .8)










One word changed. But a line is an assertion about continuity: that these observations belong on a path, that 1851 follows 1850
True for a temperature record
A lie if your x axis is countries, and people draw it anyway


A default is an argument. This is the first place in the course where that bites.

title: DSVAR
section: 04 · stat — a layer that is not in the file
text:
04 · stat — a layer that is not in the file



ggplot(climate, aes(year, anomaly)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .5, alpha = .4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess",
              formula = y ~ x, span = .4,
              linewidth = .7)










A stat computes something and draws that instead of the data
This curve is nowhere in the 176 rows. It is a model of them
And it is drawn heavier than the data it is summarising, which is a choice nobody made deliberately


Week 5 spends an hour on span. Week 3 meets the same idea first, as a histogram’s bin.

title: DSVAR
section: 05 · scale — what counts as a big change
text:
05 · scale — what counts as a big change



ggplot(climate, aes(year, anomaly)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .8) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-12, 12))










The scale turns a value into a position. Change it and the same numbers occupy a different amount of the page
The warming is still in there. You cannot see it
You have met this chart already today, in Fahrenheit


Week 2 is largely about this slot.

title: DSVAR
section: 06 · coord — the space it is drawn in
text:
06 · coord — the space it is drawn in



ggplot(climate, aes(year, anomaly)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .8) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(1975, 2025))










The coordinate system is the space the marks are placed in. Every chart so far has used the default: two straight axes at right angles
Limits here move the window: the last fifty years only. All 176 rows are still in the chart, most of them just off-screen
Limits on a scale drop whatever falls outside them. It looks like the same move; it is a different slot, and it matters once a stat is computing on what is left
The slot can also bend the space: coord_polar() runs time round a circle, which is week 5’s climate spiral, and a map projection in week 6 is this slot too

title: DSVAR
text:
07 · facet — splitting is conditioning



climate |>
  mutate(era = paste0(50 * (year %/% 50), "s")) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, anomaly)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .6) +
  facet_wrap(~era, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1860, 2020, 20), expand = c(0, 0))










Facetting splits one chart into panels on the value of a variable: here, each half-century gets its own
The marks did not change. Their arrangement did, and so did what is easy to compare
scales = "free_x" gives each panel only its own fifty years. The y axis stays shared, so a height means the same thing in every panel
Tufte called these small multiples and thought them the best idea in the field. Week 4 agrees

title: DSVAR
section: 08 · theme — everything that is not data
text:
08 · theme — everything that is not data



climate |>
  mutate(era = paste0(50 * (year %/% 50), "s")) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, anomaly)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .6) +
  facet_wrap(~era, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1860, 2020, 20), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 13)










The last slide’s chart, plus one line. Same data, same marks, same panels
The theme owns everything that is not data: background, gridlines, borders, the strip above each panel, the type
theme_bw() boxes each panel and shades its label, so four panels now read as four
ggplot ships several complete themes (theme_minimal(), theme_classic(), theme_void()), and each is one line

title: DSVAR
text:
All eight, on one dataset

Interactive — click, or press Enter, to step through. Open full screen

title: DSVAR
text:
Derived principle 2

  







  Every slot is a choice


Every chart today was the same eight slots, filled in differently. The changes at the start were slots: a layer for van Langren’s answer and for every outlet, a coord for the map, a geom and a stat for the stars’ ridges
There is no right chart for a dataset. Each slot has a setting, and most settings come from a default nobody looked at
A default you did not change is still your choice, made earlier by somebody else for another purpose. Which raises the next question: are some settings better than others, or is it taste?

title: DSVAR
text:
Read these five

Answer before you click. The point is the reading, not the answer. Open full screen

title: DSVAR
text:
What just happened

The same five numbers were in all five panels. Correctly drawn in all five: no truncation, no distortion, nothing hidden
On position and length you read B against E without effort. On angle, area and saturation you guessed, or you gave up
The difference was 31 against 29. Two units, about 7%


The channel decided what you could see. Not the data, and not the designer’s skill.

title: DSVAR
text:
This has been measured










Cleveland, W. S., & McGill, R. (1984). Graphical perception: Theory, experimentation, and application to the development of graphical methods. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 79(387), 531–554. · Heer, J., & Bostock, M. (2010). Crowdsourcing graphical perception. CHI ’10.

title: DSVAR
text:
What follows from a ranking

A pie chart asks you to judge angle and area (ranks 3 and 4) to read a number that a bar chart hands you at rank 1
3-D on a 2-D screen adds a projective distortion on top of whichever channel you were already using. This is why Wilke has a section called no-3d rather than a preference
Bubble size is worse than it looks: perceived magnitude scales roughly as area to the power of 0.7, so large circles are systematically under-read


None of these are style opinions. They are findings, and you can look up the confidence intervals.


Stevens, S. S. (1957). On the psychophysical law. Psychological Review, 64(3), 153–181. · Flannery, J. J. (1971). The relative effectiveness of some common graduated point symbols. The Canadian Cartographer, 8(2), 96–109.

title: DSVAR
text:
Derived principle 3

  






  Put what matters in the strongest channel


The full sentence is the strongest channel you can afford, and “afford” is doing real work: you have one position channel per axis and a lot of variables
So the question is never “which channels are good” but which variable deserves the good one
That is an editorial decision about what your chart is for, disguised as a technical one, which is the shape of nearly every decision in this course

title: DSVAR
text:
Find the odd one out

Click the moment you have found it. The clock is the content. Open full screen

title: DSVAR
section: Some channels do not need to be searched
text:
Some channels do not need to be searched

Rounds 1 and 2: one red dot among grey ones. It jumped out, as fast among 120 dots as among 24. For colour, size and tilt your eyes take in the whole picture at once: they are preattentive
Round 3: one square among circles. A little slower: shape stands out less than colour
Round 4: one red square among red circles and grey squares. Slowest: only the combination is unique, and no feature finds a combination at once. You check marks one by one, so more marks take more time


What a reader should find has to differ from everything else in one strong feature, such as colour.


Treisman, A. M., & Gelade, G. (1980). A feature-integration theory of attention. Cognitive Psychology, 12(1), 97–136.

title: DSVAR
text:
Which is why highlighting works

Every annotated chart you admire is exploiting this. One line in colour among twenty grey ones is found in constant time, however many grey ones there are
It also explains a common failure: a legend that distinguishes eight series by hue asks for eight-way discrimination, which is not preattentive, and readers stop trying
And it is why “just make the important one red” is better advice than it sounds


Week 7 comes back to this: it is the mechanism under every annotation you will make.

title: DSVAR
section: What makes marks look like a group
text:
What makes marks look like a group










Same twenty points every time. Nothing in the data changed
Proximity, similarity, enclosure, connection: four Gestalt rules, four different answers to “which of these belong together”

title: DSVAR
text:
Bertin’s vocabulary













Jacques Bertin, a French cartographer, in 1967 listed the retinal variables: the complete set of visual properties a mark can vary
Then he asked of each one: can it express difference, can it express order, can it express amount
Colour hue can tell you two things are different. It cannot tell you which is more



Bertin, J. (1967). Sémiologie graphique. Gauthier-Villars. English edition: Semiology of Graphics, 1983.

title: DSVAR
section: The data type picks the channel
text:
The data type picks the channel



Nominal data (countries, parties, species) needs a channel that shows difference without order. Hue does that; size does not
Ordinal and quantitative data needs a channel that carries order. Position and size do; hue does not
Every Thursday starts by naming each column’s kind for this reason




The course field guide does this for you: pick the kinds of variable you have, and it branches to the charts that can carry them, each with the R that draws it.

title: DSVAR
text:
A law, in numbers













In 1975 the US Congress set a minimum fuel economy for new cars, rising every year: 18 miles per gallon for 1978, 27.5 by 1985
One row per year, eight in all, labelled on the dots
From 18 to 27.5 is a rise of 53 per cent. That is the size of the effect in the data



The standards as Tufte (1983) gives them, pp. 57–58: Energy Policy and Conservation Act, 1975, supplemented by the US Department of Transportation.

title: DSVAR
section: How the New York Times drew it
text:
How the New York Times drew it
















How to read it

Each line is one year, painted across a road that runs into the distance.
A line’s length is meant to be the standard: 1978 is the short line at the back, 1985 the long one in front.


On the page the 1985 line is 5.3 inches long and the 1978 line 0.6: nearly nine times as long, for a standard about one and a half times as high



The New York Times, 9 August 1978, p. D-2, as reproduced and measured in Tufte (1983), p. 57. Rebuilt here from his measurements.

title: DSVAR
text:
The lie factor



  The effect in the graphicthe line grew 0.6 to 5.3 inches+783%
  The effect in the datathe standard grew 18 to 27.5 mpg+53%
  
  Lie factor783 ÷ 53
  14.8
  An honest chart scores 1. Tufte allowed 0.95 to 1.05.



Tufte’s measure divides the size of a change as drawn by the size of the same change in the data
The Times let the lines grow far faster than the numbers they stood for. The chart shows the change about fifteen times larger than it was
It is one number, and you can work it out with a ruler



Tufte, E. R. (1983). The Visual Display of Quantitative Information. Graphics Press, pp. 57–58.

title: DSVAR
text:
Beautiful, competent, backwards

























Same data, same geom, one reversed axis. The lie factor is 1.0: every value is drawn to scale, and Tufte’s measure does not catch this at all


Most readers read the 2007 spike as a fall. Which is the opposite of what happened.

title: DSVAR
text:
Data-ink























Tufte’s rule: maximise the share of ink that carries data, and erase everything else. On the right is his own redrawn boxplot: same five numbers per group, a fraction of the marks


Tufte, E. R. (1983), ch. 4 and 6.

title: DSVAR
text:
Embellished charts were remembered better



Embellished: Nigel Holmes, Time, 1982




Plain: the same numbers




Bateman and colleagues showed people charts like these in pairs. Readers described both equally accurately. Two to three weeks later, they remembered the illustrated ones better.


Both from Bateman, S., Mandryk, R. L., Gutwin, C., Genest, A., McDine, D., & Brooks, C. (2010). Useful junk? CHI ’10, 2573–2582; shown for criticism and review. Holmes’s original: Time, 1982.

title: DSVAR
text:
Minimal charts were liked less



Conventional












Tufte’s minimal version












Inbar and colleagues showed students a conventional bar chart and Tufte’s minimal redesign of it, as here. Most preferred the conventional one. Data-ink helps you find what to cut; it does not prove that less is always better.


Inbar, O., Tractinsky, N., & Meyer, J. (2007). Minimalism in information visualization: Attitudes towards maximizing the data-ink ratio. ECCE ’07, 185–188.

text:
Plain, and dishonest

Life expectancy around 1970, from R’s state.x77. The states are 4.5 years apart
The axis starts at 68, so the bars’ lengths say Hawaii’s people live about 5 times as long as Alabama’s

title: DSVAR
text:
Derived principle 4

  





  A chart can be beautiful and wrong


Beauty is frequently how a chart gets past you, including past people who have taken a course like this one
Every integrity check you have been given today, the lie factor first, passes the Florida chart. Craft is not a defence, and neither is our own
The defence is having built the dishonest version yourself, on purpose, and knowing how little it took. Week 2, Thursday: you make the pair

title: DSVAR
text:
Bullshit visualization

Michael Correll’s term, after Frankfurt: charts indifferent to whether they are true. A lie at least cares what the truth is. Against a lie you check the numbers; against this you ask what the chart was for. None of these four needed bad data













Correll, M. (2019). Ethical dimensions of visualization research. CHI ’19. · Frankfurt, H. G. (2005). On Bullshit. Princeton University Press.

title: DSVAR
text:
Four steps, in this order



01 · Describe

What is on the page?
Marks, axes, ranges, labels. No evaluation yet.



02 · Analyse

Which slots were set, and how?
The grammar, named: data, mapping, geom, scale and the rest.



03 · Interpret

What claim is it making?
One sentence, with a verb, for the reader it was made for.



04 · Judge

Does the evidence carry the claim?
A verdict, and the reason for it.



Most bad critique is step 4 arriving first: “it’s a bit cluttered” before anyone has said what the chart shows. Every exhibit in the gallery runs these four steps, in this order.

title: DSVAR
text:
Who is this for?

A chart is decoded by a particular reader with particular training, and visualization literacy is not evenly distributed
So three questions belong in step 4, not step 1: how much can this reader be assumed to decode, what does the chart owe them, and what has it assumed they already know
A log axis is honest and clear to this room. On a newspaper front page it is neither


Riche, N. H., Hurter, C., Diakopoulos, N., & Carpendale, S. (Eds.) (2018). Data-Driven Storytelling. CRC Press.

title: DSVAR
section: Describe it before you judge it
text:
Describe it before you judge it






“Coronavirus deaths in Italy, Spain and the US are increasing more rapidly than they did in China”. John Burn-Murdoch, Financial Times, data to 26 March 2020. © The Financial Times Limited; shown at reduced size for criticism and review.

title: DSVAR
section: The four steps, on this chart
text:
The four steps, on this chart



01 · Describe

One line per country, labelled at its end. The vertical axis climbs in powers of ten. Faint straight guide lines run across the plot, marked with doubling times. The horizontal axis counts days since each country’s tenth death.



02 · Analyse

Two scales do the work. The log axis turns exponential growth into slope, which people read well. Aligning on the tenth death removes the fact that outbreaks started weeks apart. Direct labels keep a dozen lines readable.



03 · Interpret

The claim is about the rate: from a comparable start, some countries slowed their deaths and others did not. It is careful not to claim that one country did worse overall.



04 · Judge

For this room, it holds. On a front page in March 2020 it is harder: on a log axis a flattening line still means deaths are rising. The FT labelled the axis loudly and published linear versions too. Who is it for decides the verdict.

title: DSVAR
text:
How sure is this?





































Masur and Parry (2026):  People saw a simulated social media feed with few or with many personal posts, then rated how normal posting personal things is there: three items on a 1 to 7 scale, averaged.
Two means on their own: a big difference, and no way to tell how sure it is.



With their 95% intervals: how far each mean could be off. Here, not far.




With each group’s n: how many people each mean rests on.



The axis is cut to 3.5–6.5 so the short whiskers can be seen. The scale runs from 1 to 7: the next slide shows all of it.

title: DSVAR
section: Every person behind the two means
text:
Every person behind the two means













The whole scale, and every one of the 589 people as a dot, with a box for the middle half and the shape of each group beside it
The intervals were narrow because they are about the mean. People vary far more: in both groups, answers run across most of the scale
Week 3 comes back to this: an interval for the mean is not the spread of the data

The fourth way to show uncertainty is a sentence. For this chart: One sample, one simulated feed, and the norm asked right after it. Whether real feeds move norms this much, the chart cannot say
An interval, a range, an n or a sentence. Any one of them counts, and good charts carry more than one



Masur, P. K., & Parry, D. A. (2026). When sharing becomes the norm. Technology, Mind, and Behavior. Data: osf.io/zw6pb, CC BY 4.0.

title: DSVAR
text:
Derived principle 5

  





  Every chart carries its uncertainty


It is the second of the three things every chart you hand in has to carry, from the first portfolio entry on. A habit picked up in week 6 comes too late: by then your defaults are set
Week 3 has the techniques: intervals, the summary that hides a distribution, and the specification curve, which shows every defensible analysis instead of one
A chart that states its limits is harder to argue with. The reader can see what you claim and how far it goes

title: Privacy
text:
What this site knows about you


Privacy

This is a static teaching site. There is no account to make, no form to fill in, and nothing here that is trying to learn who you are. Apart from the request for the page itself, one thing leaves your browser, and this page says what it is.








THE SHORT VERSION

The site has no analytics, no advertising, no tracking pixels and no cookies at all. It has no comments, logins or forms, and nothing you do on these pages is reported back to anyone who teaches this course.
The one exception: the fonts are loaded from Google, so Google sees that a browser at your address asked for them. The details are below.



WHAT LEAVES YOUR BROWSER

Two requests: one to Google for the fonts, and the request for the page itself that every website receives.
The fonts, from Google. Every page asks fonts.googleapis.com and fonts.gstatic.com for Space Grotesk and Newsreader. To answer, Google receives your IP address, your browser and operating system version, and the address of the page you are reading. This is how most of the web loads fonts and it is still a transfer of data to a third party, in the United States, governed by Google’s privacy policy rather than by anything here. It can be removed by serving the font files from this site instead, which is a change to how the site is built and not to anything you can do from your end.
The page itself, from the web server. The site is published with GitHub Pages. Like every web server, GitHub’s logs the requests it answers, including your IP address and which page you asked for. That is GitHub’s processing under their privacy statement, and nobody teaching this course can read those logs or has asked for them.
Nothing else on any page makes an outside request. The charts, the interactive explainers, the gallery exhibits, the datasets and the search index are all files served from this site.



WHAT IS STORED ON YOUR DEVICE

No cookies are set, first or third party. You can confirm it in your browser’s storage inspector.
Three small values may be written to this site’s local storage, which is a private notepad your browser keeps per website. They exist so the site remembers how you like to read it:








Value
What it is for
When it appears




quarto-color-scheme
whether you chose the light or the dark version
when you use the toggle in the navigation bar


quarto-reader-mode
whether you collapsed the side margins
when you use reader mode


quarto-persistent-tabsets-data
which tab of a tabbed block you last opened
on any page load



These stay in your browser. They are never transmitted anywhere, they are not readable by this site’s authors or by anyone else, and clearing your browser data deletes them. They are set by Quarto, the publishing system this site is built with, and not by anything written for this course.



THINGS THAT ARE NOT THIS SITE

This page covers these pages. Three things you will use for this course are somewhere else and have their own terms.

Canvas is where the course runs: enrolment, submissions, grades and the route to a teacher. It belongs to Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam and is covered by the university’s privacy statement, not by this one.
Links that leave the site (to a paper, a dataset’s home, a newspaper’s chart) take you to someone else’s server on their terms. The credits page lists where the borrowed material comes from.
Downloading the datasets is an ordinary file download from this site. What you then do with the data, especially in your portfolio, is your responsibility, and the course’s rules on that are on the assessment page.




CHECKING THIS YOURSELF


This course spends eight weeks arguing that a claim should be checkable by the person receiving it, so it would be poor form to ask you to take this page on trust. Open your browser’s developer tools, load any page here with the network tab recording, and read the list of requests. You should see this site’s own files and two requests to Google’s font servers. If you ever see something else, that is a mistake and worth reporting.

Questions, or something that looks wrong: contact the course coordinator through Canvas. There is no address printed here on purpose, because an address on a public page is harvested within days.
Last checked 18 September 2026, against the site as published on that date.

title: How this course works
text:
Period 2 · 2026




Every chart makes a claim, and someone chose which one. This course teaches you to read that claim in other people’s charts, and to make your own charts in R so that the claim they make is the one your data supports.


New here? Start with Before the first work group. How you are graded is on Assessment, what you may use AI for on AI use, and every date and room on Weeks.





WHAT YOU WILL LEARN



  
    01
    
    Say what a chart claims, and whether its data supports that claim. Run a
    critique in four steps (describe, analyse, interpret, judge) on any
    published visualisation.
  

  
    02
    
    Describe any chart as eight settings, from data and mapping to theme, and
    build it in R with ggplot2, one setting at a time.
  

  
    03
    
    Choose a chart by the kind of variables you have: comparisons and
    rankings, distributions, relationships, change over time, maps, networks
    and text.
  

  
    04
    
    Show what a chart cannot tell you: an n, a range, an interval, the whole
    distribution, or the spread of defensible analyses rather than one of
    them.
  

  
    05
    
    Name the settings that change a chart's story (baseline, order, scale,
    denominator, time window) and build the misleading version on purpose, so
    you recognise it in other people's work.
  

  
    06
    
    Choose a dataset, annotate and colour your charts for a reader, and present
    the result as a data story or an explanatory blog post, with code that runs
    on someone else's machine.
  





HOW A WEEK WORKS


Seven weeks of teaching, each adding one kind of variable to what you can draw, and an eighth with no sessions, for the take-home assignment. Weeks 2 to 7 all have the same rhythm.



Tuesday · lecture



Each lecture opens with a critique of charts from the previous Thursday, without names, and then works through one kind of comparison: what it can show, the settings that change its story, and published examples that got it right or wrong.




Thursday · work group



Meet a dataset the lecture did not use, draw the chart on paper, build it in R, and then twist it into a misleading version. The pair are photographed (screenshot) at the end for the next Tuesday. Week 1 is different: it introduces R and the grammar of graphics, and nothing is handed in.




Sunday · portfolio entry



At times, you may not finish part II of the workgroups. You just finish the honest chart and its misleading twin from Thursday and submit it with code that runs. Six in total, one each Sunday of weeks 2 to 7.
How the portfolio is graded





WHAT WE EXPECT FROM YOU



Come to every lecture and every work group. Attendance is mandatory, although it is not recorded.
Bring your own laptop to every work group, with R, RStudio, the tidyverse and Quarto installed and the setup check passed.
Run everything yourself. The code on these pages is shown, not run: what it prints is for you to find out.
Draw before you code. The sketch on paper is what you are building.
Say something. The lectures open with a critique of your charts, and it only works if the room talks.
Say how you used AI. The rules are on the AI use page.





WHO TEACHES IT

Coordinator & lecturerThe Tuesday lecture: the week’s rhetorical move, the gallery, and the critique of last week’s charts.Writes the lectures and judges whether an argument holds. Contact through Canvas.Lectures in EnglishWork group teacherThe Thursday work group: the R that executes the week’s move, and the portfolio entry that comes out of it.Answers anything about R, and holds the technical quality bar on every deliverable.Work groups in English

Tuesday is about what a chart claims and whether the claim survives scrutiny; Thursday is about the R that builds it. Each half needs the other, which is why Thursday’s charts open the next Tuesday.




THE TOOL

The course uses R. Everything you produce is made with ggplot2, and so is everything you are shown: every chart on these pages and in every lecture deck is R code you could have written, styled with the same theme_dsvar() you will be given. The exceptions are a handful of historical originals in the gallery, such as Minard, Nightingale and Snow, where the original itself is the point.



THE BOOKS




Book · free online · the R Code



How to build charts in R, step by step. The online version is now a second-edition draft (R 4.5, ggplot2 4, the base pipe, Quarto), so not every recipe from the first edition transfers.

Healy, K. (2018). Data visualization: A practical introduction. Princeton University Press. https://socviz.co

Open socviz.co




Book · free online · the principles



Which chart for which job, and why. Its chapters follow the same idea as this course: a chart is organised by what it is asked to show.

Wilke, C. O. (2019). Fundamentals of data visualization. O’Reilly. https://clauswilke.com/dataviz

Open the book






WHERE THINGS LIVE



  
    Canvas
    
    Announcements, submissions and grades. If it has a deadline, it is
    submitted there.
  

  
    This site
    
    Weeks, slides, work groups, the gallery and the field guide, released
    week by week.
  

  
    Asking
    
    Questions about code or an entry go to your work group teacher, in the
    work group if at all possible: they get answered fastest and help others at
    the same time. Everything else to the coordinator, via Canvas.

title: Warming stripes
text:
Gallery · Change over time · back to the gallery


Warming stripes

A century and a half of global temperature, with no axes, no gridlines, no numbers and no legend: one encoding does all of the work. It is the cleanest demonstration in the course that a chart is a claim rather than a table.








THE ORIGINAL



“#ShowYourStripes”, global average 1850–2025, by Ed Hawkins, National Centre for Atmospheric Science, University of Reading. Licensed CC BY 4.0. Data: Met Office HadCRUT5.1.



How to read it


 Each vertical stripe is one year, in order: 1850 at the far left, 2025 at the far right. There are 176 of them.


 Blue means cooler than the 1961–1990 average for the planet as a whole.


 Red means warmer than that same average. The deeper the colour, the further from it.


 There is no axis, no scale and no number anywhere. You can see that it got warmer and roughly when; you cannot read off how much, and that is by design.





THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

176 vertical stripes of equal width, one per year, ordered left to right. Each is filled with a single colour from a blue-to-red scale. No axis, no tick, no number, no legend, no title. Nothing is encoded except fill, and nothing is labelled at all.



02 · Analyse

Time is on position, which is the most accurate channel available, but it is position without a scale, so it gives order and not distance. Temperature is on colour, which is one of the least accurate channels. The scale is diverging, with its midpoint at the long-term average, so blue and red mean below and above normal rather than simply less and more.



03 · Interpret

The claim is: it used to be colder, it is now hotter, and the change is recent and one-directional. The graphic is not arguing about rate, or cause, or magnitude, because it has given itself no vocabulary to argue about any of them.



04 · Judge

The evidence supports the claim, and the claim is narrow enough that the encoding can carry it. Putting the least accurate channel in charge would be indefensible for a chart that had to be read precisely, and this one never asks to be. That is a choice, not an oversight, and it is why it works.



Describe, analyse, interpret, judge: in that order, and no judging before describing. The same four steps we use on your charts.




THE RECREATION

Everything above is reproducible. The data is a single open CSV, and the chart is about fifteen lines of ggplot once you know the palette. The palette is the part that takes the work, so it is worked out in the open below.


Show the R code
# The palette is ColorBrewer Blues and Reds, 8 steps each, lightest dropped.
# See "how we know" below — it is not RdBu, which is the usual guess.
blues <- rev(c("#DEEBF7","#C6DBEF","#9ECAE1","#6BAED6",
               "#4292C6","#2171B5","#08519C","#08306B"))
reds  <-     c("#FEE0D2","#FCBBA1","#FC9272","#FB6A4A",
               "#EF3B2C","#CB181D","#A50F15","#67000D")
stripe_pal <- c(blues, reds)

# 16 equal bins across the scale, plus one darker red for the years that run
# off the top of it. Hawkins does the same: 2023 to 2025 are off the scale.
breaks  <- seq(-0.63, 0.99, length.out = 17)
over    <- "#440007"

stripes <- had |>
  mutate(bin = cut(anomaly, breaks, labels = FALSE, include.lowest = TRUE),
         fill = if_else(is.na(bin) & anomaly > max(breaks), over, stripe_pal[bin]))

ggplot(stripes, aes(x = year, y = 1, fill = fill)) +
  geom_col(width = 1) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  theme_void()










Global mean surface temperature anomaly, 1850–2025, relative to 1961–1990. n = 176 years. Rendered at the original’s proportions so the two can be compared directly. Data: Met Office Hadley Centre HadCRUT 5.0.2.0 (Open Government Licence v3).




Original · Hawkins





Ours · ggplot













Side by side, at the same size. If you can spot a stripe that differs, it is almost certainly one of the nine noted below.




HOW WE KNOW THAT IS THE PALETTE

The published recipe says the global scale runs from −0.9 °C to +0.9 °C, but binning the data that way does not reproduce the image. So we read the colours off the original instead: sample the centre of each of the 176 stripes, and check what came back.


Show the R code
library(png)
img <- readPNG(here::here("gallery", "img", "warming-stripes-original.png"))
n   <- nrow(had)

# one pixel from the vertical middle of each stripe
centres <- round((seq_len(n) - 0.5) * ncol(img) / n)
px      <- img[round(nrow(img) / 2), centres, ]
sampled <- toupper(rgb(px[, 1], px[, 2], px[, 3]))

tibble(year = had$year, anomaly = had$anomaly, hex = sampled) |>
  count(hex) |>
  mutate(in_brewer = hex %in% c(stripe_pal)) |>
  summarise(distinct_colours = n(),
            from_brewer      = sum(in_brewer),
            other            = paste(hex[!in_brewer], collapse = " "))


# A tibble: 1 × 3
  distinct_colours from_brewer other  
             <int>       <int> <chr>  
1               17          16 #440007


Sixteen of the seventeen are ColorBrewer Blues and Reds exactly, and they sort in perfect order with the anomaly. The seventeenth, #440007, is darker than the darkest red in either scale and is used by exactly three years: 2023, 2024 and 2025.


WHERE OUR RECREATION DIFFERS, AND WHY

The bin edges above (−0.63 to +0.99, in steps of about 0.101 °C) are fitted to the original rather than documented by it. They reproduce 164 of the 173 on-scale stripes, and all nine misses are before 1935. The likely reason is version drift: Hawkins used HadCRUT 5.1, and the file you can download today is HadCRUT 5.0.2.0, which revises the early record. We could have hidden that by adjusting the edges until they matched; saying so is the more useful lesson.




WHAT IT GIVES UP

The same 176 numbers, encoded to be read rather than felt. This chart answers questions the stripes cannot (how much, how fast, how certain), and it will not survive being printed on a mug.


Show the R code
# The claim in the title is a PERIOD comparison, not an endpoint one, and the
# difference matters: see the note below this chart.
pre_ind <- mean(had$anomaly[had$year >= 1850 & had$year <= 1900])
recent  <- mean(had$anomaly[had$year >= 2015 & had$year <= 2025])

ggplot(had, aes(year, anomaly)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#e7e3d9", linewidth = .5) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = dsvar_accent(), alpha = .18) +
  geom_line(colour = dsvar_accent(), linewidth = .8) +
  labs(title = sprintf("The last decade averaged %.1f °C warmer than 1850–1900",
                       recent - pre_ind),
       subtitle = "Annual anomaly against the 1961–1990 average, with a 95% confidence band",
       x = NULL, y = "°C",
       caption = "n = 176 years · HadCRUT 5.0.2.0, Met Office Hadley Centre / UEA CRU, OGL v3")











A CLAIM WE GOT WRONG FIRST TIME

This title originally read “rose about 1.2 °C between 1850 and 2025”. That is two errors in one line. The endpoint-to-endpoint difference on this series is 1.61 °C, not 1.2, and quoting any endpoint difference on a noisy annual series is a cherry-pick, because it is at the mercy of which two years you happen to stand on. The defensible comparison is period against period, which is what the title now states and what the code above computes. Left here rather than silently corrected, because it is the most common way a true chart acquires a false headline.


Neither chart is the better one. The stripes win an argument in four seconds with an audience that was not going to read an axis; the line chart survives someone who wants to check it. Knowing which job you are doing is the skill. Note, too, that only one of the two can show the uncertainty band at all.




THE SAME DATA, DIFFERENT CHOICES

Three variants, none of them a lie, all of them saying something different. This is what the course means by a visualization being an argument.


Show the R code
library(patchwork)

strip_plot <- function(fills, title, note) {
  ggplot(tibble(year = had$year, f = fills), aes(year, 1, fill = f)) +
    geom_col(width = 1) + scale_fill_identity() +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) + scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
    labs(title = title, subtitle = note) +
    theme_void(base_family = dsvar_font()) +
    theme(plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11, hjust = 0,
                                       margin = margin(b = 2)),
          plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9, colour = "#5a5a52", hjust = 0,
                                       margin = margin(b = 5)))
}

bin16 <- function(x, brk) {
  i <- cut(x, brk, labels = FALSE, include.lowest = TRUE)
  i[is.na(i) & x > max(brk)] <- 16L
  i[is.na(i) & x < min(brk)] <- 1L
  i
}

i_orig <- bin16(had$anomaly, breaks)

# Stated from the data, not from memory: the third caption is computed, so it
# cannot drift away from the chart it describes when the series is updated.
cross <- function(i) had$year[which(i >= 9)[1]]

seq_pal  <- colorRampPalette(c("#fff5eb", "#7f2704"))(16)   # sequential
rain_pal <- rainbow(16, start = 0.65, end = 0)              # the classic mistake
# A baseline is a choice about what counts as normal. Centre on 1991-2020 and
# most of the record becomes "cold" rather than the recent years becoming "hot".
# The breaks are recomputed over the shifted range: reusing the old ones would
# push 105 of the 176 values off the bottom of the scale, and a demonstration
# that cheats to make its point is the thing this page argues against.
rebased     <- had$anomaly - mean(had$anomaly[had$year >= 1991 & had$year <= 2020])
brk_rebased <- seq(min(rebased), max(rebased), length.out = 17)
i_recent    <- bin16(rebased, brk_rebased)

strip_plot(seq_pal[i_orig],  "Sequential palette",
           "No midpoint, so nothing reads as below normal. Warming becomes an accumulation.") /
strip_plot(rain_pal[i_orig], "Rainbow palette",
           "Invented boundaries where hues change. The eye sees steps the data does not have.") /
strip_plot(stripe_pal[i_recent], "Baseline moved to 1991–2020",
           sprintf("Same numbers, same palette. The blue/red crossover moves from %d to %d.",
                   cross(i_orig), cross(i_recent)))










All three use the identical 176 values. Only the encoding changed. Note how much smaller the baseline effect is than the palette ones: moving the reference period shifts the crossover by a decade, which is worth knowing precisely rather than describing as “it changes everything”. The first draft of this page claimed it made most of history read as cold. It does not, and the caption is now computed from the data so it cannot say so again.




SOURCES


Original graphic: Hawkins, E. #ShowYourStripes, National Centre for Atmospheric Science, University of Reading. showyourstripes.info. CC BY 4.0.
Data: Morice, C. P. et al. (2021). An updated assessment of near-surface temperature change from 1850: the HadCRUT5 data set. Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres, 126(3). Series used here: HadCRUT 5.0.2.0 global annual summary. HadCRUT.5.0.2.0 data were obtained from http://www.metoffice.gov.uk/hadobs/hadcrut5 on 16 September 2026 and are © British Crown Copyright, Met Office 2020, provided under an Open Government License, http://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/doc/open-government-licence/version/3/
Palette: Brewer, C. A. ColorBrewer 2.0, Blues and Reds, 9-class. colorbrewer2.org.
Reproduce it: Rscript R/fetch-gallery-data.R pulls the data and the original image; every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: Unknown Pleasures
text:
Gallery · Distribution & uncertainty · back to the gallery


Unknown Pleasures

A figure from a radio astronomy thesis, lifted onto an album cover, and now probably the most reproduced statistical graphic in existence. It is also a working demonstration of when letting your data overlap is the right call.








THE ORIGINAL



Unknown Pleasures sleeve, Joy Division, Factory Records, 1979. Design by Peter Saville, after Harold D. Craft Jr’s 1970 Cornell PhD thesis. Copyright Factory Records / Peter Saville. Low-resolution copy via Wikipedia, shown at 316 px for criticism and review under the Dutch citation right (Auteurswet art. 15a). Not a free licence: it cannot be reused from here.

Harold Craft plotted 80 successive radio pulses from CP 1919, the first pulsar ever detected, in his 1970 Cornell PhD thesis. The plot was reprinted in the Cambridge Encyclopaedia of Astronomy (1977), where Peter Saville found it and used it, uncredited and inverted to white-on-black, for Joy Division’s Unknown Pleasures in 1979.


How to read it


 Each line is one rotation of a neutron star: one pulse, about 1.3 seconds of radio signal. There are 80, stacked from the bottom up.


 Left to right is time within a single pulse. All 80 are aligned to the same window, so the peaks line up in the middle.


 Height is signal strength. A tall spike is a strong pulse; the wobble either side of it is noise.


 Each line is drawn opaque and hides the ones behind it. That occlusion is deliberate, and it is what gives the plot its depth.


 Nothing is labelled, at least on the album cover: no axes, no units, no scale. Craft’s thesis version has them.



The underlying plot: Craft, H. D. (1970). Radio observations of the pulse profiles and dispersion measures of twelve pulsars. PhD thesis, Cornell University. Craft’s thesis plate carries axes and units; the sleeve strips them, which is the difference the critique below turns on.




THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

Eighty line traces stacked vertically at even intervals, each one filled opaquely so it masks whatever falls behind it. The traces are noisy at the edges and spike near the middle, and the spikes vary in height and position from line to line. No axis, tick or legend.



02 · Analyse

This is a ridgeline plot, and it uses vertical position for two things at once: the baseline of each line encodes which pulse, and displacement from that baseline encodes intensity. That double duty is why the values are unreadable and why the shape is so legible. The occlusion turns a flat grid into an apparent surface.



03 · Interpret

The claim is that the pulses are regular but not identical: they arrive on schedule and vary in strength and shape from one rotation to the next. For an astronomer in 1970 that variation was the finding. You can see it without reading a single number.



04 · Judge

Defensible, for this claim. Eighty overlaid series on one axis would be an unreadable tangle; eighty separate panels would lose the comparison entirely. The ridgeline is the form that keeps both. It is a bad choice the moment anyone needs a value off it, which is why Craft’s thesis, unlike the album, carries axes.





THE RECREATION



Show the R code
# ggplot draws one layer at a time. One geom_ribbon() for all 80 pulses and
# then one geom_line() would put every line on top of every fill, and nothing
# would be hidden. So each pulse gets its own pair of layers, its ribbon and
# then its line, and the pairs are added from the back row (the top) to the
# front row (the bottom). Each pair paints over everything already behind it.
one_pulse <- function(i) {
  d <- filter(pulsar, pulse == i)
  list(
    # Filled with the ground colour: this is what hides the rows behind.
    # Leave it out and the plot becomes a flat tangle (see below).
    geom_ribbon(data = d, aes(ymin = pulse, ymax = pulse + intensity / 9),
                fill = "black", colour = NA),
    geom_line(data = d, colour = "white", linewidth = .32)
  )
}

# y is the row (which pulse) plus the signal: one position, two jobs
ggplot(pulsar, aes(x = sample, y = pulse + intensity / 9, group = pulse)) +
  map(max(pulsar$pulse):1, one_pulse) +     # back to front
  coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) +
  theme_void() +                            # no axes, as on the sleeve
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "black", colour = NA),
        plot.margin = margin(70, 80, 70, 80))   # the sleeve's wide border










80 pulses from CP 1919, 300 samples each, white on black as on the sleeve. Each pulse is drawn over the ones behind it, from the top row down. Data traced from the sleeve by Michael Zöllner, as numbers by Borgar Þorsteinsson, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, so this chart is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 too.




WHAT THE OCCLUSION IS WORTH

The only difference between these two is whether each ribbon is filled. Both draw the peaks about twice as tall as the sleeve does, so each one reaches across several rows and the difference has somewhere to show.


Show the R code
library(patchwork)
ink   <- dsvar_tokens()$ink
paper <- dsvar_tokens()$paper

# The recreation's construction, with two changes: the page's ink on its
# paper rather than the sleeve's white on black, and peaks about twice as tall
# (intensity / 4), so each one reaches across several rows. `filled` is the
# one switch between the two panels.
ridges <- function(filled, title) {
  layers <- map(max(pulsar$pulse):1, function(i) {
    d <- filter(pulsar, pulse == i)
    list(
      if (filled) geom_ribbon(data = d, aes(ymin = pulse, ymax = pulse + intensity / 4),
                              fill = paper, colour = NA),
      geom_line(data = d, colour = ink, linewidth = .3)
    )
  })
  ggplot(pulsar, aes(x = sample, y = pulse + intensity / 4, group = pulse)) +
    layers +
    coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) +
    labs(title = title) +
    theme_void() +
    theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = paper, colour = NA),
          plot.title = element_text(colour = ink, face = "bold", size = 12,
                                    family = dsvar_font(), margin = margin(b = 10)),
          plot.margin = margin(14, 18, 14, 18))
}

ridges(FALSE, "Unfilled: a tangle") + ridges(TRUE, "Filled: a surface") +
  plot_annotation(
    caption = "Identical data, identical lines, identical drawing order. The right-hand panel fills each ribbon with the ground colour.",
    theme = theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = paper, colour = NA),
                  plot.caption = element_text(colour = dsvar_tokens()$ink_3, hjust = 0,
                                              size = 9, family = dsvar_font())))










Occlusion is normally a fault, the thing we spend week 4 fixing with transparency and jitter. Here it is the encoding: hiding the far lines behind the near ones turns a stack of traces into a receding surface, and the surface makes the pattern visible. The rule is not “never overlap”: overlapping must be a decision, and you should be able to say what it buys.




THE SAME PULSES, MADE READABLE



Show the R code
hm <- ggplot(pulsar, aes(sample, pulse, fill = intensity)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = dsvar_ramp_light, name = "Intensity") +
  coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Time within pulse", y = "Pulse number",
       title = "Intensity on colour",
       subtitle = "Every value readable, the depth gone") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

prof <- pulsar |>
  summarise(m = mean(intensity),
            lo = quantile(intensity, .1), hi = quantile(intensity, .9),
            .by = sample)

pp <- ggplot(prof, aes(sample, m)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = dsvar_accent(), alpha = .2) +
  geom_line(colour = dsvar_accent(), linewidth = .7) +
  labs(x = "Time within pulse", y = "Intensity",
       title = "The average pulse, with its spread",
       subtitle = "The 10th to 90th percentile across all 80 pulses")

# patchwork's guide collection is broken against ggplot2 4.x, so these are
# placed with plain addition and themed individually. See the README.
hm + pp










Left: nothing is hidden, and the plot has become a grid you read rather than a shape you see. Right: the summary Craft would have published if he only wanted the average, which deletes the pulse-to-pulse variation that made the original interesting.




SOURCES


Original figure: Craft, H. D. (1970). Radio observations of the pulse profiles and dispersion measures of twelve pulsars. PhD thesis, Cornell University. Reprinted in the Cambridge Encyclopaedia of Astronomy (1977).
The cover: Saville, P. (1979). Unknown Pleasures, Joy Division, Factory Records. Copyright Factory Records / Peter Saville; shown above at low resolution as a quotation for criticism and review. Not reusable from here.
Data: not Craft’s own numbers. Michael Zöllner traced the waves of the album sleeve by hand (2013, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0), and Borgar Þorsteinsson turned an approximation of that tracing into 80 pulses × 300 samples (gist, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0); we took it from the unknown_pleasures_plot repository, whose MIT licence does not cover the data. Vendored here as data/raw/cp1919-pulsar.csv, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, as are the charts on this page.
The form: ridgeline plots, and the ggridges package, which does this with one geom when you do not want to hand-roll the ribbons.
Reproduce it: every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: Snow’s cholera map
text:
Gallery · Relationships & structure · back to the gallery


Snow’s cholera map

The founding case for visualization as argument, and not, as it is usually told, the moment of discovery. Snow drew this after the outbreak was over and after he had already had the pump handle removed. It was made to convince a committee.








THE ORIGINAL



Map of the 1854 Broad Street cholera outbreak, from On the Mode of Communication of Cholera (2nd ed.) by John Snow, 1855. Public domain (author died 1858); scan via Wikimedia Commons.

John Snow’s map of the 1854 Broad Street cholera outbreak in Soho, London, published in the second edition of On the Mode of Communication of Cholera (1855).


How to read it


 The base is a street plan of a few blocks of Soho. No coordinates, no grid, no legend on the plate itself.


 Each short black bar is one death, stacked outward from the front of the house it happened in. A house with five bars had five deaths.


 The marked points are the public water pumps. There were thirteen in the area.


 The argument is a shape: the bars pile up around one pump and thin out towards the others. Nothing is calculated on the plate.





THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

A street plan with two kinds of mark on it: small bars clustered against buildings, and a second symbol at thirteen scattered points. Density of the bars varies sharply across a few hundred metres. There is no scale bar, no legend and no statistic.



02 · Analyse

Position carries geography, and that is the only channel doing quantitative work. Deaths are encoded by count of marks, one per person, rather than by colour or area, so the reader does the aggregating by eye and can see the individual cases that make up the cluster. A choropleth of the same data would have hidden exactly the structure the argument needs.



03 · Interpret

The claim is that cholera came from the water at one specific pump. The map does not say that in words, and it does not need to: once deaths are plotted where they happened and pumps are plotted beside them, the reader draws the conclusion and feels they thought of it themselves.



04 · Judge

The evidence supports the claim, but not for the reason the legend suggests. The map has no control for how many people lived on each street, so density of deaths partly tracks density of housing. Snow’s actual case rested on the anomalies (the brewery whose workers drank beer and lived, the widow who had Broad Street water delivered and died miles away), and those are notes in the text, not marks on the plate.





THE RECREATION



Show the R code
ink    <- "#332B23"
pumpc  <- "#8C1C13"

ggplot() +
  # The street plan arrives as a list of vertices with an id per segment, so it
  # is a path per street, not a single line.
  geom_path(data = streets, aes(x, y, group = street),
            colour = "#cfc9bd", linewidth = .45) +
  geom_point(data = deaths, aes(x, y),
             colour = ink, alpha = .55, size = 1.5, shape = 16) +
  geom_point(data = pumps, aes(x, y),
             colour = pumpc, size = 3.4, shape = 18) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = pumps, aes(x, y, label = label),
                           size = 2.6, colour = pumpc, family = dsvar_font(),
                           seed = 3, box.padding = .45, segment.size = .2,
                           bg.color = "#faf8f4", bg.r = .12) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "578 cholera deaths and 13 pumps, Soho, 1854",
       subtitle = "Each dot is one death, placed at the house where it occurred",
       caption = "n = 578 deaths, 13 pumps · Snow (1855), digitised by Dodson & Tobler, via HistData") +
  theme_void(base_family = dsvar_font()) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12, hjust = 0,
                                  margin = margin(b = 3)),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9.5, colour = "#5a5a52", hjust = 0,
                                     margin = margin(b = 10)),
        plot.caption = element_text(size = 7.5, colour = "#7a7a70", hjust = 0,
                                    margin = margin(t = 10)))










An attempt, not a facsimile: Snow drew stacked bars per address; this uses one dot per death with transparency. The cluster is the point and both encodings carry it.




DOES THE CLUSTER SURVIVE A NUMBER?

The map asks you to believe a shape. Check whether the shape holds up when you make it arithmetic, a move Snow’s critics could have made and did not.


Show the R code
broad <- pumps |> filter(str_detect(tolower(label), "broad"))

nearest <- deaths |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(d = list(sqrt((x - pumps$x)^2 + (y - pumps$y)^2))) |>
  mutate(which_pump = pumps$label[which.min(d)],
         dist       = min(d)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(grp = if_else(which_pump == broad$label, "Nearest pump: Broad Street",
                       "Nearest pump: any other"))

nearest |>
  count(grp) |>
  mutate(share = scales::percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = .1)) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("", "Deaths", "Share"))






Deaths
Share




Nearest pump: Broad Street
359
62.1%


Nearest pump: any other
219
37.9%





Show the R code
ggplot(nearest, aes(dist, fill = grp)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, colour = "white", linewidth = .2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Nearest pump: Broad Street" = "#1e7c50",
                               "Nearest pump: any other"    = "#a5a199"),
                    name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Distance to the nearest pump (map units)", y = "Deaths",
       title = "Most deaths were not just near Broad Street, they were nearest to it",
       caption = "n = 578 deaths. Distance is straight line, not walking distance (see the note below).") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")











STRAIGHT LINES ARE NOT HOW PEOPLE FETCH WATER

The distances above are Euclidean: they go through buildings. Nobody carried a bucket through a wall. The honest version is a walking distance along the street network, and when that is computed the Broad Street cluster gets sharper, because the pump’s catchment follows the streets. Snow himself drew a boundary line of roughly this kind on a later version of the map. Our number is the easy one, and you have to say which one you computed.




THE ANECDOTE THAT IS THE COURSE’S THESIS


The map is dated 1855 and appeared in the second edition. The pump handle came off in September 1854, and the outbreak was already subsiding when it did. Snow made this to persuade a committee of a conclusion he had reached from door-to-door interviews, water samples and a mortality table. It is a superb piece of argument and a terrible piece of discovery, and it is remembered as the opposite. When you make your own charts, notice which one you are doing.




SOURCES


Original: Snow, J. (1855). On the Mode of Communication of Cholera, 2nd ed. London: John Churchill. Public domain.
Data: Snow.deaths, Snow.pumps, Snow.streets in Friendly, M., HistData, digitised from Snow’s plate by Rusty Dodson and Waldo Tobler (NCGIA). Snow’s map is public domain; HistData is GPL. Vendored here as data/raw/snow-*.csv.
The chronology: Brody, H., Rip, M. R., Vinten-Johansen, P., Paneth, N., & Rachman, S. (2000). Map-making and myth-making in Broad Street. The Lancet, 356(9223), 64–68.
Reproduce it: every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: Original against replication
text:
Gallery · Relationships & structure · back to the gallery


Original against replication

One hundred findings, each measured twice. The chart is an ordinary scatterplot, and the whole argument lives in one line that carries no data: the diagonal where the two measurements would agree.








THE ORIGINAL



“RPP_Figure3” from the Reproducibility Project: Psychology materials by the Open Science Collaboration, via osf.io/ezcuj, dedicated to the public domain under CC0 1.0. The collaboration’s own figure, not the Science typeset version, which is AAAS copyright.

The Reproducibility Project: Psychology repeated 100 published studies with high power and preregistered protocols, then plotted each original effect size against its replication. Point size is the replication’s power, and colour is whether it reached significance.


How to read it


 Each point is one study, measured twice. Horizontal position is the effect the original paper found; vertical position is what the replication found.


 The diagonal is where a point would land if the replication matched the original exactly. It encodes nothing; it is a standard of comparison drawn on the page.


 Below the line means the replication found a weaker effect. Distance from the line, not position on the page, is the quantity you are meant to read.


 Colour marks whether the replication reached significance, which is a second and much cruder summary of the same thing.





THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

A square scatterplot with identical scales on both axes, a diagonal reference line, and roughly a hundred points. The points sit overwhelmingly on one side of the line. Density curves run along the margins.



02 · Analyse

Two measurements of the same quantity on two positional axes, which is the right call. The decision that makes it work is forcing the axes to share a scale and drawing the identity line. Without those, this is an unremarkable positive correlation; with them, every point’s vertical distance from the line is a readable quantity.



03 · Interpret

The claim is that published effects in psychology are, on average, substantially larger than what a careful repeat finds. The asymmetry about the line is the finding, and it is visible before any number is read.



04 · Judge

Well made, and honest about being a distribution rather than a verdict: points above the line exist, and the figure does not hide them. What it cannot show, and does not claim to, is why each point fell where it did: publication bias, low original power and genuine differences between the studies all produce the same picture.





THE RECREATION



Show the R code
# The original's two colours are ggplot2's own defaults for a two-level factor
# — see the note below. Matching them is part of recreating the figure.
osc_pal <- c("Not Significant" = "#F8766D", "Significant" = "#00BFC4")

main <- ggplot(rpp, aes(orig, rep)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "#8a8a82", linewidth = .4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#3a3a34", linewidth = .35, linetype = "22") +
  # rug marks on both axes, as the original has
  geom_rug(aes(colour = sig_orig), sides = "b", linewidth = .3, alpha = .75,
           length = unit(.018, "npc"), show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_rug(aes(colour = sig), sides = "l", linewidth = .3, alpha = .75,
           length = unit(.018, "npc"), show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = sig, fill = sig, size = power), shape = 21,
             stroke = .35, alpha = .75) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = osc_pal, name = "p-value") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = osc_pal, guide = "none") +
  scale_size_continuous(name = "Replication Power", range = c(1, 5.5),
                        breaks = c(.6, .7, .8, .9)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-.06, 1), ylim = c(-.55, 1.05)) +
  labs(x = "Original Effect Size", y = "Replication Effect Size") +
  theme_dsvar(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "inside",
        legend.position.inside = c(.86, .62),
        legend.background = element_rect(fill = "#faf8f4", colour = NA),
        legend.key.size = unit(10, "pt"),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 7.5),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 7),
        legend.spacing.y = unit(1, "pt"))

# Marginal densities, filled and semi-transparent so the overlap shows, exactly
# as in the original.
# after_stat(count) scales each curve by its group size. Without it geom_density
# normalises every group to area 1, so the 7 non-significant originals would get
# as much ink as the 90 significant ones — which is not what the original shows,
# and is a good illustration of how a default can quietly restate the data.
top <- ggplot(rpp, aes(orig, after_stat(count), fill = sig_orig, colour = sig_orig)) +
  geom_density(alpha = .55, linewidth = .3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = osc_pal, guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = osc_pal, guide = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-.06, 1), expand = FALSE) +
  theme_void()

right <- ggplot(rpp, aes(rep, after_stat(count), fill = sig, colour = sig)) +
  geom_density(alpha = .55, linewidth = .3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = osc_pal, guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = osc_pal, guide = "none") +
  coord_flip(xlim = c(-.55, 1.05), expand = FALSE) +
  theme_void()

# patchwork's guides="collect" is broken against ggplot2 4.x, so the legend
# lives inside the main panel and the margins are laid out by design widths.
library(patchwork)
top + plot_spacer() + main + right +
  plot_layout(ncol = 2, widths = c(4, 1), heights = c(1, 4))










34 of 97 replications reached p < .05, against 90 of 97 originals. Mean effect size fell from r = 0.4 to r = 0.2, roughly halved. Each margin is coloured by its own axis’s significance, which is why the top is almost entirely teal: the originals were published findings, so nearly all of them were significant.




WHAT THE DIAGONAL IS WORTH

The line carries no data. Take it away and see what happens to the argument.


Show the R code
twice <- bind_rows(mutate(rpp, v = "Without the reference line"),
                   mutate(rpp, v = "With it")) |>
  mutate(v = factor(v, levels = c("Without the reference line", "With it")))

ggplot(twice, aes(orig, rep)) +
  geom_abline(data = filter(twice, v == "With it"),
              aes(slope = 1, intercept = 0), colour = "#5a5a52",
              linewidth = .5, linetype = "22") +
  geom_point(colour = dsvar_accent(), size = 1.5, alpha = .75) +
  facet_wrap(~v) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-.5, 1), ylim = c(-.5, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Original effect size (r)", y = "Replication effect size (r)",
       title = "Identical points. One line added.",
       caption = "n = 97 study pairs")










On the left this is a positive correlation with a lot of scatter, and a reasonable reader concludes that replications broadly recover the originals. On the right the same points are obviously lopsided. A reference line is an argument about what counts as agreement. Drawing one, or leaving it out, costs nothing and changes what the reader concludes.




WHAT THE SCATTERPLOT WILL NOT TELL YOU



Show the R code
rpp |>
  mutate(id = row_number()) |>
  pivot_longer(c(orig, rep), names_to = "stage", values_to = "r") |>
  mutate(stage = factor(stage, c("orig", "rep"), c("Original", "Replication"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(stage, r, group = id)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#a5a199", linewidth = .3, alpha = .7) +
  geom_point(colour = dsvar_accent(), size = .9, alpha = .7) +
  facet_wrap(~field) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Effect size (r)",
       title = "The same 97 studies, as paired measurements",
       subtitle = "Almost every line slopes down, and further in social than in cognitive psychology",
       caption = "n = 97 study pairs · field as classified by the original authors")











WHAT THIS PAGE IS NOT CLAIMING

That 63 of 97 findings were false. A replication that misses significance is evidence, not a verdict: it can also reflect a smaller true effect, a different sample, or an honest difference in procedure. The figure shows a distribution of outcomes, and the course’s interest is in how it shows it. The inference is a much longer argument, and the original paper makes it carefully.




SOURCES


Original: Open Science Collaboration (2015). Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science. Science, 349(6251), aac4716.
Data: the project’s master results file, osf.io/ezcuj. Columns T_r..O. and T_r..R. are the recomputed effect sizes for original and replication. Vendored as data/raw/rpp-replications.csv.
The related case: Many analysts, one dataset, where the same dataset rather than the same question is given to many teams.
Reproduce it: every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: The PISA league table
text:
Gallery · Comparison & ranking · back to the gallery


The PISA league table

Every three years PISA tests 15-year-olds in some eighty education systems, and every three years the results become a ranking. This is the US government’s 2022 table for mathematics. It is more careful than most league tables: it marks which differences are real. But it marks them against only one country, and it prints a precise order that the data does not have.








THE ORIGINAL
