Table M1. Average scores and difference from U.S. average score of 15-year-old students on the PISA mathematics literacy scale, by education system: 2022, from Highlights of U.S. PISA 2022 Results Web Report (NCES 2023-115 and 2024-103). National Center for Education Statistics, U.S. Department of Education. Data: OECD, PISA 2022. Public domain (a U.S. federal work; IES site policy). Captured from the interactive page in its default view, 7 October 2026.

PISA, the OECD’s Programme for International Student Assessment, tests a sample of 15-year-olds in each system every three years; 2022’s main subject was mathematics. The OECD publishes its own report, and each country publishes its own reading of it. This is the American one, so its reference point is the United States.


How to read it


 Sorted by average score, highest first, running down the left column and then the right. The place in the list is never printed, but it is what everyone reads.


 ▲ and ▼ mark systems significantly above or below the United States; ◆ marks the ones that are not significantly different from it. Nothing says whether two other systems differ from each other.


 ! and !! mark a difference too imprecise to trust (its standard error is 30–50 per cent, or more than half, of the difference).


 ¹ and ² mark samples that cover only 50–75 per cent, or under half, of the country’s 15-year-olds. The rest are out of school or out of reach.


 Italic names are not OECD members. The score has no natural zero: the scale was set in 2003 so that OECD countries averaged 500.





THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

A ranked list of 81 education systems in two columns, from Singapore at 575 to Cambodia at 336, with the OECD average on top. Each row gives an average score, its difference from the United States and a symbol. The US row, 34th from the top, is navy with a flag. Footnote marks flag unstable differences and thin samples.



02 · Analyse

A table, but its order makes it a chart: position in the list encodes rank, and rank is the only thing it encodes visually. The numbers carry the sizes of the gaps, but only where a gap is significant: the twelve ◆ rows get no number at all. The symbols carry the uncertainty, and only along one axis: every system against the US. The table cannot say whether any of the twelve ◆ rows differ from each other.



03 · Interpret

For its audience the claim is: the United States is middling. Below 25 systems, above 43, indistinguishable from 12, and level with the OECD average. What a reader carries away is shorter: 34th.



04 · Judge

Better than most league tables, which print a rank and nothing else. Its weakness is the one it shares with them: the order is more precise than the evidence. On the same significance tests the US could be anywhere from 26th to 38th, and only 1 system in the table, Singapore, holds a place that is certain. The coverage footnotes deserve more than a superscript. Where under half of 15-year-olds are in the sample, the score describes the ones still in school.





THE RECREATION

A table is a chart that happens to use text, so the recreation is a ggplot too: every word below is a geom_text() placed where the original puts it, and every symbol is a point.


Show the R code
sans <- c(intersect(c("Public Sans", "Helvetica", "Arial"),
                    systemfonts::system_fonts()$family), "sans")[1]
navy <- "#002868"; title_bg <- "#eef5fc"

# Layout in the original's own pixels (2224 x 3598), y measured from the top.
W <- 2224; H <- 3598
row_y <- function(i) 383 + (i - 1) * 62               # the 41 rows of each column
cols <- tibble(col = 1:2, name_x = c(124, 1172), score_x = c(668, 1700),
               diff_x = c(1000, 2032), mark_x = c(1036, 2072))

# The OECD average leads the left column, then the 81 systems in order.
rows <- bind_rows(
  tibble(system = "OECD average", oecd = 1, coverage_note = 0, caution = 0,
         score = round(oecd_average), diff = NA, vs_us = "not different", bold = TRUE),
  pisa |> transmute(system, oecd, coverage_note, caution, score = round(mean),
                    diff = if_else(code == "USA", NA, round(mean - us$mean)),
                    vs_us, bold = FALSE)) |>
  mutate(slot = row_number(), col = if_else(slot <= 41, 1, 2),
         i = if_else(col == 1, slot, slot - 41), y = H - row_y(i),
         is_us = system == "United States",
         label = paste0(system, case_when(coverage_note == 1 ~ " ¹",
                                          coverage_note == 2 ~ " ²", TRUE ~ "")),
         # the table prints a difference only where it is significant
         diff_label = if_else(is.na(diff) | vs_us == "not different", "",
                              paste0(diff, c("", " !", " !!")[caution + 1]))) |>
  left_join(cols, by = "col")

marks <- rows |> filter(!is_us) |>
  mutate(shape = case_when(vs_us == "higher" ~ 24, vs_us == "lower" ~ 25, TRUE ~ 23))

notes <- c(
  "▲  Average score is higher than U.S. average score at the .05 level of statistical significance.",
  "▼  Average score is lower than U.S. average score at the .05 level of statistical significance.",
  "◆  Average score is not significantly different from U.S. average score at the .05 level of statistical significance.",
  "! Interpret data with caution. Estimate is unstable because the standard error is between 30 and 50 percent of the estimate.",
  "!! Interpret data with caution. Estimate is unstable because the standard error represents more than 50 percent of the estimate.",
  "¹ At least 50 percent but less than 75 percent of the 15-year-old population is covered by the PISA sample.",
  "² Less than 50 percent of the 15-year-old population is covered by the PISA sample.",
  "NOTE: Scores are reported on a scale from 0 to 1,000. Differences were computed using unrounded numbers. The default graphic or table view shows education systems ordered by their average scores",
  "in 2022. The ordering of notes and special symbols in the NOTE section follows the order shown in the default graphic/table view. Education systems are marked as OECD countries if they were OECD",
  "members in 2022. All OECD members except for Luxembourg participated in the PISA 2022 cycle. The OECD average is the average of the national averages of the participating OECD member",
  "countries, with each country weighted equally. Italics indicate non-OECD countries and education systems. Some apparent differences between estimates may not be statistically significant.",
  "SOURCE: Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), Program for International Student Assessment (PISA), 2022.")
note_y <- H - c(2990, 3052, 3114, 3176, 3238, 3300, 3362, 3410, 3446, 3482, 3518, 3560)

recreation <- ggplot() +
  # the title box and the filter line
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = W, ymin = H - 150, ymax = H, fill = title_bg) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = W, ymin = 0, ymax = H - 2930, fill = title_bg) +
  annotate("text", x = 18, y = H - 46, hjust = 0, family = sans, size = 3.45,
           label = "Table M1. Average scores and difference from U.S. average score of 15-year-old students on the PISA mathematics literacy scale, by") +
  annotate("text", x = 18, y = H - 106, hjust = 0, family = sans, size = 3.45,
           label = "education system: 2022") +
  annotate("text", x = W / 2, y = H - 212, family = sans, size = 2.5, fontface = "bold",
           label = "Filter by:   ◉ All education systems   ○ OECD members only") +
  # column heads and the rule under them
  annotate("text", x = cols$name_x, y = H - 318, hjust = 0, family = sans, size = 2.4,
           fontface = "bold", label = "Education system") +
  annotate("text", x = cols$score_x, y = H - 318, hjust = 1, family = sans, size = 2.4,
           fontface = "bold", label = c("Average\nscore", "Average score"), lineheight = .9) +
  annotate("text", x = cols$mark_x + 30, y = H - 318, hjust = 1, family = sans, size = 2.4,
           fontface = "bold", lineheight = .9,
           label = c("Difference from U.S.\naverage score", "Difference from U.S. average\nscore")) +
  annotate("segment", x = cols$name_x, xend = cols$mark_x + 30, y = H - 350, yend = H - 350,
           linewidth = .6) +
  # hairlines between rows, the US row, the text and the symbols
  geom_segment(data = rows, aes(x = name_x, xend = mark_x + 30, y = y - 31, yend = y - 31),
               colour = "#e3e3e3", linewidth = .25) +
  geom_rect(data = filter(rows, is_us), aes(xmin = name_x - 8, xmax = mark_x + 30,
                                            ymin = y - 30, ymax = y + 30), fill = navy) +
  geom_text(data = rows, aes(name_x, y, label = label,
                             fontface = case_when(bold | is_us ~ "bold",
                                                  oecd == 0 ~ "italic", TRUE ~ "plain"),
                             colour = is_us),
            hjust = 0, family = sans, size = 2.35) +
  geom_text(data = rows, aes(score_x, y, label = score, colour = is_us,
                             fontface = if_else(bold | is_us, "bold", "plain")),
            hjust = 1, family = sans, size = 2.35) +
  geom_text(data = rows, aes(diff_x, y, label = diff_label), hjust = 1, family = sans,
            size = 2.35) +
  geom_point(data = marks, aes(mark_x, y, shape = shape), size = 1.5, fill = "black",
             colour = if_else(marks$shape == 23, "black", "#9a9a9a"), stroke = .3) +
  scale_shape_identity() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#1b1b1b", `TRUE` = "white"), guide = "none") +
  # the notes
  annotate("text", x = 24, y = note_y, hjust = 0, family = sans, size = 2.05,
           label = notes, colour = "#1b1b1b") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, W), ylim = c(0, H), expand = FALSE) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA))

recreation










81 education systems and the OECD average (the equal-weighted mean of the 37 OECD members, 472). The symbols are computed from NCES’s own pairwise tests, which give the table’s split exactly: 25 above the US, 43 below, 12 not different.




Original · NCES, 2023





Ours · ggplot













Side by side, at the same size. Every number and every symbol is computed; the font is the nearest one installed, and the flag beside the US row is left out.




HOW WE KNOW

The numbers. The table is drawn in the browser from NCES’s data service, the same service behind its PISA Data Explorer. Asking it for the 2022 mathematics means, and for every pairwise comparison between the 81 systems, returns exactly the published table: the same scores to the unit, and the same 25, 43 and 12 against the US.
What we checked first. The page also ships an older cached copy of the comparisons, and that one does not match: it marks France and Spain as significantly above the US, where the table, and the live service, say they are not. An exhibit about how fragile a ranking is should not rest on the wrong file, so the cached copy is not used.
The footnote marks are drawn by the page’s stylesheet, not written in its text, so they were transcribed by eye from the rendered table: 13 systems marked ¹, 2 marked ², and 4 differences marked ! or !!.
The rank ranges below need no new statistics, only the table’s own tests applied to every pair. A system is certainly below every system that is significantly higher than it, and certainly above every system it is significantly higher than. Everything in between is a place it could hold.



THE SAME SCORES, WITHOUT THE PLACES



Show the R code
ranked <- pisa |>
  mutate(system = fct_reorder(system, mean),
         who = factor(case_when(code == "USA" ~ "United States",
                                coverage_note > 0 ~ "sample covers <75%",
                                TRUE ~ "other systems"),
                      levels = c("United States", "other systems", "sample covers <75%")))
who_cols <- c(`United States` = "#b3122e", `other systems` = dsvar_accent(),
              `sample covers <75%` = p$muted)

scores <- ggplot(ranked, aes(mean, system, colour = who)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = us$mean, colour = p$hairline, linewidth = .6) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = mean - 1.96 * se, xmax = mean + 1.96 * se),
                width = 0, linewidth = .5, orientation = "y", na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = who_cols, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Average score, with a 95% interval", x = "PISA mathematics score", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "left",
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = p$hairline, linewidth = .3),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 7.2))

places <- ggplot(ranked, aes(y = system, colour = who)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = best, xend = worst, yend = system), linewidth = 1.6, alpha = .55) +
  geom_point(aes(x = place), size = 1.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = who_cols, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_reverse(breaks = c(1, 20, 40, 60, 81)) +
  labs(title = "The places it could hold, and the one it is given",
       x = "rank (1 = top)", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = p$hairline, linewidth = .3),
        legend.position = "none")

library(patchwork)
(scores | places) + plot_layout(widths = c(1.15, 1))










Left: the scores themselves, with the uncertainty the table compresses into three symbols; grey marks a sample covering under 75 per cent of the country’s 15-year-olds. 2 systems, Cyprus and Baku, have no standard error in NCES’s file and are drawn without an interval. Right: the range of places each system could hold on the table’s own tests, with its printed place as the dot. The United States could be anywhere from 26th to 38th, and 43 of the 81 systems could move five places or more.


Why not bars


Show the R code
top <- pisa |> filter(place <= 10 | code == "USA") |>
  mutate(system = fct_reorder(system, mean), us = code == "USA")

bars <- ggplot(top, aes(mean, system, fill = us)) +
  geom_col(width = .7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(dsvar_accent(), "#b3122e"), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Bars from zero", subtitle = "The lengths look alike, and mean nothing",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())

dots <- ggplot(top, aes(mean, system, colour = us)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(dsvar_accent(), "#b3122e"), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Positions on the scale", subtitle = "The gaps, in the units PISA reports",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_blank())

bars | dots










A bar’s length is a claim about a ratio: twice as long, twice as much. PISA’s zero is not no mathematics; the scale was set so that OECD countries averaged 500, and a score of 575 is not 24 per cent more mathematics than 465. Position makes no such claim, which is why the left panel is the wrong chart and the right one is not.


A ranking prints one place per row, and the data supports a range. The NCES table is honest about the gaps it tests and silent about the rest, which is what every league table does with less care. Before you sort anything, ask which differences between neighbours are real, and draw the answer, not just the order.





SOURCES


Original: National Center for Education Statistics (2023). Table M1, Highlights of U.S. PISA 2022 Results Web Report (NCES 2023-115 and 2024-103). U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences. nces.ed.gov/surveys/pisa/pisa2022. Public domain.
Data: OECD, PISA 2022, as served by NCES’s data service: means and pairwise significance tests for mathematics, plus the standard-error file the same page loads. Source: OECD (2023), PISA 2022 Database, via NCES. The OECD’s terms allow reuse with that credit, and ask anyone reusing it from here to keep it. Vendored here as data/raw/pisa-2022-math.csv.
The OECD’s own report: OECD (2023). PISA 2022 Results (Volume I): The State of Learning and Equity in Education. doi:10.1787/53f23881-en.
Reproduce it: every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: Why outbreaks spread exponentially
text:
Gallery · The whole story · back to the gallery


Why outbreaks spread exponentially

The most-read article in the Washington Post’s history is less a chart than a simulation you watch, and its argument is that you watched it happen rather than being told the result. That is a different kind of evidence, with a different set of obligations.








THE ORIGINAL



“Why outbreaks like coronavirus spread exponentially, and how to ‘flatten the curve’” by Harry Stevens, The Washington Post, 14 March 2020. Copyright The Washington Post. A single frame of an animated work, reproduced for criticism and review under the Dutch citation right (Auteurswet art. 15a). Not a free licence: it cannot be reused from here. The Post published it free to read.

Harry Stevens, 14 March 2020. Dots bounce around a box; when an infected dot touches a healthy one, it infects it. Four scenarios run in sequence (free-for-all, an attempted quarantine, moderate distancing, extensive distancing), each with its curve building underneath.


How to read it


 Each dot is a person moving in a box. Pale blue-grey is healthy.


 Orange-brown is currently sick. Contact between a sick dot and a healthy one makes the healthy one sick.


 Pink is recovered, and cannot be infected again. The running counts sit beside the box.


 The chart underneath fills in as it runs: a stacked area of healthy, sick and recovered, built in real time rather than shown finished. The empty grey stretch on its right is time that has not happened yet.


 Each scenario changes one thing: how many dots are allowed to move. Nothing else differs between the runs.





THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

An animated box of moving points above a stacked area chart that accumulates as the animation plays. Both are small. The sequence repeats four times with a different movement rule each time, and the reader can restart it.



02 · Analyse

The dots are not data but a model, generated in the reader’s browser. The chart underneath is real data about that model. So the piece is doing two things at once: demonstrating a mechanism, and plotting the output of the demonstration. The join between them is what makes it persuasive, because you see the curve being caused.



03 · Interpret

The claim is mechanistic, not empirical: given that transmission works by contact, reducing contact flattens the curve. The piece is careful to claim nothing about how COVID-19 actually behaved.



04 · Judge

It holds, and it carries a risk the form cannot remove. A simulation is enormously convincing (you watched it), and how convincing it is has nothing to do with whether its assumptions match the world. Stevens’s dots recover with permanent immunity, mix at random, and never travel. None of that is true. The piece works because the claim it makes is narrow enough to survive the simplification. Most simulations shown to the public are not.





THE RECREATION

Every other exhibit in this gallery plots data that already existed. Here the data does not exist until the code runs, which is what this case is about.


Show the R code
set.seed(42)

simulate <- function(n = 250, moving = 1, steps = 420, box = 100,
                     radius = 2.2, recover = 90, v = 1.1) {
  # state: 0 healthy, 1 infected, 2 recovered
  state <- c(1L, rep(0L, n - 1))
  sick_since <- rep(NA_integer_, n)
  sick_since[1] <- 0L

  x <- runif(n, 0, box); y <- runif(n, 0, box)
  mobile <- rep(FALSE, n); mobile[sample(n, round(n * moving))] <- TRUE
  ang <- runif(n, 0, 2 * pi)
  dx <- ifelse(mobile, cos(ang) * v, 0); dy <- ifelse(mobile, sin(ang) * v, 0)

  out <- vector("list", steps)
  for (s in seq_len(steps)) {
    x <- x + dx; y <- y + dy
    # bounce off the walls
    dx[x < 0 | x > box] <- -dx[x < 0 | x > box]
    dy[y < 0 | y > box] <- -dy[y < 0 | y > box]
    x <- pmin(pmax(x, 0), box); y <- pmin(pmax(y, 0), box)

    inf <- which(state == 1L)
    sus <- which(state == 0L)
    if (length(inf) && length(sus)) {
      d <- as.matrix(dist(cbind(x, y)))[sus, inf, drop = FALSE]
      hit <- sus[rowSums(d < radius) > 0]
      state[hit] <- 1L; sick_since[hit] <- s
    }
    done <- which(state == 1L & (s - sick_since) > recover)
    state[done] <- 2L

    out[[s]] <- tibble(step = s,
                       healthy   = sum(state == 0L),
                       infected  = sum(state == 1L),
                       recovered = sum(state == 2L))
  }
  bind_rows(out)
}

scenarios <- tibble(
  moving = c(1, .75, .35, .12),
  label  = c("Everybody moves", "Three in four move",
             "One in three moves", "One in eight moves")
) |> mutate(label = fct_inorder(label))

runs <- scenarios |>
  mutate(sim = map(moving, \(m) simulate(moving = m))) |>
  unnest(sim) |>
  pivot_longer(c(healthy, infected, recovered),
               names_to = "status", values_to = "n") |>
  mutate(status = factor(status, c("recovered", "infected", "healthy"),
                         c("Recovered", "Infected", "Healthy")))

ggplot(runs, aes(step, n, fill = status)) +
  geom_area() +
  facet_wrap(~label, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Healthy = "#c2cdc7", Infected = "#8C1C13",
                               Recovered = "#1e7c50"), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(title = "Same model, same population, one parameter changed",
       subtitle = "250 people in a box. The only difference is how many of them move",
       x = "Time step", y = "People",
       caption = "Simulated data, 250 agents × 420 steps × 4 scenarios, seed 42") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")










The peak falls and widens as fewer people move. That is what “flatten the curve” means, and why the phrase is about the shape rather than the total.




WHAT THE ANIMATION ADDED



Show the R code
set.seed(7)
snap <- local({
  n <- 250; box <- 100; radius <- 2.2; recover <- 90; v <- 1.1
  state <- c(1L, rep(0L, n - 1)); sick_since <- rep(NA_integer_, n); sick_since[1] <- 0L
  x <- runif(n, 0, box); y <- runif(n, 0, box)
  ang <- runif(n, 0, 2 * pi); dx <- cos(ang) * v; dy <- sin(ang) * v
  want <- c(1, 40, 80, 140, 220, 380); keep <- list()
  for (s in seq_len(max(want))) {
    x <- x + dx; y <- y + dy
    dx[x < 0 | x > box] <- -dx[x < 0 | x > box]; dy[y < 0 | y > box] <- -dy[y < 0 | y > box]
    x <- pmin(pmax(x, 0), box); y <- pmin(pmax(y, 0), box)
    inf <- which(state == 1L); sus <- which(state == 0L)
    if (length(inf) && length(sus)) {
      d <- as.matrix(dist(cbind(x, y)))[sus, inf, drop = FALSE]
      hit <- sus[rowSums(d < radius) > 0]; state[hit] <- 1L; sick_since[hit] <- s
    }
    done <- which(state == 1L & (s - sick_since) > recover); state[done] <- 2L
    if (s %in% want) keep[[length(keep) + 1]] <-
      tibble(step = s, x = x, y = y,
             status = factor(state, 0:2, c("Healthy", "Infected", "Recovered")))
  }
  bind_rows(keep)
})

ggplot(snap, aes(x, y, colour = status)) +
  geom_point(size = .8) +
  facet_wrap(~paste("step", step), nrow = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Healthy = "#a5a199", Infected = "#8C1C13",
                                 Recovered = "#1e7c50"), name = NULL) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Six frames from one run", x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = "The reader of the original saw this move. A static page cannot, and loses something real.") +
  theme_void(base_family = dsvar_font()) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11, hjust = 0),
        plot.caption = element_text(size = 7.5, colour = "#7a7a70", hjust = 0),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 8, colour = "#5a5a52"),
        legend.position = "bottom")










Six frames are not the animation, and the gap between them is what made the original work. Watching a single red dot become a wall of red is an experience; reading six panels is an inspection. Both carry the same information. Only one of them was shared by tens of millions of people, and being honest about that is not the same as recommending it.




WHAT THE SIMULATION ASSUMES



A MODEL IS PERSUASIVE WHETHER OR NOT IT IS RIGHT

Read the code above and notice what it takes for granted. Everyone is identical. Contact is a fixed radius. Recovery happens on a fixed schedule and confers permanent immunity. Nobody dies, nobody travels, and the population is closed. Change any one of those and the curves change shape. None of that weakens the narrow claim, that the peak falls when contact is reduced, which is the only claim Stevens made. It would demolish any attempt to read a number off these curves, and a reader who has just watched a simulation is in the worst possible frame of mind to remember that.




SOURCES


Original: Stevens, H. (2020). Why outbreaks like coronavirus spread exponentially, and how to “flatten the curve”. The Washington Post, 14 March 2020. Reported as the most-read article in the paper’s history.
The predecessor: the piece credits Kevin Simler’s Outbreak explorable as inspiration.
Data: none. Everything on this page is generated by the code shown, seeded for reproducibility.
Related: Pandemic trajectories on a log scale, which plots what actually happened rather than what a model does.
Reproduce it: every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: Minard’s march on Moscow
text:
Gallery · The whole story · back to the gallery


Minard’s march on Moscow

Six variables in one figure, none of them a chart type you could pick from a menu. Tufte called it the best statistical graphic ever drawn. It is the course’s strongest argument for composing a figure rather than choosing one.








THE ORIGINAL



Carte figurative des pertes successives en hommes de l’Armée Française dans la campagne de Russie 1812–1813 by Charles Joseph Minard, 1869. Public domain (author died 1870); scan via Wikimedia Commons.



How to read it


 The tan band is the Grande Armée marching east, from the Niemen river on the left to Moscow on the right, in the summer of 1812.


 The black band is the same army retreating west, back the way it came, through the winter.


 The width of a band is the number of men still alive. 422,000 set out and 10,000 came back. Nothing else on the map encodes that: the collapse is the narrowing.


 The army is not one band but three. It splits into separate columns that march apart and rejoin, so at any point you may be looking at a branch rather than the whole force.


 The names along the route are towns and rivers. Each place where the black band suddenly thins is a river crossing.


 The panel underneath is the temperature during the retreat, lining up with the map above by longitude. It is in degrees Réaumur, not Celsius.


 There is no legend, no scale bar and no axis on the map itself. Minard explains all of this in the French text at the top, which is one reason a key is needed here.





THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

A band crosses a map from left to right and back again. Going out it is tan and wide; coming back it is black and much thinner, and it thins further at each branch. Below the map sits a separate line plot falling from zero to −30. City names are lettered along the route. There is no legend and no vertical axis on the map.



02 · Analyse

Six variables, on five channels. Longitude and latitude on position; army size on band width; direction of travel on colour, as a two-value split; date and temperature in the panel below, tied back to the map by shared longitude. Width is the load-bearing channel, and it is used for the one quantity that matters most.



03 · Interpret

The claim is that the army was destroyed, and the figure says where, when, and in what cold. It is not arguing that the cold caused the losses: the band is already a third of its width before the temperature panel begins. The graphic lets you notice that yourself, which is a stronger move than asserting it.



04 · Judge

It works, and it is not a template. The variables are coupled (a place, a time, and a number that changes because of both), so composing them into one figure buys something that six separate charts would not. But it carries no uncertainty at all, its geography is loose, and you cannot read a value off it. It earns those omissions; most charts that imitate its density do not.





THE RECREATION

This is an attempt, not a facsimile. The aim is to get the encoding right, six variables in one figure, without the hand lettering, the French annotations, the river-crossing branches or the paper. Michael Friendly calls reproducing this “Minard’s Challenge”, and the point of the challenge was always the grammar rather than the calligraphy.


Show the R code
# Minard's two inks: tan out, black back.
ink  <- c(A = "#D9BC7E", R = "#332B23")
xlim <- c(23.6, 38.2)

march <- ggplot(troops, aes(long, lat)) +
  # group must combine direction AND group: the numbering restarts for the
  # retreat, so `group = group` silently joins the advance to the retreat.
  geom_path(aes(linewidth = survivors, colour = direction,
                group = interaction(direction, group)),
            lineend = "round", linejoin = "round") +
  geom_point(data = cities, size = 1, colour = "#8C1C13") +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = cities, aes(label = city),
                           size = 2.7, colour = "#8C1C13", family = dsvar_font(),
                           seed = 7, box.padding = 0.5, point.padding = 0.25,
                           max.overlaps = Inf, force = 6, max.iter = 20000,
                           min.segment.length = 0.25, segment.size = 0.2,
                           segment.colour = "#B08A84",
                           bg.color = "#faf8f4", bg.r = 0.12) +
  # Width is proportional to survivors and the scale starts at zero, which is
  # what makes the collapse readable. The 0.45 floor is a compromise: see below.
  scale_linewidth(range = c(0.45, 12), limits = c(0, max(troops$survivors))) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = ink) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = xlim, ylim = c(53.8, 56.15)) +
  theme_void(base_family = dsvar_font()) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# Minard's thermometer is in degrees REAUMUR, not Celsius. See the note below.
temp_panel <- ggplot(temps, aes(long, temp)) +
  geom_line(colour = ink[["R"]], linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(colour = ink[["R"]], size = 1.3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(temp, "°")), vjust = -1.1, size = 2.7,
            colour = ink[["R"]], family = dsvar_font()) +
  geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(is.na(date), "", date)), vjust = 2.1, size = 2.4,
            colour = "#7a7a70", family = dsvar_font()) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, -10, -20, -30)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = xlim, ylim = c(-34, 6)) +
  labs(y = "°Réaumur, on the retreat", x = NULL) +
  theme_dsvar(base_size = 9, grid = "y") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.line.x = element_blank(),
        axis.title.y = element_text(size = 7.5))

march / temp_panel + plot_layout(heights = c(2.7, 1))










Survivors, route and retreat temperatures of the Grande Armée, 1812–1813. n = 51 route points, 20 cities, 9 temperature readings. Data digitised by Leland Wilkinson for The Grammar of Graphics, distributed in the HistData package and vendored into this repo as CSV.




FOUR THINGS THAT BIT



1 · THE UNITS ARE NOT CELSIUS

Minard.temp$temp is documented only as “Temperature”. The obvious reading is Celsius, and it is wrong: Minard’s thermometer is Réaumur, a scale where water boils at 80°. His −30° is −37.5 °C, so calling it Celsius understates the cold by a quarter. Nothing in the data says so; only the original does, where Minard writes it on the chart. A column with no units is a column you do not yet understand.



2 · GROUP IS NOT WHAT YOU THINK

The group column numbers 1–3 for the advance and then starts again at 1 for the retreat. Mapping group = group therefore joins the end of each advance to the start of the unrelated retreat, drawing three phantom bands across the map. It looks like a rendering glitch rather than a data error, which is why it is worth meeting once. The fix is group = interaction(direction, group).



3 · THE HEADLINE NUMBERS ARE SUMS, NOT THE WIDEST BAND

The famous figures are 422,000 out and 10,000 back, and neither appears in any single row of the data. The widest advance band is 340,000; read that as the army and you understate it by a fifth. 422,000 is the three advance columns added at the Niemen; 10,000 is the two retreat columns that get back there, since the third stops at longitude 28.3 and never reaches the river. Both reconcile exactly once you sum the right branches, which is how you know you have understood the structure.



4 · PROPORTIONAL WIDTH HAS A FLOOR

Minard’s bands are proportional to the number of men. But 4,000 survivors is 1.2% of the 340,000 who set out, so at any sensible size for the widest band the thinnest one is less than a pixel and disappears. We set a floor of 0.45, so the last stretch is drawn slightly wider than it should be: a small but real departure from proportionality. Minard had the same problem and solved it with an engraver.




WHAT THE COMPOSITION BUYS

Here is the same headline number, the army’s size, as a chart you would reach for. It is more precise than Minard on the one variable it shows, and it has lost the argument.


Show the R code
troops |>
  mutate(leg = if_else(direction == "A", "Advance", "Retreat")) |>
  ggplot(aes(long, survivors, colour = leg,
             group = interaction(direction, group))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Advance = "#B8912F", Retreat = "#332B23")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "The same collapse, as a chart you would reach for",
       subtitle = "Surviving troops against longitude. Readable, precise, and no longer about a place",
       x = "Longitude", y = NULL, colour = NULL,
       caption = "n = 51 route points · Minard (1869), digitised by Wilkinson")











LOOK AT THE RETREAT LINE AGAIN

It rises. Plotted against longitude, the retreat runs east to west, so it has to be read right to left. Read the way everyone reads a line chart, it shows an army growing from 4,000 to 100,000. The information is all still there and the chart is not lying; it has dropped the one channel, direction, that made the original impossible to misread.


This is the mirror image of the warming-stripes lesson. There, the plain chart was the one that could be checked and the famous graphic was the one that landed. Here the famous graphic is the one carrying more information, and the plain chart is the reduction. The moral is neither “be like Minard” nor “be plain”: the form follows the claim, and you have to know what your claim is before you can choose.




SOURCES


Original graphic: Minard, C. J. (1869). Carte figurative des pertes successives en hommes de l’Armée Française dans la campagne de Russie 1812–1813. Public domain.
Data: digitised by Leland Wilkinson for The Grammar of Graphics (Springer), distributed in Friendly, M., HistData. Minard’s figures are public domain; HistData is GPL. Vendored here as data/raw/minard-*.csv.
Minard’s Challenge: Friendly, M. (2002). Visions and re-visions of Charles Joseph Minard. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, 27(1), 31–51. See also datavis.ca/gallery/re-minard.html.
The claim about it: Tufte, E. R. (1983). The Visual Display of Quantitative Information. Graphics Press.
Reproduce it: Rscript R/fetch-gallery-data.R; every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: Mayr’s radar chart
text:
Gallery · Comparison & ranking · back to the gallery


Mayr’s radar chart

Twelve numbers drawn four ways around a circle, in a German book on statistics from 1877. The third panel is usually credited as the first radar chart. On the page before it, its inventor says when it may be used, and the rule he gives rules out most of the radar charts drawn since.








THE ORIGINAL



Figur 4, Linien-Diagramme im Kreise, from Georg Mayr, Die Gesetzmässigkeit im Gesellschaftsleben: Statistische Studien (Munich: R. Oldenbourg, 1877), p. 78. Public domain (author died 1925); scan of the University of Toronto copy via the Internet Archive, cropped to the figure.

Georg Mayr, later von Mayr, was a Bavarian statistician, and this is a popular book on what statistics could say about society. Its first part is a short course in drawing statistics: points, then lines, then areas, then solids. Figure 4 belongs to the lines. Having shown that one series can be drawn on a straight baseline in several ways, Mayr bends the baseline into a circle, and says on the facing page when that is allowed:

Zur Darstellung von Verhältnissen, welche thatsächlich einen Kreislauf darstellen, kann das in den Kreis gezeichnete Linien-Diagramm mit einiger Berechtigung angewendet werden. Solches ist beispielsweise der Fall, wenn die Sterblichkeit nach Monaten nicht für ein einzelnes Kalenderjahr, sondern nach dem Durchschnitte einer Jahresreihe darzustellen ist. In diesem Falle steht thatsächlich der Januar dem Dezember eben so nahe wie dem Februar, was nur bei der Darstellung im Kreise, nicht aber auf der Basis einer Geraden zu erreichen ist. (p. 77)

“For relations that really are a cycle, the line diagram drawn in a circle can be used with some justification. That is the case, for instance, when deaths by month are shown not for a single calendar year but as the average of a run of years. Then January really does stand as close to December as to February, which only the circle can show, and a straight baseline cannot.” (Our translation.)


How to read it


 The column on the left is the data: a Zahlen-Reihe, a series of twelve numbers, with no unit and no labels. Read it as a year of months, as Mayr’s own example suggests.


 Each number is one radius, starting at twelve o’clock and running clockwise. The largest, 10, reaches the rim.


 In a and c the lines start at the centre; in b and d they start at the rim and run inwards. The dotted part of each radius is the empty rest of the scale.


 In c and d the ends are joined by straight lines. Panel c is the radar chart as it is drawn today.





THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

A framed square under the title Linien-Diagramme im Kreise, “line diagrams in a circle”. A column of twelve numbers runs down the left. Four circles of equal size fill the rest, each cut by twelve radii at equal angles. In a and b the values are heavy strokes along the radii, out from the centre in a and in from the rim in b. In c and d the same strokes are reduced to points, joined into a polygon. There is no scale, and nothing on the radii says which number is which.



02 · Analyse

One variable, twelve values, encoded as length along a radius. Length is a good channel, but every radius points a different way, so no two are measured against the same baseline: the eye compares lengths at an angle. Panels b and d measure from the rim, which turns the encoding inside out: the largest value is the shortest stroke in b, and in d the polygon shrinks as the values grow. The polygons in c and d add a channel the series does not have, shape and area, and the shape depends on which values happen to be neighbours.



03 · Interpret

The figure makes no claim about the world: the series has no subject. Its claim is about method. One series can be drawn in several forms that look nothing alike, and the circle is one more of them, which Mayr allows only when the data is a cycle. Then the circle shows something a straight line cannot: that the last value is the neighbour of the first.



04 · Judge

Mayr got the rule right in 1877, and the rule did not travel with the form. His own four panels already show the risks: b and d invert the reading, and c and d draw a shape that the order of the radii decides. Panel c is now the default for comparing profiles, whose axes have no order at all, which is the case his justification excludes. The figure is better than most of its descendants, because it came with a rule for when to use it.





THE RECREATION

The data is the column of twelve numbers. Each panel is drawn by hand with trigonometry, for a reason given in HOW WE KNOW.


Show the R code
ink <- p$ink
R <- 10   # the rim is the series' largest value, as Mayr drew it

# The engraver's lettering: a narrow grotesque for the title and the panel
# letters, an italic serif for the numbers. Use the closest faces installed.
grotesk <- c(intersect(c("DIN Condensed", "Arial Narrow"),
                       systemfonts::system_fonts()$family), dsvar_font())[1]
serif <- c(intersect(c("Hoefler Text", "Baskerville", "Georgia"),
                     systemfonts::system_fonts()$family), "serif")[1]

# The layout, measured off the scan in units of the scale (a unit is 28.6 px
# of the crop, so the circles are 20 across). Circle a is centred on the
# origin; the frame runs from -14.5 to 30 across and from -30 to 14.5 up, with
# the number column and the title band each 4.5 units deep.
centres <- tibble(panel = c("a", "b", "c", "d"),
                  from  = c("centre", "rim", "centre", "rim"),
                  cx = c(0, 20, 0, 20), cy = c(0, 0, -20, -20))
xy <- function(r, spoke, cx, cy) spoke_xy(r, spoke) |> mutate(x = x + cx, y = y + cy)

# For each radius: where its solid stroke starts and ends, and where its dotted
# rest runs. a and c measure from the centre, b and d from the rim.
radii <- cross_join(centres, mayr) |>
  mutate(tip   = if_else(from == "rim", R - value, value),
         start = if_else(from == "rim", R, 0),
         rest  = if_else(from == "rim", 0, R))
solid   <- radii |> mutate(xy(start, spoke, cx, cy) |> rename(x0 = x, y0 = y),
                           xy(tip, spoke, cx, cy))
dotted  <- radii |> mutate(xy(tip, spoke, cx, cy) |> rename(x0 = x, y0 = y),
                           xy(rest, spoke, cx, cy))
polygon <- radii |> filter(panel %in% c("c", "d")) |> mutate(xy(tip, spoke, cx, cy))
rims    <- cross_join(centres, tibble(t = seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 361))) |>
  mutate(x = cx + R * sin(t), y = cy + R * cos(t))

# a and b draw the values as heavy strokes; c and d keep the radii thin and put
# the weight on the polygon, as the engraver did.
heavy <- c(a = 1.5, b = 1.5, c = .35, d = .35)

# The frame's inner rules: under the title, beside the column, between panels.
rules <- tibble(x = c(-14.5, -10, 10, -10), xend = c(30, -10, 10, 30),
                y = c(10, 10, 10, -10), yend = c(10, -30, -30, -10))

recreation <- ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -14.5, xmax = 30, ymin = -30, ymax = 14.5,
           fill = NA, colour = ink, linewidth = .5) +
  geom_segment(data = rules, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
               colour = ink, linewidth = .4) +
  geom_path(data = rims, aes(x, y, group = panel), colour = ink, linewidth = .35) +
  geom_segment(data = dotted, aes(x0, y0, xend = x, yend = y),
               colour = ink, linewidth = .45, linetype = "11") +
  geom_segment(data = solid, aes(x0, y0, xend = x, yend = y,
                                 linewidth = I(heavy[panel])),
               colour = ink, lineend = "round") +
  geom_polygon(data = polygon, aes(x, y, group = panel), fill = NA,
               colour = ink, linewidth = 1.05) +
  annotate("text", x = 8, y = 12.25, label = "Linien - Diagramme im Kreise :",
           family = grotesk, size = 9.6, colour = ink) +
  geom_text(data = centres, aes(cx - 9.3, cy + 8.2, label = paste0(panel, ".")),
            hjust = 0, family = grotesk, size = 9, colour = ink) +
  annotate("text", x = -12.25, y = c(8.6, 7.5, 6.4), label = c("Zah-", "len-", "Reihe."),
           family = serif, fontface = "italic", size = 4.2, colour = ink) +
  geom_text(data = mayr, aes(-12.25, 3.46 - 2.49 * (spoke - 1), label = value),
            family = serif, fontface = "italic", size = 5.4, colour = ink) +
  annotate("text", x = 8, y = -31.7, label = "Figur 4.", family = serif,
           size = 4, colour = ink) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-15.3, 30.9), ylim = c(-32.7, 15.2), expand = FALSE) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = p$paper, colour = NA),
        plot.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0))

recreation










n = 12 values, as printed in the figure. The rim is 10, the largest value; zero is the centre in a and c and the rim in b and d. Drawn at the scan’s proportions, 1320 × 1369, with the frame, the column and the circles where the engraving puts them, so the two can be compared directly.




Original · Mayr, 1877





Ours · ggplot















HOW WE KNOW

The numbers are printed in the figure, so they did not need digitising. What is not printed is which radius belongs to which number.
Where the series starts, and which way it runs. Only one stroke in panel a reaches the rim, at two o’clock, and only one number is 10, the third. So the first number sits at twelve o’clock and the series runs clockwise. That is a guess from one stroke, and the other eleven test it: below, rings are drawn over the scan at every value the series uses, and each stroke ends on or close to the ring for its number.


Show the R code
# Panel a of the cropped scan, in its own pixels. Its frame was measured on the
# image: the panel runs from x = 151 to 723 and y = 148 to 720, so the circle
# is centred at (437, 434) with a radius of 286 px. Image rows count down.
scan <- jpeg::readJPEG(here::here("gallery", "img", "mayr-radar-original.jpg"))
cx <- 437; cy <- 434; r_px <- 286
panel_a <- scan[(cy - r_px):(cy + r_px), (cx - r_px):(cx + r_px), ]

rings <- crossing(value = sort(unique(mayr$value)),
                  t = seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 241)) |>
  mutate(x = value / 10 * sin(t), y = value / 10 * cos(t))
numbers <- mayr |> mutate(spoke_xy(1.07, spoke), label = paste0(spoke, ": ", value))

ggplot() +
  annotation_raster(panel_a, -1, 1, -1, 1) +
  geom_path(data = rings, aes(x, y, group = value), colour = "#c0392b",
            linewidth = .35, alpha = .7) +
  geom_text(data = numbers, aes(x, y, label = label), size = 3,
            colour = "#c0392b", family = dsvar_font()) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-1.15, 1.15), ylim = c(-1.15, 1.15), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Each stroke ends at or near the ring for its number",
       subtitle = "Panel a of the scan, with a ring at each value. Labels give radius: value",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
        axis.line.x = element_blank())










Rings at the values 4 to 10, with the rim at 10 and zero at the centre. The engraving is hand-made, and some strokes stop a little past their ring, but none is out by as much as a whole unit.

Why straight edges need trigonometry. Mayr joins the ends of the radii with straight lines, “die lineare Verbindung der Endpunkte”. The obvious way to draw this in ggplot, coord_polar(), does not: it draws the line between two neighbouring values as a straight line in the data, which on the circle is a spiral. The difference is small with twelve spokes and large with five, and it is why every chart on this page computes its points with sin() and cos().


Show the R code
straight <- mayr |> mutate(spoke_xy(value, spoke)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_polygon(fill = NA, colour = dsvar_accent(), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(colour = dsvar_accent(), size = 1.8) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-R, R), ylim = c(-R, R)) +
  labs(title = "Straight edges, by hand", subtitle = "What Mayr drew",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_blank())

# An open path through a 13th point that repeats the first: a closed polygon
# would draw its closing edge from 12 back to 1 the long way round.
curved <- bind_rows(mayr, mutate(mayr[1, ], spoke = 13)) |>
  ggplot(aes(spoke, value)) +
  geom_path(colour = dsvar_accent(), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(colour = dsvar_accent(), size = 1.8) +
  coord_polar() +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(1, 13)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, R)) +
  labs(title = "coord_polar()", subtitle = "Each edge bends into a curve",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_blank())

straight + curved










The same twelve points. Between them, the left panel draws what Mayr drew; the right panel draws a line that is straight in the data and curved on the page. Neither line is data: the values exist only at the points.




THE SAME DATA, DIFFERENT CHOICES


On a straight baseline
Two pages earlier, Mayr’s figure 3 draws a different series on a straight base: a dotted upright at each value, and a line joining their tops, which he prefers to the uprights alone. Here are figure 4’s twelve numbers drawn the same way.


Show the R code
mayr |>
  ggplot(aes(spoke, value)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = spoke, y = 0, yend = value), colour = p$ink_3,
               linewidth = .4, linetype = "11") +
  geom_line(colour = dsvar_accent(), linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(colour = dsvar_accent(), size = 2.2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = value), vjust = -1, size = 3.4, colour = p$ink_2,
            family = dsvar_font()) +
  annotate("text", x = 12.6, y = 9.3, hjust = 1, size = 3.2, colour = p$ink_3,
           family = dsvar_font(), label = "…and 12 is next to 1 again") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 11.2), breaks = c(0, 5, 10), expand = expansion(0)) +
  labs(title = "On one baseline every value can be compared with every other",
       subtitle = "What the line cannot show is that the series wraps around",
       x = "position in the series (a month, by Mayr's example)", y = NULL,
       caption = "n = 12. Mayr (1877), figure 4.")










Easier to read than any of the circles: each value is a height above one baseline, the most accurate comparison there is. What it gives up is the one thing Mayr wanted the circle for. The step from 7 back up to 8 at the turn of the year is split between the two ends of the axis. Figure 3 makes a further point that holds here: drawn tall and narrow the same line looks dramatic, and drawn flat it looks calm, and nothing in the data decides which.



Where the spokes have no order
A radar chart of a profile puts several different measures on the spokes, and the measures have no order of their own. Here are V-Dem’s five democracy indices for two autocracies in 2025, drawn once in the order V-Dem lists them and once with one spoke moved.


Show the R code
pair <- c("Belarus", "Venezuela")
indices <- c("electoral", "liberal", "participatory", "deliberative", "egalitarian")
orders <- list(`In V-Dem's order` = indices,
               `One spoke moved` = c("electoral", "liberal", "deliberative",
                                     "egalitarian", "participatory"))

two <- vdem |> filter(year == max(year), country %in% pair) |>
  select(country, all_of(indices))
stopifnot(nrow(two) == 2)

drawn <- imap_dfr(orders, \(o, name) {
  two |> pivot_longer(-country, names_to = "index") |>
    mutate(spoke = match(index, o), order = name)
}) |> arrange(order, country, spoke) |>
  mutate(spoke_xy(value, spoke, n = 5))

areas <- drawn |> summarise(area = radar_area(value), .by = c(order, country)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = country, values_from = area) |>
  mutate(ratio = Belarus / Venezuela)
first  <- areas$ratio[areas$order == names(orders)[1]]
second <- areas$ratio[areas$order == names(orders)[2]]
stopifnot(first > 1, second < 1)   # the claim in the title, checked

top  <- .25                                    # the scale's outer ring
grid <- expand_grid(order = names(orders), ring = c(.1, .2, top), spoke = c(1:5, 1)) |>
  mutate(spoke_xy(ring, spoke, n = 5))
axes <- imap_dfr(orders, \(o, name) tibble(order = name, index = o, spoke = 1:5)) |>
  mutate(spoke_xy(top, spoke, n = 5),
         spoke_xy(top * 1.14, spoke, n = 5) |> rename(lx = x, ly = y))

ggplot(drawn, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_path(data = grid, aes(group = ring), colour = p$hairline, linewidth = .35) +
  geom_segment(data = axes, aes(0, 0, xend = x, yend = y), colour = p$hairline) +
  geom_text(data = axes, aes(lx, ly, label = index), size = 3.1, colour = p$ink_3,
            family = dsvar_font()) +
  geom_polygon(aes(fill = country, colour = country), alpha = .25, linewidth = .8) +
  facet_wrap(~ order) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = dsvar_cat[c(1, 2)], name = NULL) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = dsvar_cat[c(1, 2)], name = NULL) +
  coord_equal(clip = "off") +
  labs(title = sprintf("The same ten numbers: Belarus's polygon is %d%% larger, or Venezuela's is %d%% larger",
                       round(100 * (first - 1)), round(100 * (1 / second - 1))),
       subtitle = "V-Dem's five democracy indices. Rings at 0.1, 0.2 and 0.25 of V-Dem's 0 to 1 scale",
       x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = sprintf("V-Dem v16, %d. Area computed from the drawn polygons.", max(vdem$year))) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
        axis.line.x = element_blank(), legend.position = "top",
        strip.text = element_text(hjust = .5), panel.spacing = unit(4, "lines"))










Nothing changed but where the participatory index sits. Its value is the largest difference between the two countries, and its neighbours decide how much area that difference buys. The averages of the five indices are almost the same, 0.103 for Belarus and 0.095 for Venezuela, and the chart offers a verdict either way.



The comparison without the circle


Show the R code
long <- two |> pivot_longer(-country, names_to = "index")

# The title's claim, checked: the two largest gaps, and who leads on each.
gaps <- long |> pivot_wider(names_from = country) |>
  mutate(gap = Venezuela - Belarus) |> arrange(desc(abs(gap)))
stopifnot(setequal(gaps$index[1:2], c("participatory", "egalitarian")),
          gaps$gap[gaps$index == "participatory"] > 0,
          gaps$gap[gaps$index == "egalitarian"] < 0)

long |>
  mutate(index = fct_reorder(index, value, .fun = max)) |>
  ggplot(aes(value, index)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = index), colour = p$hairline, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = country), size = 3.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = dsvar_cat[c(1, 2)], name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, .25), breaks = c(0, .1, .2)) +
  labs(title = "Venezuela is higher on participation, Belarus on equality; the rest is close",
       subtitle = "Each index on one common scale, so no order of the indices can change the reading",
       x = "V-Dem index (0 to 1)", y = NULL,
       caption = sprintf("V-Dem v16, %d.", max(vdem$year))) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = p$hairline, linewidth = .35))










The comparison the radar chart was being asked for, with nothing hanging on the order of the rows. They are sorted by the larger of the two values, which is a choice too, but one that moves dots, not areas.


“Daraus ergibt sich, daß dieselbe statistische Reihe in einer Anzahl äußerlich einander mehr oder weniger unähnlicher Diagramme dargestellt werden kann.” The same statistical series can be drawn as several diagrams that look more or less unlike one another. Mayr wrote it on page 77, and it is still the argument of this course. His circle is a good diagram for a cycle, because the order of the spokes is the order of the year. For anything else the order is yours, and so is the shape.





SOURCES


Original: Mayr, G. (1877). Die Gesetzmässigkeit im Gesellschaftsleben: Statistische Studien. Munich: R. Oldenbourg, figure 4 on p. 78, the quoted passages on p. 77. Public domain; scan via the Internet Archive.
Data: the twelve numbers are printed in the figure. V-Dem: Coppedge, M., et al. (2026). V-Dem Dataset v16. Varieties of Democracy Project. doi:10.23696/vdemds26. CC BY-SA 4.0; vendored as data/raw/vdem-indices.csv.
On radar charts and order: Feldman, R. (2013). Filled radar charts should not be used to compare social indicators. Social Indicators Research, 111(3), 709–712. doi:10.1007/s11205-012-0028-6
Reproduce it: every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: Iraq’s bloody toll
text:
Gallery · Change over time · back to the gallery


Iraq’s bloody toll

An inverted vertical axis, which is on every list of things you must not do. Here it is the best decision on the chart. Read this one beside Gun deaths in Florida, where the identical technique produces the opposite verdict. The two pages are written as a pair.








THE ORIGINAL



“Iraq’s bloody toll” by Simon Scarr, South China Morning Post, 2011. Copyright Simon Scarr / SCMP, reproduced for criticism and review under the Dutch citation right (Auteurswet art. 15a). Not a free licence: it cannot be reused from here.

Simon Scarr’s graphic for the South China Morning Post (2011), published as coalition forces withdrew from Iraq. Deaths hang downward from a heavy title in deep red.


How to read it


 Each bar is a month of documented civilian deaths, running left to right from the 2003 invasion to the 2011 withdrawal.


 The bars hang down from the top, not up from the bottom. The axis is inverted: further down means more deaths.


 The title sits on top of the bars so they read as running out of it, and the whole thing is a single deep red.


 The resemblance to dripping blood is deliberate. The headline is “Iraq’s bloody toll”.





THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

A bar chart on a dark red field, with the bars descending from a title block at the top of the frame. The vertical axis is labelled and its numbers increase downward. Annotations mark specific events along the timeline.



02 · Analyse

Quantity is on length, which is accurate, and the length is anchored to a common baseline, which keeps it honest. The only unconventional decision is the direction of growth. Colour carries no data; it does rhetorical work, and the chart does not hide it.



03 · Interpret

The claim is that the war’s human cost was enormous and sustained. The inversion is what makes the bars read as bleeding rather than as growth, and the graphic wants you to feel the accumulation before you read a number.



04 · Judge

It works because there is no plausible wrong reading. A viewer who ignores the axis entirely still concludes “a lot, and worse in the middle years”, which is the true story. The inversion adds a metaphor without opening a route to a false conclusion. The Florida chart fails this same test.





THE RECREATION



Show the R code
blood <- "#8C1C13"

ggplot(ibc, aes(factor(year), civilian_deaths)) +
  geom_col(fill = blood, width = .78) +
  # The inversion: reverse the y scale so bars grow downward from the top.
  scale_y_reverse(expand = expansion(mult = c(.06, 0)),
                  labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_x_discrete(position = "top") +
  labs(title = "IRAQ'S BLOODY TOLL",
       subtitle = "Documented civilian deaths from violence, per year",
       x = NULL, y = "Deaths",
       caption = "n = 9 years · Iraq Body Count, documented civilian deaths. Annual totals, not monthly.") +
  theme_dsvar(base_size = 11, grid = "y") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(colour = blood, face = "bold", size = rel(1.6)),
        axis.text.x.top = element_text(colour = "#5a5a52"),
        axis.line.x = element_blank())










Scarr’s original runs monthly across 2003–2011 and is far denser; Iraq Body Count publishes annual totals openly, so this is the annual version. The encoding decision under discussion is identical.




THE SAME DATA, THE RIGHT WAY UP



Show the R code
ggplot(ibc, aes(factor(year), civilian_deaths)) +
  geom_col(fill = dsvar_accent(), width = .78) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .06)),
                     labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "Documented civilian deaths in Iraq, 2003–2011",
       subtitle = "Identical numbers, conventional axis, neutral colour",
       x = NULL, y = "Deaths",
       caption = "n = 9 years · Iraq Body Count")










This version is more conventional and less honest about what it is doing. It presents 100,000 documented deaths in the register of a quarterly sales report, and the neutrality is itself a rhetorical choice, only an invisible one. Scarr’s chart announces that it is making an argument. Most charts make one and do not say so.




THE TEST THIS CHART PASSES



IS THERE A PLAUSIBLE WRONG READING?

Ask it of any unconventional encoding; it is more useful than a rule about which way an axis may point. Here, a reader who misses the inversion still gets “many deaths, peaking in the middle”. The bars are anchored, the quantity is on length, and the metaphor points the same direction as the data. Apply the same test to Gun deaths in Florida, which uses this exact technique, cites this exact chart as its inspiration, and fails.




SOURCES


Original: Scarr, S. (2011). Iraq’s bloody toll. South China Morning Post. Copyright Simon Scarr / SCMP; shown above at low resolution as a quotation for criticism and review. Not reusable from here.
Data: Iraq Body Count, documented civilian deaths from violence, annual totals. iraqbodycount.org. © Iraq Body Count; free for not-for-profit use with iraqbodycount.org cited. The nine totals are drawn here, but the file is not offered for download.
The pair: Gun deaths in Florida, Christine Chan, Reuters (2014).
Reproduce it: every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: Headlines turning negative
text:
Gallery · Change over time · back to the gallery


Headlines turning negative

Twenty-three million headlines from 47 American news outlets, each scored by a language model, averaged by year: the news got more negative between 2000 and 2019. The trend holds up when you check it. The number printed on the chart, “−314%”, does not mean anything.








THE ORIGINAL



Fig 1 of Longitudinal analysis of sentiment and emotion in news media headlines using automated labelling with Transformer language models by David Rozado, Ruth Hughes and Jamin Halberstadt, PLOS ONE 17(10): e0276367, 2022. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0276367. Licensed CC BY 4.0, reproduced unaltered.

The study scraped the headlines of 47 outlets, from Jacobin and Democracy Now to Breitbart and Newsmax, and ran each through a pretrained sentiment model. The paper’s other figures split the same series by the outlets’ political leaning and by emotion (anger, fear, sadness and so on). Everything is deposited openly: the scored headlines, the models and the analysis notebooks.


How to read it


 Each headline is scored between −1 and +1: the model’s verdict, negative or positive, times how sure it is. There is no neutral class. Zero is where the model is undecided, or where verdicts cancel out.


 Each year’s value is an average of averages: first over an outlet’s headlines, then over the outlets, every outlet counting the same.


 The band is how far the outlets differ from each other that year (1.96 standard deviations, divided by the square root of the number of outlets), not the uncertainty of the trend.


 The two annotations are a percentage change from 2000 to 2019, and a test of a straight line fitted to the twenty yearly values.





THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

One thick blue line over twenty years, inside a pale band, falling from about +0.08 to about −0.16 with a flat stretch in the 2000s and a steeper fall after 2013. The y axis runs from −0.2 to 0.15. Two annotations, a percentage and a t-test, sit in the corners, and the 47 outlets are listed in a footnote.



02 · Analyse

Time on x, a mean score on y, cropped to the 0.4 of a two-point scale where the line lives. The band looks like a confidence interval but measures the spread between outlets. The number of outlets inside the average grows from 18 to 47. The percentage is computed on a scale whose zero is a classifier’s decision boundary, and the t-test treats twenty consecutive years as independent observations.



03 · Interpret

The claim is that American news headlines became markedly more negative over two decades, and the annotations are there to say markedly and certainly. −314% reads as a collapse; p = 1.6 × 10⁻⁸ reads as beyond doubt.



04 · Judge

The trend is real: it survives every check below. The decoration oversells it. A percentage change needs a true zero, and this scale does not have one: score the same headlines with the authors’ other model, which starts a little below zero, and the same kind of fall becomes +2,528%. About 34 per cent of the fall comes from outlets joining the average, not from any outlet changing. Drop the percentage, say how many outlets each year contains, and the chart would be both honest and still alarming.





THE RECREATION

From the authors’ deposited data, with the paper’s own inclusion rule. The annotations are computed, not copied.


Show the R code
# matplotlib's defaults, the look of the original
sans <- c(intersect(c("DejaVu Sans", "Helvetica", "Arial"),
                    systemfonts::system_fonts()$family), "sans")[1]
mpl_blue <- "#1f77b4"

outlets_note <- paste(
  "* Alternet, Democracy Now, Daily Beast, Huffington Post, The Intercept, Jacobin, Mother Jones, The New Yorker, The Nation, Slate,",
  "Vox, CNN, New York Times, ABC News, The Atlantic, Buzzfeed, CBS News, The Economist, The Guardian, NBC News, POLITICO, TIME,",
  "Washington Post, NPR, Associated Press, BBC, Bloomberg, Christian Science Monitor, REUTERS, The Hill, USA Today, Wall Street",
  "Journal, Reason, Washington Examiner, Washington Times, Fox News, American Spectator, Breitbart, The Blaze, Christian",
  "Broadcasting Network, The Daily Caller, The Daily Mail, The Daily Wire, The Federalist, National Review, New York Post, Newsmax",
  sep = "\n")

recreation <- ggplot(yearly, aes(year, mean)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = mean - ci, ymax = mean + ci), fill = mpl_blue, alpha = .1,
              colour = alpha(mpl_blue, .15), linewidth = .3) +
  geom_line(colour = mpl_blue, linewidth = 1.9) +
  annotate("text", x = 2000.1, y = .125, hjust = 0, family = sans, size = 5.4,
           label = sprintf("2000–2019Δ=%.0f%%", delta_pct)) +
  annotate("text", x = 2000.2, y = -.215, hjust = 0, family = sans, size = 5.2,
           label = sprintf("β₁≠0, t(%d)=%.2f, p=%.2e", nrow(yearly) - 2, fit["t value"],
                           fit["Pr(>|t|)"])) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2000:2019, expand = expansion(add = .9)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(-.2, .15, .05), labels = \(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-.235, .158), expand = FALSE, clip = "off") +
  labs(title = "Average Yearly Sentiment of News Articles Headlines in 47* Popular News Media Outlets (N=23 Million)",
       x = NULL, y = "Sentiment\n(Negative to Positive)", caption = outlets_note) +
  theme_classic(base_family = sans, base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
        panel.border = element_rect(fill = NA, colour = "black", linewidth = .6),
        axis.line = element_blank(),
        axis.text = element_text(colour = "black", size = 12),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 13),
        axis.title.y = element_text(size = 11, lineheight = .95),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = .5, size = 14.5, margin = margin(b = 4)),
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 11.2, lineheight = 1.05,
                                    margin = margin(t = 26)),
        plot.caption.position = "plot",
        plot.margin = margin(6, 10, 8, 6))

recreation










655 outlet-years from 47 outlets, 23,361,697 headlines. Drawn at the original’s proportions in matplotlib’s colours, so the two can be compared.




Original · Rozado, Hughes & Halberstadt, 2022





Ours · ggplot













Side by side. The same twenty values, the same band, and the same two annotations, to the last printed digit.




HOW WE KNOW

The data. The deposit includes the authors’ own per-outlet, per-year averages, the step just before the figure. Those are the numbers on this page; the 23 million scored headlines behind them are in the same deposit, at three quarters of a gigabyte per model.
The rule that is not in the code. Averaging the deposited values directly gives a line that matches the figure from 2014 onwards and misses it before: +0.102 for 2000 instead of +0.077. The difference is a sentence in the paper’s methods: an outlet-year is included only if it has at least 100 headlines. The deposit keeps the thin years, the smallest of them a single headline. Apply the rule and every value matches.


Show the R code
all_rows |>
  summarise(`outlet-years` = n(),
            `with fewer than 100 headlines` = sum(headlines < 100),
            `smallest` = min(headlines)) |>
  knitr::kable()





outlet-years
with fewer than 100 headlines
smallest




679
24
1





The −314%. It is the 2019 value minus the 2000 value, divided by the 2000 value: (-0.164 − 0.077) / 0.077. The arithmetic is right. The trouble is the denominator. On a scale from −1 to +1 whose zero is where a classifier cannot decide, 0.077 is not a baseline, it is a point close to zero, and dividing by a number close to zero makes any change look enormous. The fall itself is 0.24 points, about 12 per cent of the scale’s range.
The t-test. A straight line through twenty yearly means, tested as if the years were twenty independent draws. Consecutive years of the same outlets are not independent, so the p-value is too small, by an amount the chart cannot tell you. The trend does not need it.



THE SAME HEADLINES, OTHER CHOICES


Who is in the average


Show the R code
lines <- bind_rows(
  yearly |> transmute(year, mean, series = "all outlets, as published"),
  balanced |> mutate(series = sprintf("the %d outlets present every year", length(always))))

ggplot(lines, aes(year, mean, colour = series)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = p$hairline) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_text(data = \(d) filter(d, year == 2019), aes(label = series), hjust = -.04,
            family = dsvar_font(), fontface = "bold", size = 3.3) +
  geom_text(data = yearly, aes(year, -.215, label = n), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            family = dsvar_font(), size = 3, colour = p$muted) +
  annotate("text", x = 1999.6, y = -.215, label = "outlets:", hjust = 1,
           family = dsvar_font(), size = 3, colour = p$muted) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(p$ink_3, dsvar_accent()), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2000, 2019, 3), expand = expansion(add = c(1.2, 7.5))) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-.23, .13)) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(title = sprintf("About %.0f%% of the fall comes from who joined the average",
                       100 * (1 - drop_bal / drop_all)),
       subtitle = "Mean headline sentiment; outlets with 100+ headlines that year",
       x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = "Rozado, Hughes & Halberstadt (2022), deposited data, CC BY 4.0.")










The outlets that enter the series later are, on average, more negative than the ones that were there from the start, so the published line falls partly because the room changed. The 18 that were there throughout still fall, by 0.16 points rather than 0.24. Both are true. Only one is labelled “47”.



Forty-seven lines, not one


Show the R code
ggplot(heads, aes(year, sentiment, group = outlet)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = p$hairline) +
  geom_line(colour = p$ink_3, alpha = .28, linewidth = .45) +
  geom_line(data = yearly, aes(year, mean), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            colour = dsvar_accent(), linewidth = 1.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2000, 2019, 3)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-1, 1), breaks = seq(-1, 1, .5)) +
  labs(title = "Outlets differ from each other far more than years do",
       subtitle = "Each grey line is one outlet; green is their average. The y axis is the model's whole scale",
       x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = sprintf("In 2019 alone, outlets range from %.2f to %.2f.",
                         min(heads$sentiment[heads$year == 2019]),
                         max(heads$sentiment[heads$year == 2019])))










On the model’s full scale the trend is a modest drift inside a wide spread. That is not the opposite of the published chart; it is the context the published chart cropped away. Which outlet you read matters more than which year you read it in.



Another model, the same headlines


Show the R code
two <- heads |>
  summarise(`RoBERTa (the published figure)` = mean(sentiment),
            `DistilBERT SST-2 (the authors' other model)` = mean(sentiment_sst2),
            .by = year) |>
  pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "model", values_to = "mean")
pct_of <- two |> summarise(first = mean[year == 2000], last = mean[year == 2019], .by = model) |>
  mutate(pct = 100 * (last - first) / first,
         label = sprintf("%s\nwould print \"Δ=%s%%\"", model, trimws(format(round(pct), big.mark = ","))))

ggplot(two, aes(year, mean, colour = model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = p$hairline) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_text(data = left_join(filter(two, year == 2019), pct_of, by = "model"),
            aes(label = label), hjust = -.04, lineheight = .95,
            family = dsvar_font(), size = 3.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(p$ink_3, dsvar_accent()), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2000, 2019, 3), expand = expansion(add = c(1, 9.5))) +
  labs(title = sprintf("Two classifiers agree on the direction, and their percentages disagree by %s points",
                       format(round(abs(diff(pct_of$pct)), -2), big.mark = ",")),
       subtitle = "Mean headline sentiment across outlets, the same headlines scored twice",
       x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = "Rozado, Hughes & Halberstadt (2022), deposited data, CC BY 4.0.")










A smaller model starts the series a little below zero, and the same fall, divided by a small negative number, comes out as a rise of over two thousand per cent. The direction is the finding. The percentage was never a measure of it.


A percentage change needs a zero that means none. Temperatures in Celsius do not have one, sentiment scores do not have one, and an index set to 100 in a chosen year has one only by decree. On those scales report the change in the scale’s own units, and say how many cases sit behind each point, because an average over a growing room is two trends at once.





SOURCES


Original: Rozado, D., Hughes, R., & Halberstadt, J. (2022). Longitudinal analysis of sentiment and emotion in news media headlines using automated labelling with Transformer language models. PLOS ONE, 17(10), e0276367. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0276367. CC BY 4.0.
Data: the authors’ deposit on Zenodo, 10.5281/zenodo.5144113 (CC BY 4.0): the per-outlet yearly averages from both models and the headline counts, from analysisScripts.rar. Vendored here as data/raw/rozado-headline-sentiment.csv.
Reproduce it: every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: Income and life expectancy
text:
Gallery · Relationships & structure · back to the gallery


Income and life expectancy

Four variables in one scatterplot, and a fifth added by making it move. Hans Rosling’s bubble chart is the most-watched statistical graphic of the last twenty years, and almost everything that makes it work is a choice you could have made differently.








THE ORIGINAL



“Gapminder World 2015” (version 15), Gapminder Foundation, CC BY 4.0. Based on a free chart from www.gapminder.org. Reproduced unaltered. Gapminder’s own data lines: income from the World Bank’s GDP per capita (PPP, 2011 international $), population from the UN Population Division, life expectancy from IHME GBD-2015.

Gapminder World was developed by Hans Rosling, Ola Rosling and Anna Rosling Rönnlund, and performed rather than published. This is the still poster, the one thing about Gapminder World that holds still. Most people met it in the 2006 TED talk, a man talking over a moving chart, and the live tool is a third thing again. Which of the three you have in mind changes what the critique below is about.


How to read it


 Each bubble is a country. Horizontal position is income per person, vertical position is life expectancy.


 The size of the bubble is population, so China and India dominate visually without dominating the trend.


 Colour is the region: an unordered grouping, so it gets hue rather than lightness.


 The horizontal axis is logarithmic. Equal steps are equal multiples of income, not equal dollars. It is the decision the chart rests on.


 In the original it moves, one frame per year, and the fifth variable is time.



Gapminder Foundation. Data and tools at gapminder.org, released CC BY 4.0. The original interactive is not embedded here. The recreation runs on the poster’s own data: Gapminder’s figures for 2015 as they stood in October 2016, in 2011 dollars. Every section after it uses Jenny Bryan’s gapminder extract: 142 countries, every five years from 1952 to 2007.




THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

A scatterplot of a few hundred circles. Two positional channels, one size channel, one colour channel and, in the original, an animation control. Both axes are labelled and the horizontal one is unevenly spaced.



02 · Analyse

The two variables the argument is about get position, the most accurate channel, which is right. Population goes on area, which is weak, and that is also right: nobody is asked to compare populations, only to notice that some dots are big. The log axis converts a violently skewed variable into something a straight line can pass through.



03 · Interpret

The claim is that there is no first world and third world, only a continuum. When it moves, it adds that essentially every country is travelling up and to the right. Rosling built it to destroy a specific mental model, and the shape of the cloud is the rebuttal.



04 · Judge

It holds, with one asterisk. The log axis is what makes the relationship look tidy, and a reader who does not notice it will badly underestimate how large the income gaps are in absolute terms. That is a defensible choice, clearly labelled, but the chart is much more persuasive about convergence than the underlying dollars warrant.





THE RECREATION



Show the R code
# Drawn at the poster's proportions, 3166 x 2238 px, and on the poster's own
# data: Gapminder's 2015 figures as of October 2016, the vintage its footer
# names. The gapminder extract used everywhere else on this page stops in 2007
# and is in older dollars, which put India and Nigeria a whole income level
# below where the poster has them. See R/fetch-gallery-data.R.
w15 <- read_csv(here::here("data", "raw", "gapminder-world-2015.csv"),
                show_col_types = FALSE)
tok <- dsvar_tokens()

# The poster's four regions, each in the palette colour nearest the poster's:
# Africa blue, the Americas green, Asia red, Europe yellow.
region_pal <- c(africa = dsvar_cat[[2]], americas = dsvar_cat[[1]],
                asia   = dsvar_cat[[3]], europe   = dsvar_cat[[7]])

# Gapminder's four income levels. The poster prints no numbers for them, so the
# cut-offs are measured off its pixels: one dashed line sits exactly on $8,000
# and the others are equal steps either side on the log axis, a factor of about
# 2.94 each. Each label goes in the middle of its band, as on the poster.
level_step  <- 2.94
level_lines <- 8000 * level_step^(-1:2)     # about $2,700, $8,000, $23,500, $69,000
level_mids  <- 8000 * level_step^(-1.5:1.5)

# Bubble AREA proportional to population, starting from zero, which is what
