# scale_size_area() does and what the poster does. Plain scale_size() rescales
# from the smallest country, adding a floor that makes 10 million look barely
# bigger than 1 million; the size key below would then be drawing a lie.
# scale_radius() would map radius instead and square the impression — the same
# trap as Nightingale. The chart and its key share this one scale, so the key's
# circles are the chart's circles. max_bubble is measured too: it makes the
# 1,000 million circle as wide, for the width of the chart, as the poster's
# (251 px of 3166).
max_bubble <- 31
pop_scale  <- scale_size_area(max_size = max_bubble,
                              limits = c(0, max(w15$population)), guide = "none")

# A few countries named, to anchor the cloud: the two giants, a spread of rich
# ones, the two ends, and the ones that sit far from the curve, like South
# Africa, which is about as rich as Brazil and lives thirteen years less.
# Every country gets a row here, most with an empty label, so the labels are
# pushed clear of all 193 bubbles and not only the eleven named ones. point.size
# is each bubble's drawn size, worked out the way pop_scale does it, so a label
# cannot land inside India or China. The names are the poster's.
named <- w15 |>
  mutate(label = case_match(country,
                            c("China", "India", "Japan", "Germany", "Russia",
                              "Brazil", "Nigeria", "South Africa", "Qatar") ~ country,
                            "United States" ~ "USA",
                            "Central African Republic" ~ "Central African Rep.",
                            .default = ""),
         drawn = max_bubble * sqrt(population / max(population)))

# A dark hairline round each bubble, as on the poster: a white one swallows the
# smallest countries whole, and shows nothing where two bubbles overlap.
bubbles <- ggplot(w15, aes(gdp_per_capita, life_expectancy)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = level_lines, linetype = "22",
             colour = tok$muted, linewidth = .35) +
  geom_point(aes(size = population, fill = region), shape = 21,
             colour = alpha(tok$ink, .45), stroke = .25, alpha = .85) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = named,
                           aes(gdp_per_capita, life_expectancy, label = label,
                               point.size = drawn),
                           inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3.1, family = dsvar_font(),
                           colour = tok$ink_2, seed = 4,
                           box.padding = .4, min.segment.length = 0,
                           max.overlaps = Inf, segment.size = .25,
                           segment.colour = "grey55",
                           bg.colour = tok$paper, bg.r = .12) +
  # The poster's frame, read off it like the levels: $574 to $144,000, widened
  # here to $150,000 so Macao ($148,000), which the poster leaves out, stays
  # in; 46.5 to 85 years. Breaks in doublings, as on the poster, which is what
  # puts $8,000 on a level line. The level names ride on a second axis along
  # the top, where the poster has them.
  scale_x_log10(breaks = 1000 * 2^(0:7), limits = c(574, 150000),
                expand = expansion(0), labels = scales::label_dollar(),
                sec.axis = dup_axis(name = NULL, breaks = level_mids,
                                    labels = paste("Level", 1:4))) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(50, 85, 5), limits = c(46.5, 85),
                     expand = expansion(0)) +
  pop_scale +
  scale_fill_manual(values = region_pal, guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Richer countries live longer, and the gain flattens out",
       subtitle = "Each bubble is a country. Dashed lines split income into Gapminder's four levels; note the log axis",
       x = "GDP per person (2011 dollars, adjusted for prices; log scale)",
       y = "Life expectancy (years)",
       caption = sprintf("n = %d countries, 2015 · Gapminder, data as of October 2016 · income levels measured off the poster",
                         nrow(w15))) +
  theme(axis.text.x.top = element_text(colour = tok$ink_3, face = "bold",
                                       size = rel(.85), margin = margin(b = 4)))

# THE KEY, after the poster's: a map that is the colour legend, and four
# circles that are the size legend. It is one ggplot in map coordinates
# (Robinson, in metres), with the row of circles placed under the map in the
# same units. Each country on the map takes its region from the data, so the
# map agrees with the bubbles (Russia and Turkey are Europe, Australia is Asia).
# The few Natural Earth shapes with no row, like Western Sahara and Taiwan,
# fall back on their UN region, with Oceania folded into Asia as Gapminder
# does. Antarctica has no region, so it goes.
fallback <- c(Africa = "africa", Americas = "americas", Asia = "asia",
              Europe = "europe", Oceania = "asia")
world <- sf::st_transform(rnaturalearth::countries110, "+proj=robin") |>
  left_join(transmute(w15, ADM0_A3 = toupper(geo), region), by = "ADM0_A3") |>
  mutate(region = coalesce(region, fallback[REGION_UN])) |>
  filter(!is.na(region))

bb <- sf::st_bbox(world)
w  <- bb$xmax - bb$xmin               # everything below is placed in map widths
size_key <- tibble(pop   = c(1, 10, 100, 1000) * 1e6,
                   label = c("1", "10", "100", "1,000"),
                   x     = bb$xmin + w * c(.04, .18, .36, .72))
y_head <- c(bb$ymax + .14 * w, bb$ymin - .07 * w)
y_row  <- bb$ymin - .42 * w
y_lab  <- bb$ymin - .74 * w

key <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = world, aes(fill = region), colour = NA) +
  annotate("text", x = bb$xmin, y = y_head, hjust = 0, vjust = 1,
           label = c("Colour by region", "Size by population, millions"),
           size = 3.2, fontface = "bold", colour = tok$ink_3,
           family = dsvar_font()) +
  geom_point(data = size_key, aes(x, y_row, size = pop), shape = 21,
             fill = tok$hairline, colour = tok$muted, stroke = .3) +
  geom_text(data = size_key, aes(x, y_lab, label = label), size = 3.1,
            colour = tok$ink_3, family = dsvar_font()) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = region_pal, guide = "none") +
  pop_scale +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(bb$xmin, bb$xmax), ylim = c(y_lab - .05 * w, y_head[1]),
           expand = FALSE, datum = NA, clip = "off") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = tok$surface, colour = tok$hairline,
                                       linewidth = .5),
        plot.margin = margin(10, 12, 10, 12))

# Into the empty lower right, where the poster puts it, over the last level
# line as on the poster. No country sits under it.
bubbles + patchwork::inset_element(key, left = .78, bottom = .03, right = .977,
                                   top = .55, align_to = "panel")












THE DECISION THE CHART RESTS ON

Take the log axis away and change nothing else.


Show the R code
# The transform has to be applied to the VALUE, not requested via scale_x_log10:
# a scale applies to the whole plot, so one facet cannot be log and the other
# linear. The first version of this figure used scale_x_log10 outside the facet
# and silently drew the identical linear panel twice.
both <- bind_rows(
  latest |> mutate(x = gdpPercap,        scale = "Linear income axis"),
  latest |> mutate(x = log10(gdpPercap), scale = "Log income axis")
) |> mutate(scale = factor(scale, levels = c("Linear income axis", "Log income axis")))

ggplot(both, aes(x, lifeExp, size = pop, fill = continent)) +
  geom_point(shape = 21, colour = "white", stroke = .25, alpha = .85) +
  facet_wrap(~scale, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_size(range = c(1, 11), guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cont_pal, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "GDP per person · left: dollars · right: log10(dollars)",
       y = "Life expectancy (years)",
       title = "Same 142 countries, same year, one axis changed",
       subtitle = "On the left almost every country is crushed against the axis; on the right the relationship appears",
       caption = sprintf("n = %d countries, %d · Gapminder", nrow(latest), max(gap$year))) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")











Show the R code
inc <- bind_rows(
  mutate(latest, how = "Income, linear", v = gdpPercap),
  mutate(latest, how = "Income, log10",  v = log10(gdpPercap))
) |> mutate(how = factor(how, levels = c("Income, linear", "Income, log10")))

ggplot(inc, aes(v)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = dsvar_accent(), colour = "white", linewidth = .2) +
  facet_wrap(~how, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Countries",
       title = "Why the log axis is not a trick",
       subtitle = "Income across countries is roughly log-normal; the transform is the shape of the variable, not a flattering choice",
       caption = sprintf("n = %d countries, %d", nrow(latest), max(gap$year)))











WHAT THE LOG AXIS GIVES AND TAKES

It gives a readable relationship, because income across countries is close to log-normal and the transform turns a wall of points into a line. It takes away your sense of absolute distance: on that axis the gap between $500 and $5,000 looks the same as the gap between $5,000 and $50,000, and those are not the same thing to live through. Both are true at once. State the axis, and expect readers to misjudge the dollars anyway.




WHAT THE ANIMATION WAS DOING

The famous version moves. Here the same fifth variable is drawn as small multiples, the static answer to animation.


Show the R code
ggplot(gap, aes(gdpPercap, lifeExp, size = pop, fill = continent)) +
  geom_point(shape = 21, colour = "white", stroke = .15, alpha = .8) +
  facet_wrap(~year, ncol = 6) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale())) +
  scale_size(range = c(.4, 5), guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cont_pal, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "GDP per person (log scale)", y = "Life expectancy (years)",
       title = "Every country moving up and to the right, 1952 to 2007",
       caption = sprintf("n = %d countries × 12 years · Gapminder", length(unique(gap$country)))) +
  theme_dsvar(base_size = 8.5) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")










The small multiples are better for anything you want to check: you can compare 1972 with 1992 by moving your eyes, which an animation makes impossible. The animation is better for the thing Rosling actually wanted, which was for you to feel a world in motion and abandon a category you had been carrying since school. Neither is the correct chart. They are answers to different questions, and only one of them can be argued with.




SOURCES


Original: Gapminder Foundation, gapminder.org. Data and tools CC BY 4.0. Rosling, H. (2006). The best stats you’ve ever seen, TED.
Data: Based on free material from GAPMINDER.ORG, CC-BY LICENSE. The recreation: Gapminder’s income (GDP per capita, 2011 PPP dollars), life expectancy and population for 2015, from the open-numbers repository pinned to its commit of 31 October 2016, the poster’s vintage; vendored as data/raw/gapminder-world-2015.csv. Everything else: Bryan, J. gapminder, an excerpt of the Gapminder data, 142 countries, 1952–2007; vendored as data/raw/gapminder.csv.
Map: Natural Earth country outlines at 1:110m, public domain, via the rnaturalearth package.
On area versus radius: see the Nightingale exhibit, where the same trap has a bigger consequence.
Reproduce it: every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: Two centuries of extreme poverty
text:
Gallery · The whole story · back to the gallery


Two centuries of extreme poverty

Two hundred years of the world’s population, split into the people living in extreme poverty and everyone else. It answers the objection a falling share always meets, that the world just got bigger, by drawing the count and the total together. It does not show how little is known about its left half.








THE ORIGINAL



“World population living in extreme poverty, 1820 to 2015”, Our World in Data, from the topic page Poverty by Joe Hasell, Bertha Rohenkohl, Pablo Arriagada, Esteban Ortiz-Ospina and Max Roser, OurWorldinData.org/poverty. Licensed CC BY 4.0; reproduced unaltered. Data: Ravallion (2016), updated with World Bank (2019), from Bourguignon & Morrisson (2002) and the World Bank.

The visualisation goes back to Martin Ravallion’s The Economics of Poverty (2016). Our World in Data redrew it and brought it up to 2015 from the same sources: Bourguignon and Morrisson’s reconstruction of the world income distribution for the years before 1981, and the World Bank’s household surveys after. It is one of the most shared charts Our World in Data has made, and one of the most argued over.


How to read it


 The red band is the number of people in extreme poverty: living on less than $1.90 a day, in dollars adjusted for prices in each country and for inflation.


 The green band is everyone else. It is stacked on the red, so the top edge of the chart is the whole world population.


 Only the red band starts from zero. Read the green as the distance between the two edges, not as a height.


 The two halves are measured differently. Before 1981 the numbers are reconstructed from historical GDP; from 1981 they come from household surveys. The chart draws them as one surface.





THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

A stacked area from 1820 to 2015, red under green, on an axis from 0 to 8 billion. The total climbs from 1.1 to 7.3 billion. The red band grows slowly to about 1.9 billion around 1980, then falls to 0.7 billion. Both bands are labelled at the right; the subtitle defines the poverty line; the footer names the sources and links to a page on their limits.



02 · Analyse

Two counts, stacked, so position on a common scale works for the red band and the total, and the green band is only a difference. Nothing marks where the data is: 10 estimates between 1820 and 1980, joined by straight lines across gaps of up to forty years, then a point every year or three from 1981. The change of method at 1981 is invisible, and so is any uncertainty. The red is the conventional colour for a bad thing and the green for a good one, which tells the reader which way to feel before they read a number.



03 · Interpret

The claim is that for most of modern history most people were extremely poor, that their number kept rising until about 1980, and that it has since fallen by more than half while the world population kept growing. Share and count are both on the page: in 1820 the red band is 89% of the total, in 2015 10%. The design choice that matters is showing counts: the decline cannot be explained away by a bigger denominator.



04 · Judge

A whole-story chart that earns the name: the outcome, the population it belongs to, and two centuries, in one picture with direct labels and a zero baseline. Its weakness is that it is equally confident everywhere. The left half rests on 10 reconstructions from historical GDP, and Our World in Data’s own methods page says “there are substantial questions that introduce uncertainty which need to be taken seriously”. The result also depends on the line: $1.90 a day is very low, and Our World in Data’s current charts use the World Bank’s newer $3 line. A chart that marked its data points and its seam would make the same argument and say how much of it is measured.





THE RECREATION

From Our World in Data’s own data, in its house style, at the original’s proportions.


Show the R code
serif <- c(intersect(c("Playfair Display", "Georgia"), systemfonts::system_fonts()$family), "serif")[1]
sans  <- c(intersect(c("Lato", "Helvetica", "Arial"), systemfonts::system_fonts()$family), "sans")[1]
red_fill   <- "#913d45"; red_ink   <- "#760d17"   # sampled off the original
green_fill <- "#368960"; green_ink <- "#046c38"
grey_ink   <- "#5b5b5b"

stack <- pov |>
  select(year, poor, not_poor) |>
  pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "who", values_to = "n") |>
  mutate(who = factor(who, c("not_poor", "poor")))   # poor drawn at the bottom

labels <- tibble(
  y   = c(4e9, .6e9),
  lab = c("Number of people\nnot in extreme\npoverty", "Number of people\nliving in extreme\npoverty"),
  col = c(green_ink, red_ink))

recreation <- ggplot(stack, aes(year, n, fill = who)) +
  geom_area(position = "stack", colour = NA) +
  geom_text(data = labels, aes(x = 2018, y = y, label = lab), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            colour = labels$col, hjust = 0, lineheight = .95, size = 4.3, family = sans) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(poor = red_fill, not_poor = green_fill), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1820, 1850, 1900, 1950, 2015), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 8e9, 1e9), limits = c(0, 8.05e9), expand = c(0, 0),
                     labels = \(x) if_else(x == 0, "0", paste(x / 1e9, "billion"))) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(title = paste0("World population living in extreme poverty ",
                      "<span style='font-family:\"", sans, "\"; color:#767676; font-size:15pt'>",
                      "1820 to 2015</span>"),
       subtitle = paste("Extreme poverty is defined as living on less than 1.90 international-$ per day.",
                        "International-$ are adjusted for price differences between countries and for price changes over time (inflation).",
                        sep = "\n"),
       x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = "**Data source:** Ravallion (2016) updated with World Bank (2019)<br>**Note:** Recreated in ggplot from Our World in Data's own series; the original links to a page on the strengths and limitations of this data.") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = sans, base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
        plot.title = ggtext::element_markdown(family = serif, face = "bold", size = 21,
                                              colour = "#2d2e2d", margin = margin(b = 6)),
        plot.title.position = "plot",
        plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = grey_ink, size = 11.6, lineheight = 1.15,
                                     margin = margin(b = 14)),
        plot.caption = ggtext::element_markdown(colour = "#767676", hjust = 0, size = 9.6,
                                                lineheight = 1.3, margin = margin(t = 12)),
        plot.caption.position = "plot",
        panel.grid.major.y = element_line(colour = "#dddddd", linetype = "33", linewidth = .4),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        axis.text = element_text(colour = grey_ink, size = 12),
        axis.line.x = element_line(colour = "#999999", linewidth = .4),
        axis.ticks.x = element_line(colour = "#999999", linewidth = .4),
        plot.margin = margin(16, 140, 10, 16))

recreation










n = 25 years, 10 of them before 1981. The two bands add up to the world population in every year. Our World in Data’s logo and CC BY stamp are left off: this is our drawing of their data, not their chart.




Original · Our World in Data





Ours · ggplot















HOW WE KNOW

The data is the chart’s own. Our World in Data publishes the numbers behind every chart as a CSV next to it, and that file is what this page draws. Its metadata names the sources and the date it was last changed, 1 February 2019. The series is frozen there: the poverty line is the $1.90 of 2011 prices, which the World Bank has since replaced twice.
Two kinds of number, one surface. Our World in Data’s methods page explains that the estimates before 1981 come from Bourguignon and Morrisson’s “reconstruction of the global income distribution using the Maddison Project’s database of historical GDP per capita series”, and the later ones from household surveys collected by the World Bank. The file has both a 1980 and a 1981 value, one from each:


Show the R code
pov |>
  filter(year %in% 1970:1984) |>
  transmute(year, source,
            `in extreme poverty (bn)` = round(poor / 1e9, 3),
            `world population (bn)`   = round(total / 1e9, 3),
            share = scales::percent(share, .1)) |>
  knitr::kable()

The two methods meet almost exactly, a sign that the joining was done with care. That does not make the left half as well measured as the right.



THE SAME NUMBERS, OTHER CHOICES


Where the estimates are


Show the R code
ggplot(pov, aes(year, poor / 1e9)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 1815, xmax = 1980.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = p$hairline, alpha = .55) +
  annotate("text", x = 1822, y = 2.25, hjust = 0, size = 3.2, family = dsvar_font(),
           colour = p$ink_3, label = "Reconstructed from historical GDP\n(Bourguignon & Morrisson 2002)") +
  annotate("text", x = 1985, y = 2.25, hjust = 0, size = 3.2, family = dsvar_font(),
           colour = p$ink_3, label = "Household surveys\n(World Bank)") +
  geom_line(colour = p$ink_3, linewidth = .5, linetype = "22") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = source), size = 2.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(reconstruction = p$ink_2, surveys = dsvar_accent()), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1820, 1850, 1900, 1950, 1981, 2015), expand = expansion(add = c(5, 3))) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 2.5), breaks = seq(0, 2.5, .5),
                     labels = \(x) paste(x, "bn"), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(title = sprintf("%d estimates cover the first 160 years; from 1981 there is one every year or three",
                       n_reconstructed),
       subtitle = "People living in extreme poverty ($1.90 a day), with every point the series actually contains. Dashes join them",
       x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = "Our World in Data, after Ravallion (2016), Bourguignon & Morrisson (2002) and the World Bank")










The same red band as a line, with its data points drawn and the change of method shaded. The shape is the same, but now the reader can see that the slow rise of the nineteenth century is ten numbers, each built from a country’s GDP and an assumed distribution, and that the steep fall after 1990 is measured year by year.



The share instead of the count


Show the R code
ggplot(pov, aes(year, share)) +
  geom_area(fill = dsvar_accent(), alpha = .18) +
  geom_line(colour = dsvar_accent(), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(colour = dsvar_accent(), size = 1.6) +
  annotate("text", x = first$year + 2, y = first$share + .06, hjust = 0, size = 3.4,
           family = dsvar_font(), colour = p$ink_2,
           label = sprintf("%d: %.0f%%", first$year, 100 * first$share)) +
  annotate("text", x = last$year - 1, y = .035, hjust = 1, size = 3.4,
           family = dsvar_font(), colour = p$ink_2,
           label = sprintf("%d: %.0f%%", last$year, 100 * last$share)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1820, 1850, 1900, 1950, 2015), expand = expansion(add = c(3, 3))) +
  labs(title = sprintf("As a share, the fall runs the whole two centuries: from %.0f%% of the world to %.0f%%",
                       100 * first$share, 100 * last$share),
       subtitle = "Share of the world population living in extreme poverty ($1.90 a day)",
       x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = "The same file: people in extreme poverty divided by the two bands' total")










As a share, poverty has been falling since the first estimate; as a count, it rose for 160 years and has fallen for 35. Both are true. Which one a chart shows decides whether the industrial revolution looks like the start of the decline or a long prelude to it, and the original is the rare chart that shows both at once.


A whole-story chart is a promise to show everything that matters at once: the thing, its denominator, and enough time to see the change. This one keeps the promise about the numbers and breaks it about the evidence. The fix is cheap: draw the points, mark the seam, and the same chart tells the reader where it is sure.





SOURCES


Original: Our World in Data, “World population living in extreme poverty, 1820 to 2015”, in Hasell, J., Rohenkohl, B., Arriagada, P., Ortiz-Ospina, E., & Roser, M. (2022). Poverty. OurWorldinData.org/poverty. CC BY 4.0, checked against the chart’s own stamp and Our World in Data’s FAQ, 9 October 2026.
The visualisation it updates: Ravallion, M. (2016). The Economics of Poverty: History, Measurement, and Policy. Oxford University Press.
Data: Our World in Data’s series for the chart, from Bourguignon, F., & Morrisson, C. (2002). Inequality among world citizens: 1820–1992. American Economic Review, 92(4), 727–744; and the World Bank’s PovcalNet, now the Poverty and Inequality Platform (CC BY 4.0). Cited as Ravallion, Bourguignon and Morrisson, and World Bank (2019) – processed by Our World in Data. Vendored as data/raw/owid-extreme-poverty-1820-2015.csv.
On the methods: Hasell, J., & Roser, M. (2019). How do we know the history of extreme poverty? OurWorldinData.org/extreme-history-methods.
Reproduce it: every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: Du Bois’s data portraits
text:
Gallery · Comparison & ranking · back to the gallery


Du Bois’s data portraits

In 1900 W. E. B. Du Bois and his students at Atlanta University, a historically Black university, drew some sixty charts of Black life in America, by hand, for the Paris Exposition. They were made to answer the racist “science” of the day with evidence. This one makes the case in ten bars: one generation after slavery, Black Americans were already less illiterate than the people of several European nations.








THE ORIGINAL



Illiteracy of the American Negroes compared with that of other nations, from A series of statistical charts illustrating the condition of the descendants of former African slaves now in residence in the United States of America. W. E. B. Du Bois and students of Atlanta University, for the Exhibit of American Negroes, Exposition Universelle, Paris, 1900. Ink and watercolour on board. Library of Congress, Daniel Murray collection (LCCN 2014645352). Public domain in the United States (published 1900); scan via Wikimedia Commons, shown at half its resolution.

The charts were made for the American section of the 1900 Exposition, in the Library of Congress’s words “to show the economic and social progress of African Americans since emancipation.” That purpose was a reply to the racist writing of the period, which dressed itself in statistics: in 1896 the American Economic Association published Frederick Hoffman’s Race Traits and Tendencies of the American Negro, which argued that Black Americans had declined since emancipation and were headed for extinction. Du Bois, a sociologist trained in statistics, took its methods apart in a review the following year. The Paris charts answered the same kind of claim with better data, drawn by Black students, in front of the world.
There were two sets of charts: one on Georgia, and this one on the United States as a whole. Every caption is in English and French, because the audience was in Paris. The pencilled “P 1124” and “[47]” on the board are later catalogue marks, not part of the chart.


How to read it


 Each bar is one population, and its length is the share who could not read or write. Longer is worse.


 The red bar is Black Americans. Every green bar is a nation, labelled in French: Roumanie is Romania, Servie Serbia, Russie Russia, Hongrie Hungary, Autriche Austria, Suède Sweden. Ireland is left in English.


 The bars are ranked, longest at the top, so the position of the red bar is the finding: fourth of ten.


 There is no scale and no number anywhere on the board, and no year. You can read only which bar is longer, and by how much relative to another.


 “Negroes” is the plate’s own word, the standard term in 1900. This page says Black Americans, except when quoting the plate.





THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

Ten horizontal bars on a cream board, starting from a common left edge and ranked from longest at the top to a sliver at the bottom. Nine are green and carry the names of nations in French; one, fourth from the top, is red and reads “Negroes, U. S. A.” The title sits above in English and French, with “Done by Atlanta University.” No numbers, no axis, no source.



02 · Analyse

Length from a common baseline, the strongest channel after position, and the only one in use. The bars are sorted by value, so rank reads instantly. Colour is spent once, on one category, and red against green finds the eye before anything is read. With no scale, the reader can compare only ranks and ratios, never levels: the chart says less than Russia, not how many.



03 · Interpret

An argument against racism, made as a ranking. The question racist writers asked about Black Americans in 1900, wanting the answer to be no, was whether they could advance at all. Under slavery, teaching an enslaved person to read had been a crime in most of the slave states. Thirty-five years after emancipation, this chart answers: Black Americans are already less illiterate than the people of Romania, Serbia and Russia, and level with Hungary. Shown in Paris, it places them among the nations its audience counted as peers.



04 · Judge

A masterpiece, as argument and as craft: a true common baseline, bars in consistent proportion, colour spent on exactly one thing. The choice of company is not a trick: it answers the racist question of its day with the comparison that question deserved, nations rather than a hierarchy of races. Its one weakness is the missing scale; printed numbers would have made the case even harder to wave away. The gap with white Americans, which the chart does not draw, was imposed by law and by segregated schooling, and the last chart on this page shows how quickly it narrowed.





THE RECREATION

The bars below are drawn from the measured values, not traced: each length is its share of illiteracy times one fixed number of pixels per point. The colours are read off the scan.


Show the R code
serif <- c(intersect(c("Hoefler Text", "Baskerville", "Georgia"),
                     systemfonts::system_fonts()$family), "serif")[1]

# Colours sampled from the scan: the average of each kind of watercolour.
in_bars <- function(want_red) {
  b <- filter(bars, red == want_red)
  idx <- unlist(map(seq_len(nrow(b)), \(i) {
    rr <- b$top[i]:b$bottom[i]; cc <- b$left[i]:b$right[i]
    as.vector(outer(rr, (cc - 1) * nrow(R), `+`))
  }))
  idx <- idx[paint[idx]]
  rgb(mean(R[idx]), mean(G[idx]), mean(B[idx]))
}
board  <- rgb(mean(R[1500:1560, 300:900]), mean(G[1500:1560, 300:900]), mean(B[1500:1560, 300:900]))
ink    <- "#3b3631"
green  <- in_bars(FALSE)
red    <- in_bars(TRUE)

# Pixel space of the half-resolution scan, y flipped so the top is up.
H <- nrow(R); W <- ncol(R); px_per_point <- plate$px[plate$red] / ANCHOR
x0 <- median(bars$left)

recreation <- ggplot(plate) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = x0, xmax = x0 + pct * px_per_point,
                ymin = H - bottom, ymax = H - top, fill = red),
            colour = ink, linewidth = .2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = green, `TRUE` = red), guide = "none") +
  annotate("segment", x = x0, xend = x0, y = H - 400, yend = 0 + 60,
           colour = "#cfc6b5", linewidth = .3) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 52, y = H - (top + bottom) / 2, label = label),
            hjust = 0, family = serif, size = 3, colour = ink) +
  annotate("text", x = W / 2, y = H - 98, family = serif, size = 4.1, colour = ink,
           label = "Illiteracy of the American Negroes compared with that of other nations.") +
  annotate("text", x = W / 2, y = H - 158, family = serif, size = 2.6, colour = ink,
           label = "Proportion d' illettrés parmi les Nègres Americains comparée à celle des autres nations.") +
  annotate("text", x = W / 2, y = H - 213, family = serif, size = 2.2, colour = ink,
           label = "Done by Atlanta University.") +
  annotate("segment", x = W / 2 + c(-90, -90), xend = W / 2 + c(90, 90),
           y = H - c(128, 186), yend = H - c(128, 186), colour = "#b9b0a0", linewidth = .25) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, W), ylim = c(0, H), expand = FALSE) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = board, colour = NA))

recreation










Ten bars, as measured off the scan below. Drawn at the plate’s proportions so the two can be set side by side. The title is set in a period serif; the original’s lettering is the student draughtsman’s.




Original · Du Bois and Atlanta University, 1900





Ours · ggplot













Side by side, at the same size. The bar ends are the data. The wobble of the watercolour, and the fact that no two of the original bars are quite the same height, are not.




HOW WE KNOW

The bar lengths. A chart with no scale has to be measured. The code finds every pixel of green or red watercolour on the board, groups them into the ten bands, and measures each band from the shared left edge to where the paint stops. Nothing is typed in.


Show the R code
plate |>
  transmute(bar = label, `length (px)` = px,
            `relative to the red bar` = round(ratio, 3)) |>
  knitr::kable()

From lengths to percentages. The plate gives only ratios, so one number has to come from outside it. Black Americans’ illiteracy in the 1890 census series was 56.8 per cent, and setting the red bar to that value puts every other bar on the same scale. If Du Bois’s students worked from a slightly different figure, every value below moves by the same proportion, and the ranking does not move at all.


Show the R code
# Anthony Starks measured the same bars on the printed reproduction in
# Battle-Baptiste & Rusert (2018), in centimetres, against the same anchor
# (dubois-data-portraits, plate 47, CC BY-NC 4.0).
starks <- c(72.9363, 72.2908, 72.2908, 56.8, 55.509, 43.8909,
            34.8545, 25.1727, 12.9091, 0.645454)

plate |>
  transmute(bar = english,
            `ours, from the scan` = round(pct, 1),

Two measurements, made from different reproductions with different tools, agree to within 0.7 points on every bar. That is the best evidence available that the board was drawn to scale, not by eye.



WHY THE COMPARISON MATTERED


The plate, with its numbers


Show the R code
plate |>
  mutate(who = fct_reorder(english, pct)) |>
  ggplot(aes(pct, who, fill = red)) +
  geom_col(width = .68) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.0f%%", pct)), hjust = -.15, size = 3.4,
            family = dsvar_font(), colour = p$ink_2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = dsvar_accent(), `TRUE` = "#b3122e"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 82), breaks = seq(0, 80, 20),
                     labels = \(x) paste0(x, "%"), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .02))) +
  labs(title = "One generation after slavery, already among the nations of Europe",
       subtitle = "Share unable to read or write: the plate's bars as measured, given the scale it left off",
       x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = "Bars measured from the scan, anchored on the 1890 census figure for Black Americans (56.8%).") +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = p$hairline, linewidth = .35))










The same ranking, with the numbers the board leaves off. Printing them costs the chart nothing it needs and lets anyone check it, which an argument against prejudice should welcome.



The distance travelled


Show the R code
gap <- nces |> filter(year %in% c(1870, 1930)) |> mutate(gap = black - white)

nces |>
  pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "group", values_to = "pct") |>
  mutate(group = if_else(group == "black", "Black Americans", "White Americans")) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, pct, colour = group)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 1897, xmax = 1903, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = p$hairline, alpha = .6) +
  annotate("text", x = 1900, y = 92, label = "the Paris\nExposition", size = 3,
           lineheight = .9, family = dsvar_font(), colour = p$ink_3) +
  # the gap, at both ends
  annotate("segment", x = gap$year, xend = gap$year, y = gap$white + 1.5, yend = gap$black - 1.5,
           colour = p$ink_3, linewidth = .4, arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(1.6, "mm"))) +
  annotate("text", x = gap$year + c(1.2, -1.2), y = (gap$white + gap$black) / 2,
           hjust = c(0, 1), size = 3.1, family = dsvar_font(), colour = p$ink_3,
           label = sprintf("gap: %.0f points", gap$gap)) +
  annotate("text", x = 1871.5, y = 84, hjust = 0, size = 3.1, family = dsvar_font(),
           colour = "#b3122e", lineheight = .95,
           label = "Five years after emancipation. Under slavery,\nteaching an enslaved person to read was a crime") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) + geom_point(size = 2.3) +
  geom_text(data = \(d) filter(d, year == 1930), aes(label = group),
            hjust = -.08, family = dsvar_font(), fontface = "bold", size = 3.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#b3122e", p$ink_3), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1870, 1930, 10), expand = expansion(mult = c(.02, .2))) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 95), labels = \(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(title = sprintf("Illiteracy among Black Americans fell from %.0f%% to %.0f%% in sixty years",
                       nces$black[nces$year == 1870], nces$black[nces$year == 1930]),
       subtitle = "Share unable to read or write, by census year",
       x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = "NCES (1993), 120 Years of American Education, table 6. Its series is 'Black and other races'.")










Literacy is learned, not inherited. A population that had been barred by law from learning to read went from four in five unable to read to one in six within a single lifetime, through schools that were segregated and starved of money. The gap with white Americans was imposed, and it narrowed from 68 points to 13 as schooling became possible. Du Bois’s ranking shows where Black Americans stood in 1900; this line shows how far they had already come, against everything put in their way. The ranking is week 2’s form, the line week 5’s.


Every comparison answers “compared to what?”, and the answer is a decision. Du Bois made his deliberately, as an argument against racism: he measured Black Americans against nations rather than against a racial hierarchy, and showed that they already stood among them. Most charts make the same choice silently, by which rows they include. Make yours openly, as he did, and know what it says.





SOURCES


Original: W. E. B. Du Bois and Atlanta University (1900). Illiteracy of the American Negroes compared with that of other nations. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs, Daniel Murray collection, LCCN 2014645352. Public domain in the US; scan via Wikimedia Commons.
The collection in print: Battle-Baptiste, W., & Rusert, B. (Eds.) (2018). W. E. B. Du Bois’s Data Portraits: Visualizing Black America. Princeton Architectural Press.
What the exhibit answered: Hoffman, F. L. (1896). Race Traits and Tendencies of the American Negro. Publications of the American Economic Association, 11(1–3). Du Bois’s review: Du Bois, W. E. B. (1897). The Annals of the American Academy of Political and Social Science, 9, 127–133. doi:10.1177/000271629700900108.
The cross-check: Starks, A. dubois-data-portraits, plate 47, GitHub (CC BY-NC 4.0).
The anchor and the trend: Snyder, T. D. (Ed.) (1993). 120 Years of American Education: A Statistical Portrait, table 6. National Center for Education Statistics, via NCES.
Reproduce it: every value on this page is measured from the scan by the code shown above it.

title: Conditional effects
text:
Gallery · Distribution & uncertainty · back to the gallery


Conditional effects

The plot you reach for when an effect is supposed to depend on something else. It comes in two flavours (sample the moderator at three points, or draw the effect across all of it), and they lead readers to different conclusions from the same model. This one is from my own data, and the choices below are ones I actually had to make.








THE ORIGINAL



Figure 3 from Masur, P. K., & Parry, D. A. (2026). When sharing becomes the norm: How disclosure prevalence and relational similarity shape social norms on social media. Technology, Mind, and Behavior. © American Psychological Association; reproduced here by one of its authors for teaching. Data: osf.io/zw6pb.

Study 1 sat participants in front of a simulated social feed in which the share of personal disclosures was high or low, and afterwards asked them what they thought was normal on that platform and how likely they were to post something personal themselves. The question the figure answers is whether that chain runs differently for people who felt similar to the others in the feed.


How to read it


 The x axis is the moderator: felt similarity, mean-centred, so 0 is the average participant.


 The y axis is an effect, not an outcome: the slope you would get if you ran the analysis on people at that value of the moderator. That is what makes the genre hard: every point on the line is a whole regression coefficient.


 The horizontal dashed line is zero, i.e. no effect. Where the ribbon crosses it, the effect is no longer distinguishable from nothing.


 The vertical dashed line is the Johnson–Neyman point: the value of the moderator at which the interval first excludes zero. Teal to the right of it, red to the left: significant, then not.


 Panels A–C are the visual-disclosure route, D–F the written one: the effect of the feed on what people think is normal (path a), the effect of that perception on their own intention (path b), and the indirect effect, the two multiplied.





THE RECREATION

The top row of the original, rebuilt from the open data in ggplot. Two changes: the x axis carries the raw 1–7 similarity scale rather than the centred one, because “similarity = 0” is not a thing a reader can picture, and the significant/not split is stated in the legend rather than left to be inferred from two colours.


Show the R code
# The indirect effect is a product of two estimated slopes, so its interval is
# not a delta-method sum. Percentile bootstrap: resample participants, refit
# both equations, multiply, and read the quantiles off the 1000 curves.
set.seed(2026)
boot <- replicate(1000, {
  s  <- d1[sample.int(nrow(d1), replace = TRUE), ]
  fa <- lm(norm ~ prev_vis * sim_c + prev_wri, data = s)
  fb <- lm(intention ~ norm * sim_c + inj + prev_vis + prev_wri, data = s)
  (coef(fa)[["prev_vis"]] + coef(fa)[["prev_vis:sim_c"]] * w_grid) *
  (coef(fb)[["norm"]]     + coef(fb)[["norm:sim_c"]]     * w_grid)
})

panels <- c(
  "A · Path a: effect of the feed on what people think is normal",
  "B · Path b: effect of that perception on their own intention",
  "C · a × b: the indirect effect of the feed on intention")

ce <- bind_rows(
  cond_effect(m_a, "prev_vis", "prev_vis:sim_c", w_grid) |> mutate(panel = panels[1]),
  cond_effect(m_b, "norm",     "norm:sim_c",     w_grid) |> mutate(panel = panels[2]),
  tibble(w   = w_grid,
         est = (coef(m_a)[["prev_vis"]] + coef(m_a)[["prev_vis:sim_c"]] * w_grid) *
               (coef(m_b)[["norm"]]     + coef(m_b)[["norm:sim_c"]]     * w_grid),
         lwr = apply(boot, 1, quantile, .025),
         upr = apply(boot, 1, quantile, .975),
         panel = panels[3])
) |>
  mutate(panel      = factor(panel, levels = panels),
         similarity = w + mean_sim,
         sig = if_else(lwr > 0 | upr < 0, "95% CI excludes zero", "95% CI includes zero"))

# The Johnson-Neyman point is simply where that label changes.
jn <- ce |>
  group_by(panel) |>
  filter(sig != lag(sig, default = first(sig))) |>
  slice(1) |>
  ungroup()

pal_sig <- c("95% CI excludes zero" = dsvar_cat[1],
             "95% CI includes zero" = dsvar_cat[3])

ggplot(ce, aes(similarity, est)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = .4, colour = dsvar_light$hairline) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr, fill = sig), alpha = .16) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = sig, group = 1), linewidth = .9) +
  geom_vline(data = jn, aes(xintercept = similarity), linetype = "22",
             linewidth = .4, colour = dsvar_light$muted) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free_y", labeller = label_wrap_gen(34)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_sig, name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal_sig, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Felt similarity to the people in the feed (1–7)",
       y = "Conditional effect") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")










n = 589 participants. Path a from norm ~ prevalence * similarity, path b from intention ~ norm * similarity, both holding the written-disclosure manipulation constant and path b also holding the injunctive norm constant. Ribbons are 95% intervals: delta method for a and b, 1000-sample percentile bootstrap for the product. Dashed verticals mark the Johnson–Neyman points.



CHECKED AGAINST THE PUBLISHED FIGURE

The shapes match and the moderation is the same in sign and size, but the recreation sits a little higher than the printed panels and its cut points sit further left. Published panel A runs from about 2.26 down to 1.06 across the similarity range; ours runs from 2.65 to 1.49: the same −0.2 per scale point, shifted up. Published panel B turns significant at about −1.6 centred; ours at about −2.2. The paper applies exclusions derived from participants’ browsing logs which are not in the open file, so our 589 is the larger sample. Nothing in the conclusion moves, but the Johnson–Neyman point does, by most of a scale point. The cut point is the least stable number on the whole figure, and it is the one readers quote.




THE SAME MODERATION, PICK-A-POINT

The other way to draw this. Instead of the effect at every value of the moderator, choose a few values (by convention the mean and one standard deviation either side) and plot the ordinary outcome-by-condition picture once per value. It uses the same model and the same data, and estimates nothing new.


Show the R code
pts <- c(-sd_sim, 0, sd_sim)
lab <- c("low similarity (−1 SD)", "average similarity", "high similarity (+1 SD)")

# Predicted norm perception in each feed, at each of the three chosen values.
pap <- expand_grid(prev_vis = 0:1, sim_c = pts) |>
  mutate(prev_wri = mean(d1$prev_wri))
pap <- bind_cols(pap, as_tibble(predict(m_a, pap, interval = "confidence"))) |>
  mutate(level = factor(lab[match(sim_c, pts)], levels = lab),
         feed  = factor(if_else(prev_vis == 1, "many personal posts", "few personal posts"),
                        levels = levels(d1$feed)))

# The slope of each of those three lines is one conditional effect.
slopes <- cond_effect(m_a, "prev_vis", "prev_vis:sim_c", pts) |>
  mutate(level = factor(lab, levels = lab), similarity = w + mean_sim)
curve_a <- cond_effect(m_a, "prev_vis", "prev_vis:sim_c", w_grid) |>
  mutate(similarity = w + mean_sim)

pal3 <- setNames(dsvar_ramp_light[c(1, 3, 5)], lab)

p_pap <- ggplot(pap, aes(feed, fit, colour = level, group = level)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .9) +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), linewidth = .9, alpha = .45) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal3, name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(1, 7)) +
  labs(title = "Pick-a-point",
       subtitle = "The moderator sampled at three values",
       x = "Feed the participant browsed", y = "Perceived norm (1–7)") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

p_curve <- ggplot(curve_a, aes(similarity, est)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), fill = dsvar_cat[1], alpha = .14) +
  geom_line(colour = dsvar_cat[1], linewidth = .9) +
  geom_linerange(data = slopes, aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr, colour = level),
                 linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(data = slopes, aes(colour = level), size = 2.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal3, guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "… are three points on this curve",
       subtitle = "Panel A again, with those three values marked",
       x = "Felt similarity (1–7)",
       y = "Effect of the feed on perceived norm")

p_pap + p_curve










Left: predicted perceived norm from m_a, with the written-disclosure manipulation held at its sample mean; vertical bars are 95% intervals on the prediction. Right: panel A of the recreation, with the three chosen values of the moderator marked. The three slopes on the left are the three points on the right: 2.11, 1.87 and 1.62 scale points.




WHICH ONE TO DRAW




What pick-a-point gets right

Its y axis is a quantity the reader already understands, a score on the scale the study measured, so it can be checked against the data and against common sense. It shows the size of the thing: the feed moves perceived norms by roughly two points on a seven-point scale at every level of similarity, which is large, and the moderation shrinks it by a quarter of a point, which is not. Three near-parallel lines are an honest picture of that.



What pick-a-point hides

The three values are a choice, and the plot does not admit it. ±1 SD is a convention, not a fact about the moderator; on a skewed or bounded moderator the “high” line can sit at a value almost nobody scored. Worse, the picture is unfalsifiable at a glance: three lines that are not quite parallel look like a moderation whether the interaction is significant or noise, which is exactly how a small wobble gets promoted into a finding.



What the conditional-effect plot gets right

It stops choosing. The whole moderator range is on the page, the interval is drawn everywhere, and the reader can see that path a is comfortably non-zero across the entire scale while path b is not. It is also the only one of the two that makes the uncertainty in the interaction visible: the ribbon fans out towards the ends of the scale, where there are few participants, and that fanning is the honest reason not to extrapolate.



What it hides: the significance-region trap

Colouring the line by whether the interval excludes zero invites the reading that the effect switches on at the cut point. It does not. Nothing happens at similarity 2.8; an interval that just includes zero and one that just excludes it are the same estimate with a rounding error between them. And as the check above shows, moving that cut point by most of a scale point took nothing more than a different exclusion rule. Draw the ribbon; be very careful about quoting the number where it crosses.



The verdict

Draw both, in this order. Pick-a-point first, because it answers “how big, on what scale” and keeps the reader anchored to the measurement. The conditional-effect plot second, because it answers “does this hold everywhere” and shows the uncertainty the first one leaves out. Neither is a substitute for the other, and a paper that shows only the second (which is most of them) has told you where an effect is significant without ever telling you how large it is.





WHAT THE MODEL ACTUALLY SAYS



Show the R code
bind_rows(
  broom::tidy(m_a, conf.int = TRUE) |> mutate(equation = "Path a · norm"),
  broom::tidy(m_b, conf.int = TRUE) |> mutate(equation = "Path b · intention")
) |>
  filter(str_detect(term, ":")) |>
  transmute(Equation = equation,
            `Interaction term` = str_replace_all(term, c("prev_vis" = "prevalence",
                                                         "sim_c"    = "similarity",
                                                         "norm"     = "perceived norm")),
            estimate = round(estimate, 3),
            `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", conf.low, conf.high),
            p = round(p.value, 3)) |>
  knitr::kable()












Equation
Interaction term
estimate
95% CI
p




Path a · norm
prevalence:similarity
-0.193
[-0.36, -0.02]

Path b · intention
perceived norm:similarity

Both interactions are real but small. The feed’s effect on perceived norms weakens by 0.19 scale points per point of similarity, against a main effect of 1.87, so over the whole observed range the effect shrinks from about 2.6 to 1.5, and never comes close to vanishing. That is the number the pick-a-point panel puts in front of you and the conditional-effect panel makes you infer from an axis of slopes.


THE SENTENCE TO AVOID

“The effect of the feed was significant only for participants high in similarity.” Look at panel A: it is significant everywhere, and it is stronger for participants low in similarity. The sentence is about path b, where the cut point lives, and even there it means “our sample was too small to resolve a small effect down at that end of the scale”, not “the effect is absent there”. A conditional-effect plot is a map of what this study could detect, not of where the effect exists.




THE RULE THIS CASE EXISTS FOR


A conditional-effects plot is a picture of a model, not of the world. Put the effect size on a scale the reader can hold (pick-a-point), then put the uncertainty everywhere it goes, across the whole moderator (the conditional-effect curve). Show one without the other and you have either a moderation nobody can falsify or a cut point nobody should quote.




SOURCES


Study and data: Masur, P. K., & Parry, D. A. (2026). When sharing becomes the norm. Technology, Mind, and Behavior. Materials and data: osf.io/zw6pb, CC BY 4.0; download the data there; this site does not serve its own copy. The original figure is Figure 3; this page recreates panels A–C.
The method: Johnson, P. O., & Neyman, J. (1936). Tests of certain linear hypotheses and their application to some educational problems. Statistical Research Memoirs, 1, 57–93. Modern treatment: Hayes, A. F. (2022). Introduction to Mediation, Moderation, and Conditional Process Analysis (3rd ed.), ch. 12.
On drawing the interval: Wilke, C. O. (2019). Fundamentals of Data Visualization, ch. 16, “Visualizing uncertainty”.
Reproduce it: Rscript R/fetch-gallery-data.R pulls the study data; every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: The Bible’s cross-references
text:
Gallery · Relationships & structure · back to the gallery


The Bible’s cross-references

Sixty-three thousand arcs over a bar chart of the Bible’s 1,189 chapters. Its makers say they aimed for something more beautiful than functional, and they got it. The arc diagram is the right form for it, for a reason one of them gives on the same page: the chapters come in an order.








THE ORIGINAL



Bible Cross-References, Chris Harrison and Christoph Römhild, 2007. © Chris Harrison, all rights reserved; chrisharrison.net. Shown at the low resolution the author’s own page serves, under the Dutch citation right (Auteurswet art. 15a), because this page is a critique of it. Not reusable from here.

Christoph Römhild, a Lutheran pastor, had assembled a digital set of the cross-references found in the King James Bible, the links that some editions print in their margins, and asked Chris Harrison to draw it. Harrison’s page says what they were after:

“The pastor and I struggled to find an elegant solution to render the data – 63,779 cross references in total. We set our sights on something more beautiful than functional. At the same time, we wanted a visualization that honored and revealed the complexity of the Bible at every level – as one leans in, smaller details should become visible.”



How to read it


 The bars along the bottom are the chapters, Genesis 1 on the far left to Revelation 22 on the far right. Each bar’s length is the number of verses. The very long one is Psalm 119.


 Books alternate light and dark grey. The two white stretches are Genesis and Matthew, where the Old and New Testaments begin.


 Each arc is one cross-reference between two chapters. The farther apart they are, the wider and higher the arc.


 Colour is distance too, violet for neighbours to green and yellow for links across the whole book.


 There is no text on the graphic: no book names, no counts, no legend.





THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

On black, a half-disc of thin coloured arcs, so many that they read as a texture with bands of colour. Under it a dense strip of grey bars hangs from a baseline, with a single long spike near the middle. No labels, no axes, no legend, no title on the image itself.



02 · Analyse

An arc diagram: every node on one line, here 1,189 chapters in the order of the book, and every link drawn as a semicircle between two of them. Position along the line says which chapters are linked, and an arc’s span and height say how far apart they are. Colour encodes that distance a second time. At 63,779 arcs, no single link can be followed. What the eye reads is density: where many faint arcs overlap, the image is bright.



03 · Interpret

The claim is about the whole book: that the Bible refers to itself everywhere, from end to end. The dome of long arcs is the claim made visible, links from the Old Testament to the New. It is a picture of scale and connectedness, the “first hyperlinked book”, in the phrase Harrison’s page quotes.



04 · Judge

It does what its makers said they wanted, and says so. As an image of scale it is hard to beat, and the arc diagram earns its place, because the chapters have an order and the span of an arc means something. As evidence it answers almost nothing you could ask: not which books cite which, nor how often, nor whether the density is in the text or in the overlap of faint lines. The rainbow adds beauty and no information. As a picture it is honest, but it is not a finding to cite.





THE RECREATION

Römhild’s dataset was never published, so this is drawn from another: OpenBible.info’s cross-references, links that OpenBible’s readers have voted on. Keeping the links with at least 8 votes leaves 61,282, within 4% of the original’s 63,779.


Show the R code
arcs <- arc_paths(links)
recreation <- arc_figure(arcs)
recreation










n = 59,035 links between different chapters, from OpenBible.info’s cross-references with at least 8 votes. Drawn at the original’s proportions, 850 × 500. The colours are ours: the original’s are not published.




Original · Harrison & Römhild, 2007





Ours · ggplot












The two differ most on the right. The New Testament here carries a denser dome of short links within itself than it does in the original. That comes from the two datasets, not from how they are drawn: each shows the choices of whoever compiled it.



HOW WE KNOW

Which links. OpenBible’s file draws mostly on the public-domain Treasury of Scripture Knowledge, and each link carries a count of readers’ votes. How many count as “the” cross-references is a threshold, and the original’s total picks it.


Show the R code
by_threshold <- tibble(min_votes = 5:30) |>
  mutate(links = map_int(min_votes, \(v) sum(refs$votes >= v)))
chosen <- filter(by_threshold, min_votes == MIN_VOTES)
stopifnot(which.min(abs(by_threshold$links - HARRISON_N)) == MIN_VOTES - 4)

ggplot(by_threshold, aes(min_votes, links)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = HARRISON_N, colour = p$ink_3, linewidth = .5) +
  geom_line(colour = dsvar_accent(), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = chosen, colour = dsvar_accent(), size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = 30, y = HARRISON_N, vjust = -.6, hjust = 1, size = 3.2,
           colour = p$ink_3, family = dsvar_font(),
           label = sprintf("the original: %s", format(HARRISON_N, big.mark = ","))) +
  annotate("text", x = MIN_VOTES - .3, y = chosen$links - 6000, hjust = 1, vjust = 1,
           size = 3.2, colour = p$ink_2, family = dsvar_font(),
           lineheight = .95,
           label = sprintf("%d votes or more:\n%s", MIN_VOTES,
                           format(chosen$links, big.mark = ","))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(), limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(title = sprintf("At %d votes or more, OpenBible's count comes closest to the original's",
                       MIN_VOTES),
       subtitle = "Cross-references kept, by the fewest readers' votes a link needs",
       x = "minimum votes", y = NULL,
       caption = "OpenBible.info cross-references, export of 2026-10-12.")









The chapter bars. OpenBible does not list verse counts, so each chapter’s length is the highest verse number cited anywhere in its full file. That gives 31,083 verses against the King James Bible’s 31,102: the last verse of a few chapters is never cited, and those bars are a verse short.
The arcs. Each arc is a semicircle, so its height is half its span: the height and the colour both encode the distance between the two chapters. A link within a single chapter has no span and no arc; there are 2,247 of those, left out. Links run in one direction in the file and are drawn without one, as in the original.



THE SAME DATA, DIFFERENT CHOICES


What the colour adds


Show the R code
arc_figure(arcs, colour = "#c9c9c9")










The same arcs in one colour. Nothing that could be read off the original is lost, because the colour repeated what each arc’s height already said. What is lost is most of the reason anyone hangs it on a wall, which is a fair account of what “more beautiful than functional” means.



What the order does


Show the R code
set.seed(1189)
shuffle <- sample(nrow(chapters))   # chapter at position i moves to shuffle[i]
shuffled_links <- links |>
  mutate(a = shuffle[lo], b = shuffle[hi],
         lo = pmin(a, b), hi = pmax(a, b), span = hi - lo)
canonical_bars <- bars
bars <- bars |> mutate(pos = shuffle[pos])     # arc_figure() draws `bars`
arc_figure(arc_paths(shuffled_links))









Show the R code
bars <- canonical_bars



Every link the same, every chapter put somewhere at random on the line. The arcs now say only that the Bible’s chapters are linked to each other, which the first picture said too, and nothing about where. The canonical order is what gave an arc’s span a meaning: links between neighbouring chapters, within a book, across the two Testaments. This is the rule the field guide gives for arc diagrams.



Book by book


Show the R code
book_names <- chapters |> distinct(book_index, book)
# Each pair counted once, then mirrored, so the grid reads the same both ways.
pairs <- links |>
  mutate(from = chapters$book_index[lo], to = chapters$book_index[hi]) |>
  count(from, to)
by_book <- bind_rows(pairs, pairs |> filter(from != to) |> rename(from = to, to = from))
top <- pairs |> filter(from != to) |> slice_max(n, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

ggplot(by_book, aes(to, from, fill = n)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_tile(data = bind_rows(top, rename(top, from = to, to = from)),
            width = 1, height = 1, fill = NA, colour = p$ink, linewidth = .6) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = book_names$book_index, labels = book_names$book,
                     expand = expansion(0), position = "top") +
  scale_y_reverse(breaks = book_names$book_index, labels = book_names$book,
                  expand = expansion(0)) +
  scale_fill_dsvar_o(transform = "log10", name = "links") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = sprintf("Between two different books, %s and %s are linked most: %s times",
                       BOOK_NAMES[top$from], BOOK_NAMES[top$to],
                       format(top$n, big.mark = ",")),
       subtitle = "Cross-references between every pair of books, in canonical order. Darker is more, on a log scale",
       x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = sprintf("n = %s links, OpenBible.info, %d votes or more.",
                         format(nrow(links), big.mark = ","), MIN_VOTES)) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 0, vjust = .5, size = rel(.6)),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = rel(.6)),
        panel.grid.major = element_blank(), axis.line.x = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "right")










The same links counted, not drawn. Every pair of books has a cell, so this can answer what the arcs cannot: which books cite which, and how often. It is an adjacency matrix, the form the field guide gives for dense networks.


Harrison drew a second graphic from the Bible, of who is named in the same verse as whom (2,619 people and places), and did not use arcs for it. “Because such relationships had no ordering or structure (unlike the cross references), I used a spatial clustering algorithm.” That sentence is the rule for an arc diagram: it needs an order the nodes already have, because an arc’s span is only worth drawing when the distance it spans means something. The same holds for the spokes of a radar chart.





SOURCES


Original: Harrison, C., & Römhild, C. (2007). Bible Cross-References. chrisharrison.net. © Chris Harrison; shown here at low resolution under the citation right.
Data: OpenBible.info, cross-references, export of 2026-10-12, CC BY 4.0; mostly from the public-domain Treasury of Scripture Knowledge. Links with at least 5 votes vendored as data/raw/openbible-cross-references.csv, chapter lengths as data/raw/openbible-chapters.csv; see R/fetch-gallery-data.R.
The arc diagram: Wattenberg, M. (2002). Arc diagrams: Visualizing structure in strings. IEEE Symposium on Information Visualization, 110–116.
Reproduce it: every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: Field guide
text:
A decision tree


Field guide

The idea behind this field guide is to help you choose the right type of chart for your specific data. What kind of variable(s) you have and what you want to show with them decides which types of chart you can use. Pick the variable kind below and follow the branches to the relevant charts. Every form opens onto what it claims and the R code that draws it.




Categorieswk 2Category & numberwk 2Numberswk 3Timewk 5Spacewk 6Networks & textwk 6
Categories from week 2Counts of things, and parts of a whole. Every variable here is
categorical; the only number is how many fall in each category.One categorical variableBar chart of countsLollipop chartWaffle chartThink twicePie chartTwo categorical variablesCompare inside each groupGrouped barsThe make-up of each groupStacked to 100%Every combination at onceCount gridThe same cases, followed acrossAlluvial flows
Category & number from week 2One categorical variable and one continuous one: the simplest chart
there is, and the commonest. The first question is whether each category
has one value, two, or many.One value per categoryRank themSorted barsDot plotAgainst a referenceDiverging barsParts of a whole, nestedTreemapTwo values per categorySlopegraphDumbbellMany values per categoryShow every pointStrip plotRaincloudShow the shapeViolinRidgelineSummarise each groupBox plotThink twiceMean and intervalThink twiceBar with error bars
Numbers from week 3Continuous variables only. One of them is a distribution, two are a
relationship, and several are a search for which relationship to argue
about. One estimate, made many defensible ways, is a test of whether the
argument survives.One variableHistogramDensity curveTwo variablesTens to hundreds of pointsScatterplotScatter with a fitted lineBubble chartThousands of pointsTransparent scatter2D binsSeveral variablesSmall multiplesScatterplot matrixCorrelation heatmapThink twiceRadar chartOne effect, estimated many waysSpecification curve
Time from week 5One variable is time, and time is ordered. That order is the whole
reason a line is allowed here and nowhere else on this page.One seriesThrough timeLine chartLine with a smootherArea chartWarming stripesAround a cycleSeasonal gridThink twiceRose diagramThink twiceRadar chartSeveral seriesOn the same unitsSeveral linesSmall multiplesParts of a totalThink twiceStacked areaTwo series against each otherConnected scatterplotThink twiceTwo y axes
Space from week 6The data has a place attached. The first question is whether the
value belongs to an area, to a point or to a route between two, and the
second is whether it is a count or a rate.A value for each areaDrawn as the land isChoroplethEvery area the same sizeTile mapValues at placesA count at each placeProportional symbolsEach event where it happenedPoint mapMovement between placesFlow map
Networks & text from week 6Connections between things, and words. Both turn out to be
applications of forms met earlier: a matrix is a heatmap, a word count
is a sorted bar chart, and a word embedding is a scatterplot.ConnectionsA few hundred nodes or fewerNode-link diagramDense, or many nodesAdjacency matrixNodes that have an orderArc diagramWordsHow often each is usedTerm frequencyThink twiceWord cloudWhich go togetherEmbedding map
Every form, in full
Week 2 · Comparison & rankingBar chart of countsHow many fall in each category — and because length is the count, the
bars start at zero.Use it whenOne categorical variable, and the question is which category is most
common.Watch forLeaving the categories in alphabetical order. fct_infreq()
sorts by count; alphabetical hides the finding.The code
ggplot(mpg, aes(y = fct_infreq(class))) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Cars in the mpg data, by class",
       x = "number of cars", y = NULL)

Week 2 · Comparison & rankingLollipop chartHow many fall in each category, as a stem from zero to a dot: a bar with
most of its ink taken away.Use it whenMany categories, where a wall of bars would be mostly ink and the ends
of the bars are what matter.Watch forCutting the axis above zero. The stem is a length, so it needs zero just
as a bar does. A dot plot has no stem, which is why it does not.The code
count(mpg, manufacturer) |>
  mutate(manufacturer = fct_reorder(manufacturer, n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, manufacturer)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = n, yend = manufacturer)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Cars in the mpg data, by manufacturer",
       x = "number of cars", y = NULL)

Week 2 · Comparison & rankingWaffle chartParts of a whole, in units the reader can count: 38 squares of every
100.Use it whenOne share, or two or three, for an audience that should be able to count
it.Watch forMore than three or four categories. Beyond that the grid is noise, and a
sorted bar chart says it better.The code
tibble(cell = 1:100,
       answer = rep(c("Yes", "No"), times = c(38, 62))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = (cell - 1) %% 10, y = (cell - 1) %/% 10, fill = fct_inorder(answer))) +
  geom_tile(width = 0.85, height = 0.85) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Thirty-eight in every hundred said yes",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())

Week 1 · The argument in the graph Think twicePie chartParts of a whole, encoded as angle — one of the channels people read
least accurately.Use it whenTwo or three parts, when “about a quarter” is precise enough.Watch forSlices of similar size, or more than three of them. Week 1’s ranking of
channels is the reason: position beats angle.The code
mpg |>
  mutate(drv = recode(drv, f = "front", r = "rear", "4" = "four-wheel")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = "", fill = drv)) +
  geom_bar(width = 1) +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  labs(title = "Cars in the mpg data, by drive",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())

Week 2 · Comparison & rankingGrouped barsCounts for every combination of two categories, compared within each
group.Use it whenThe comparison that matters is between the bars inside one group.Watch forMore than three or four bars per group. Facet instead, and keep the
colours.The code
as_tibble(UCBAdmissions) |>
  count(Dept, Admit, wt = n) |>
  ggplot(aes(Dept, n, fill = Admit)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Applications to six Berkeley departments, 1973",
       x = "department", y = "applicants", fill = NULL)

Week 2 · Comparison & rankingStacked to 100%The make-up of each group as shares that sum to one. The sizes of the
groups are deliberately thrown away.Use it whenComposition is the point, and how big each group is, is not.Watch forComparing the middle segments. Only the first and the last share a
baseline; everything between floats.The code
as_tibble(UCBAdmissions) |>
  count(Dept, Admit, wt = n) |>
  ggplot(aes(Dept, n, fill = Admit)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(title = "Share of applicants admitted, Berkeley, 1973",
       x = "department", y = NULL, fill = NULL)

Week 2 · Comparison & rankingCount gridHow many fall in every combination of two categories, encoded as colour.Use it whenMany combinations, where the pattern matters more than any exact count.Watch forExpecting the reader to read numbers off a colour. If the values matter,
print them in the cells, as this one does.The code
as_tibble(HairEyeColor) |>
  count(Hair, Eye, wt = n) |>
  ggplot(aes(Eye, Hair)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = n)) +
  geom_label(aes(label = n)) +
  labs(title = "Hair and eye colour of 592 statistics students",
       x = "eye colour", y = "hair colour", fill = "students")

Alluvial flowsHow the same individuals divide across several categorical variables, in
sequence.Use it whenThree or so categorical variables measured on the same cases, where the
paths are the finding.Watch forMany categories per axis, or axes with no natural order. The ribbons
become a tangle, and the order of the axes is itself a claim.The code
library(ggalluvial)

as_tibble(Titanic) |>
  ggplot(aes(axis1 = Class, axis2 = Sex, axis3 = Survived, y = n)) +
  geom_alluvium(aes(fill = Survived)) +
  geom_stratum() +
  geom_text(stat = "stratum", aes(label = after_stat(stratum)), size = 3) +
  scale_x_discrete(limits = c("Class", "Sex", "Survived")) +
  labs(title = "Everyone aboard the Titanic, by class, sex and survival",
       y = "people", fill = "survived")
In the gallery Sankey and alluvial flows
Week 2 · Comparison & rankingSorted barsOne value per category, ranked. Length is the value, so the axis starts
at zero.Use it whenComparing amounts across categories. The commonest chart there is, and
usually the right one.Watch forCutting the axis above zero. A bar whose length is not its value lies in
the strongest channel you have.The code
tibble(city = names(precip), inches = precip) |>
  slice_max(inches, n = 10) |>
  ggplot(aes(inches, fct_reorder(city, inches))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "The ten wettest of 70 US cities",
       x = "average rainfall per year (inches)", y = NULL)
In the gallery Du Bois’s data portraits
Week 2 · Comparison & rankingDot plotOne value per category, as a position — so, unlike a bar, the axis does
not have to start at zero.Use it whenThe values sit close together and far from zero, so bars would all look
the same length.Watch forAdding a stem from zero. That turns it back into a length, and a length
needs zero again.The code
tibble(city = names(precip), inches = precip) |>
  slice_max(inches, n = 10) |>
  ggplot(aes(inches, fct_reorder(city, inches))) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(title = "The ten wettest of 70 US cities",
       x = "average rainfall per year (inches)", y = NULL)
In the gallery The PISA league table
Week 2 · Comparison & rankingDiverging barsHow far each category sits above or below a reference, and in which
direction.Use it whenThe reference means something: an average, a target, no change.Watch forA reference chosen to make one side look large. Say what zero is, in the
caption.The code
mpg |>
  group_by(manufacturer) |>
  summarise(hwy = mean(hwy)) |>
  mutate(gap = hwy - mean(mpg$hwy),
         side = if_else(gap > 0, "above average", "below average")) |>
  ggplot(aes(gap, fct_reorder(manufacturer, gap), fill = side)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Highway fuel economy of 15 makes, against the average car",
       x = "miles per gallon above or below the average", y = NULL, fill = NULL)

Week 2 · Comparison & rankingSlopegraphTwo values per category, and the change between them as the slope of a
line.Use it whenBefore and after, or two conditions on the same units. The direction of
each line is the finding.Watch forMore than two points per line, or so many lines that they cannot be
labelled.The code
ggplot(sleep, aes(group, extra, group = ID)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Extra sleep on two drugs, the same ten patients",
       x = "drug", y = "extra hours of sleep")

Week 3 · Distribution & uncertaintyStrip plotEvery observation in every group, so the reader sees the shape and the n
at once.Use it whenUp to a few hundred points per group. The most honest distribution chart
there is.Watch forJittering along the measured axis. Only ever jitter across the
categorical one, or the values move.The code
ggplot(mpg, aes(hwy, class)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.2, width = 0, alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "Highway fuel economy, by car class",
       x = "highway miles per gallon", y = NULL)
