  cross_join(tibble(name = people)) |>
  filter(str_detect(text, fixed(name)))

# Along the line, in the order the novel first names them.
nodes <- named |> slice_min(line, by = name) |> arrange(line) |> select(name)

# Two characters are linked once for every chapter that names both.
in_chapter <- distinct(named, chapter, name)
edges <- inner_join(in_chapter, in_chapter, by = "chapter",
                    relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  filter(name.x < name.y) |>
  count(from = name.x, to = name.y)

tidygraph::tbl_graph(nodes, edges, directed = FALSE) |>
  ggraph(layout = "linear") +
  geom_edge_arc(aes(edge_width = n, edge_alpha = n), fold = TRUE) +
  geom_node_point() +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name), angle = 90, hjust = 1, nudge_y = -0.3,
                 size = 3) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.2, 2.5)) +
  scale_edge_alpha(range = c(0.1, 0.6)) +
  expand_limits(y = -3) +
  labs(title = "Characters named in the same chapter of Pride and Prejudice",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, edge_width = "chapters", edge_alpha = "chapters") +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
In the gallery The Bible’s cross-references
Week 6 · Structure in space and textTerm frequencyWhich words occur most, ranked by a count that can be read off an axis.Use it whenAny question about frequent terms. It is a category against a number, so
week 2’s rules apply.Watch forTreating frequency as importance. After the stop words go, the most
common words are usually names.The code
library(tidytext)
library(sotu)

sotu_meta |>
  mutate(text = sotu_text) |>
  filter(year > 2000) |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text) |>
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 15) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, fct_reorder(word, n))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "The commonest words in the State of the Union, 2001 to 2020",
       x = "times used", y = NULL)

Week 6 · Structure in space and text Think twiceWord cloudFrequency as font size, at positions that mean nothing — and long words
look important because they are long.Use it whenDecoration. Never as evidence.Watch forAny comparison at all. The sorted bar chart beside it says the same
thing, and it can be read.The code
library(tidytext)
library(sotu)
library(ggwordcloud)

sotu_meta |>
  mutate(text = sotu_text) |>
  filter(year > 2000) |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text) |>
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 80) |>
  ggplot(aes(label = word, size = n)) +
  geom_text_wordcloud(rm_outside = TRUE, seed = 1) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 11) +
  labs(title = "The same words, as a cloud")

Embedding mapWords placed so that words used in similar sentences sit close together.
Each word is a long vector, and the page shows two of its directions.Use it whenExploring which words a corpus treats as related, before choosing a
claim that a count can test.Watch forReading the axes, or the distance between far-apart words. They come
from one projection among many, and a different method redraws the map.The code
library(tidytext)
library(sotu)

words <- sotu_meta |>
  mutate(text = sotu_text) |>
  filter(year > 2000) |>
  unnest_tokens(sentence, text, token = "sentences") |>
  mutate(id = row_number()) |>
  unnest_tokens(word, sentence) |>
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") |>
  filter(!word %in% c("applause", "laughter")) |>
  distinct(id, word) |>
  add_count(word) |>
  filter(n >= 40)

# how much more often two words share a sentence than chance says they should
co <- as.matrix(crossprod(cast_sparse(words, id, word)))
pmi <- log(co * sum(co) / outer(rowSums(co), colSums(co)))
pmi[!is.finite(pmi) | pmi < 0] <- 0

# each row is now a word's vector; draw two of its directions
s <- svd(pmi)
tibble(word = rownames(co), n = diag(co),
       x = s$u[, 2] * s$d[2], y = s$u[, 3] * s$d[3]) |>
  slice_max(n, n = 70) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, label = word)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(vjust = -0.7, size = 3, check_overlap = TRUE) +
  labs(title = "State of the Union words, placed by the company they keep",
       x = "second dimension", y = "third dimension") +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())




Every thumbnail is the code on its card, run exactly as written (except for small layout additions to match the course design). The data is all built into R or its packages, so the code runs in a fresh session after library(tidyverse). Forms marked think twice are ones this course argues against (but breaking these rules is sometimes necessary!). The shape of this page is inspired by From Data to Viz by Yan Holtz and Conor Healy.

title: Three types of Assignments
text:
Assessment · 2026




The course has three graded assignments: a portfolio built over the course of all weeks, two written critiques, and one visualization project with your own on data. What you may use AI for, and how to say so, is on the AI use page. Every deadline is on the Weeks page and on Canvas.





  
    25%
    Portfolio
    Weeks 2 to 7 · individual · six entries
  
  
    25%
    Two critique pieces
    After weeks 4 and 6 · individual · two PDFs
  
  
    50%
    Take-home assignment
    End of week 8 · individual · your own data
  


Note: The final grade is the weighted average of the three. Every component is graded on a 0–10 scale, with 5.5 the passing mark. The final grade is rounded to the nearest half point (5.5 becomes 6.0). Every component must be passed with at least 5.5, and one component cannot compensate for another.




WHAT EVERY CHART HAS TO CARRY

Three things, on every chart you hand in, from the first portfolio entry to the take-home:

A claim, written as a sentence. Not a description of the variables, but the thing you claiming the chart shows.
Uncertainty, in some form the chart can show. This could be a confidence interval, a range, an sample size, or a concrete sentence naming what the chart cannot show.
Code that runs on someone else’s machine. We ask you to submit the code that build the figure. It should be reproducible. Thus data is loading from a path that exists and the code runs without errors. If you use a dataset that is not public, you must provide it in the submission.

A chart missing any of the three is incomplete.




25%



Assignment 1 of 3




One entry a week, started in the work group


Weeks 2 to 7 · six entries, each due the Sunday after its work group · individual






Each Thursday from week 2 ends with a chart and its misleading twin. You finish the pair at home as that week’s portfolio entry and hand it in on the Sunday after the work group; there is no final submission. The next Tuesday’s lecture opens with a critique of some of the entries, without names, and what it shows you goes into your next entry. Each entry is graded fail (4), pass (8) or high pass (10), and your portfolio grade is the average of the six. It counts for 25% of the final grade.



THE HONEST/DISHONEST PAIR


Every entry has two versions of the week’s chart: the one you would defend and think is honest, and one that uses only defensible-looking choices to tell a different, dishonest story. Take the second as seriously as the first: building the misleading version on purpose is the clearest evidence that you know which choice was doing the work, and it is much harder to be fooled by a chart once you have made that chart yourself.




HOW IT IS GRADED









Grade
What it looks like




High pass (10)
Everything a pass needs, and a twin that changes the one choice doing the work, with a sentence that names that choice precisely


Pass (8)
Complete: the sketch, the chart and its twin, the sentence on which choice did the work, what the charts cannot tell you, and the AI statement. The chart carries its claim and its uncertainty, and the file renders


Fail (4)
Something is missing: one of the six things, the claim or the uncertainty on the chart, or a file that does not render










25%



Assignment 2 of 3




A published chart, taken apart


Due Wednesday 25 November and Wednesday 9 December, 23:59 · individual · PDF on Canvas






Two written analyses of a chart someone else published, using the method from the lectures: describe, analyse, interpret, and judge. This is the half of the skill the portfolio cannot test: reading a chart you did not make, and saying precisely where its claim and its evidence part ways.
You find the chart yourself, in a newspaper, a report, a research paper or on social media. It has to be one the course has not shown, and the second piece takes a different chart from the first.



TWO DEADLINES




Critique 1 · Wednesday 25 November



Due once weeks 3 and 4 have covered distributions, uncertainty and relationships, so you have those to work with as well as comparisons. The lecture the day before opens with a critique of the week 4 entries: treat it as practice.




Critique 2 · Wednesday 9 December



Due once weeks 5 and 6 have covered change over time, maps, networks and text, so you have those to work with too. The lecture the day before opens with a critique of the week 6 entries: treat it as practice.






WHAT GOES IN THE PDF

Each piece is one PDF with at most two A4 pages of text, handed in on Canvas. The figure and its credit line come on top of that, and so does your AI statement. It has four parts, in this order:

The figure, in the file. Put the chart itself into your document, large enough to read, with a credit line under it: who made it, where and when it was published, and a link. A link alone is not enough, because published charts change and disappear.
The four steps, in order. Describe what is on the page: marks, axes, ranges, and no evaluation yet. Analyse which slots of the grammar were set. Interpret the claim the chart makes, in one sentence with a verb. Judge whether the evidence supports that claim: a verdict, and a reason.
What you like and what you do not. Your own view as a reader: which choices work and which do not, each with a reason that points at a specific choice in the chart.
How you would improve it. Outline a better version: what you would change, and what a reader would then see that they cannot see now. You do not have to build it.




AI

AI may improve your language, not add content. Grammar, spelling and translation are fine; the description, the arguments and the verdict have to be your own. End the piece with an AI statement that says what the tool changed, or No AI used.



HOW IT IS GRADED

Each piece is scored on five criteria, each at one of four levels: Excellent (10), Good (8), Sufficient (6) or Insufficient (4). The grade for a piece is the weighted average of its five scores, and your critique grade is the average of the two pieces.











Criterion
Excellent (10)
Good (8)
Sufficient (6)
Insufficient (4)




Describe and analyse · 25%
A complete and neutral account of marks, axes, scales and ranges, and every setting of the grammar named with what it does
An accurate account of what is on the page, and the main settings named, with little judgement slipping in
The main elements described and some settings named, but parts are missing or judgement arrives early
Description skipped or inaccurate, or the piece judges before it says what is on the page


Interpret · 20%
The claim in one precise sentence with a verb, including what the chart implies but does not say
The claim in one clear sentence with a verb
A claim is given, but it is vague or names the topic more than the argument
No claim, or only a description of the variables


Judge · 25%
A clear verdict argued from specific choices and from the limits of the data, including what the chart cannot show
A clear verdict with a reason that points at a specific choice in the chart
A verdict, but its reasons are general (“misleading”, “cluttered”) rather than tied to a choice
No verdict, or a verdict without reasons


Reflect and improve · 20%
Strengths and weaknesses tied to specific choices, and an improvement argued from the claim that lets a reader see something new
Strengths and weaknesses tied to choices, and a concrete improvement
Likes and dislikes given but general, or an improvement that stays vague
Missing, or matters of taste without reasons


Form · 10%
Figure legible with a full credit line, within two pages, precise and concise writing, complete AI statement
All parts present and within two pages, with small lapses in the credit line or in clarity
Over length, an incomplete credit line, or writing that is hard to follow in places
Figure or credit line missing, or no AI statement










50%



Assignment 3 of 3




One new piece, on data of your own choosing


Due Sunday 20 December, 23:59 · end of week 8 · individual · your own dataset






A new piece of work on a dataset you choose yourself: one met in the course, or one you bring. You present it either as a data story or as an explanatory blog post. Week 7 is where you choose the dataset and find two claims it supports. Week 8 has no sessions: the whole week is yours to write the piece.
The dataset has to support at least two defensible stories. You tell one of them, and your note says why not the other: a file with only one story in it cannot show that you chose.



FINDING DATA


Finding the data is where many projects stall. The safest start is a file the course has used, with a question the course did not ask of it. If you bring your own, choose it in week 7 and test it before you commit.



THE FIVE-MINUTE TEST

Before you commit to a dataset, answer three questions. If it fails any of them, choose another.

Can you download it today, without filing an application, and hand it in with your code?
Can you say in one sentence what one row is, and what each column you need means?
Does it support at least two defensible stories?











Source
What is there
The catch




The course’s own files
World Bank indicators, Gapminder and KNMI weather, in the data/ folder of earlier weeks
None, as long as you ask a question the course did not. The safest start.


Our World in Data
Thousands of indicators; every chart has a Download tab with its CSV
Already aggregated and already charted. Do not redraw their chart, and check the original source it names.


Statistics offices
CBS StatLine (cbsodataR), Eurostat (eurostat), the World Bank (WDI)
Read the definitions: a change of method can look like a change in the world.


Surveys
European Social Survey, Eurobarometer (via GESIS), World Values Survey
Free, after registration. Read the codebook for weights and for missing codes such as 77, 88 and 99.


Political data
V-Dem, ParlGov, the Manifesto Project
Indices built from expert ratings or coding: say what the scale measures before you chart it.


Research repositories
Harvard Dataverse, Zenodo, OSF, the replication packages of published papers
Reusing data means inheriting someone else’s decisions. Read the codebook first.


TidyTuesday
A clean dataset every week, with a short description, on GitHub
Hundreds of people have charted each one already. Your claim has to be your own.


Kaggle
Many datasets on many topics
Often no clear source. Use one only if it names its original source and you can check it.





Whatever the source, the grader has to be able to run your code on your data. If its terms do not let you hand the file in, choose another, or ask the coordinator first.




TWO FORMATS


Both formats tell one story from your data, in four charts and 1,000 to 1,500 words (charts not counted), for a reader who has not taken this course. They differ in what carries the argument: the charts, or the text.




Option A · Data story




Four charts, one question. Each chart is one step of the answer, and its title states that step as a claim.
A structure, chosen. A martini glass (you lead, then the reader explores), a drill-down (overview, then detail) or a slideshow (one claim per chart).
Describe, then explain. First what the pattern looks like, then what it goes with.
Text between the charts that takes the reader from one step to the next.
One visual language. A category keeps its colour from chart to chart.
The limit, last. What the data cannot tell the reader.





Option B · Explanatory blog post




A question in the first paragraph, and why a reader should care.
The data, introduced. Where it comes from, what one row is, what it covers and what it misses.
Four charts, each read for the reader. How to read it first: what the marks are and where to look. Then what it shows.
The choice that matters. For each chart, the setting that does the most work, and why you chose it.
The answer, with its uncertainty, and the other story the data could tell.





For both, week 7’s four settings are the checklist: the title, the annotation, the colour and the order. And every chart carries what every chart has to carry: a claim, its uncertainty, and code that runs.




WHAT YOU HAND IN

By Sunday 20 December, 23:59, on Canvas, two files:

The piece, as a PDF: the data story or the blog post as a reader would see it. Render your .qmd to HTML and print it to PDF from the browser. At the end of the PDF come two short sections:

A note on your choices, at most 250 words: who the reader is and what they can be assumed to decode, why the charts come in this order, and the other defensible story in your data and why you did not tell it.
Your AI statement, in the same format as in the portfolio. AI is allowed as in Part II of a work group: as an assistant, a thinking partner or an instrument, never as a surrogate.

The code, the data and the output, as one zip: your take-home folder, with the .qmd that builds every chart, the data it reads from data/, and the rendered HTML. Unzipped on another machine and rendered from a clean session, it has to produce the same charts.

A take-home without the PDF, the data, or code that runs is incomplete.



HOW IT IS GRADED

The take-home is scored on five criteria, each at one of four levels: Excellent (10), Good (8), Sufficient (6) or Insufficient (4). The grade is the weighted average of the five scores.











Criterion
Excellent (10)
Good (8)
Sufficient (6)
Insufficient (4)




Data and question · 15%
A sharp question the data can answer, the data fully explained (source, what one row is, what it covers and misses), and its limits used in the story
A clear question the data can answer, and the data explained: source, what one row is, what it covers
A question and a dataset, but the fit between them or the account of the data is thin
No clear question, data that cannot answer it, or data not understood


The charts · 30%
Four charts in the right form, each carrying its claim and its uncertainty, with annotation and colour that make the evidence hard to miss
Four charts in a suitable form, each with its claim and its uncertainty, annotated and coloured with care
Four charts that work, but a form is poorly chosen, or a claim, the uncertainty or the annotation is missing in places
Fewer than four charts, charts that mislead, or charts without claims or uncertainty


The story · 25%
The four charts build one argument in an order that is part of it, and the chosen format is used to full effect
One argument across the four charts, in an order the reader can follow, with what the chosen format asks for
The charts answer one question but read as separate pieces, or the format is only partly followed
No story the reader can follow, or the format and length not followed


The note on your choices · 15%
The reader, the order and the other defensible story each explained, with the trade-offs named
The reader, the order and the other story each explained
Only some of the three covered, or the choices described rather than explained
Missing, or not about the choices


Reproducibility · 15%
Renders from a clean session on another machine without changes; readable, commented code; complete AI statement
Renders from a clean session; data and output in the zip; complete AI statement
Renders only after a small fix (a path, a missing package), or the AI statement is incomplete
Does not render, data missing, or no AI statement









DEADLINES, LATE WORK AND RESITS






How it works




Deadlines
Each portfolio entry is due on the Sunday after its work group; the critique pieces and the take-home on the dates above. Every deadline is on the Weeks page and on Canvas.


Late work
If you expect to miss a deadline, message the coordinator on Canvas as soon as you can. A late submission is accepted with a reasonable justification, at most twice in the course.


Resit
There is no resit for any part of this course.


Language
Everything you hand in is written in English.

title: Using AI in this course
text:
AI use · 2026


Using AI in this course

AI tools are everywhere, and we cannot realistically make you work without them. What we can do is decide where they help your learning, and hold you accountable for what you hand in. The rule is the same every week: no AI in Part I of a work group, where you learn the code; AI for language only in the two critique pieces; and AI with a statement in Part II, the portfolio and the take-home. Wherever AI is allowed, you say how you used it, can account for every chart you hand in, and can own the claim it makes. This page explains where AI fits, the four kinds of use, the statement you write about them, and how AI was used to make this course; the Assessment page explains how the work is graded.





WHERE AI FITS


An AI tool can write a ggplot call in seconds. You can only tell whether that call draws the right chart if you can read and write one yourself, and if you know which claim the data supports and which choice in the chart does the work. That is what the first part of every work group teaches, so it is done without AI. Once you can write the code, a tool can write it faster, and you can judge what it gives you.




No AI


Part I, and the sketch
Part I of each work group is where you learn the code: you run every chunk and write the two Your turn exercises yourself. No AI, and no code completion such as GitHub Copilot: switch it off. Week 1 works the same way, and so does the sketch on paper that starts Part II.




Language only


The two critique pieces
A critique is your own reading of someone else’s chart. AI may improve your language (grammar, spelling, translation) but may not add content: no descriptions, arguments or verdicts. The piece still ends with an AI statement that says what it changed.




AI allowed, with a statement


Part II, portfolio, take-home
From the Part II build on, you may use AI as an assistant, a thinking partner or an instrument. Each piece ends with an AI statement. Never as a surrogate: you may not hand in work a tool did that you cannot defend without its output in front of you.




The reference sheet on every work group page runs on different data from the week’s file, on purpose: pasting it, or a tool’s version of it, draws a chart of the wrong thing.




FOUR KINDS OF USE


We sort AI use by what the tool did to the work, and so by what you have to be able to account for.






Kind
What it means
What we ask of you




Assistant
Syntax, error messages, help searching, and writing or fixing the code for a chart you have already designed. Editing, grammar and translation of your text. The claim, the design and the reasoning are yours; the tool touched how they are written.
Which tool, for what, and what you did with its output: what you kept, what you changed, what you rejected. And how you checked that the chart shows what the data says.


Thinking partner
The model works on your own sketch, chart or draft. You ask it what a reader might misread, which choice in your twin does the work, or what your critique has missed. The ideas you test are already yours.
Say what you discussed with it and what came out of it. You must be able to defend every claim without the output in front of you, and the text must be in your own voice.


Instrument
The model's output becomes part of your data: it sorts or labels rows, reads numbers off a document or an image, or produces a table you then chart.
A statement written like a methods section: which model, what you asked it, and how you checked its output against the source or your own judgement.


Surrogate
The model produces the work (the chart, the claim, the critique) and you put your name on it. That includes a chart the tool drew itself, in its own window, rather than the R code in your file.
Not allowed. It falls under the VU fraud and plagiarism regulation, and no AI statement makes it acceptable.






The rule from the Info page holds here too: every chart you hand in is made with ggplot2, by the code in your file, and that code has to run on someone else’s machine.




THE AI STATEMENT



WHAT IT HAS TO SAY

Every piece you hand in ends with a section headed AI use: each portfolio entry (the entry file in each week’s folder already has it), both critique pieces and the take-home. Write one short block for each kind of use, and say which parts you did without AI. For each use, answer four questions:

Which tool, and when (e.g. ChatGPT, 12 November; Claude; GitHub Copilot in RStudio)?
What for: which chart or step, and what you asked it?
What you did with it: what you kept, what you changed, and at least one thing you rejected, with the reason.
How you checked it: how you know the chart shows what the data says, not only that the code runs. For example, you compared one plotted value with the table, or the n in your caption with nrow().

If you used no AI at all, write No AI used. That is a complete statement. If you used it a lot, paste your most important prompts at the end of the file, or add a share link to the conversation.
The standard behind all of it: you must be able to explain and defend every choice in your chart (the claim, the encoding, the scale, the twin) without the output in front of you. If you cannot, the kind of use was Surrogate, whatever the statement says.




Example · light use


Only as an assistant
Assistant. ChatGPT (5 Nov), for one error in the build: “Cannot use + with a single argument”. It explained that I had started a line with + instead of ending the line before with it. I moved the + myself.
Not used for: the claim, the sketch, the twin and the sentence on which choice did the work.




Example · medium use


Assistant and thinking partner
Assistant. Claude (19 Nov), to write the geom_text_repel() call for the labels. I kept its code and rejected its suggestion to label every point: the claim is about four countries, so only those carry a name. I checked those four against the table.
Thinking partner. After building my twin, I asked which choice a reader would notice first. It said the log scale; I think the window does more of the work, and my sentence says why.
Not used for: the claim and the sketch. Prompts at the end of the file.




Example · entry 6, your own data


When the model touches the data
Instrument. ChatGPT (10 Dec), to copy a 30-row table out of the PDF report my data comes from. I checked every row against the PDF; two were shifted by a line, and I fixed them by hand. The caption names the report, not the tool, as the source.
Assistant. ChatGPT, to turn my sketch into a first ggplot() call. It mapped colour to region; I removed that, because the claim compares years, not regions.
Not used for: the claim, the twin and the text.





NOT ENOUGH


AI use: ChatGPT helped with the code and the text.

Which code? Which chart? What did you keep, what did you change, what did you reject, and how did you check it? A statement like this counts as missing.




IF IT GOES WRONG










What happens




No statement, or one like the example above
It counts as missing.


Work a tool did, handed in as yours
Surrogate use falls under the VU fraud and plagiarism regulation, with or without a statement.







OUR OWN AI STATEMENT


Because we ask you to write an AI statement, we lead by example: here is how I used AI to make this course, in the same format. It covers what I prepared as coordinator: this website, the slides, the work groups and the gallery. The standard is the same: I can account for every page, every chart and every number in them, and the errors in them are mine (tell us on Canvas when you find one).



AI statement · the coordinator

Assistant. Claude Code (Anthropic, Claude Opus models) was used to build this website, to write parts of the R code behind the slides and the gallery rebuilds, and to check all R code in the slides and the work groups for errors and consistency. I reviewed everything before it went online. I could check the code because I wrote this kind of code for years without AI, which is why Part I of every work group is done without it.
Claude also helped drafting slides and pages from my outlines and notes and from the materials of earlier editions of this course. I closely reviewed and heavily edited everything it produced. It also checked that dates, rules and numbers agree across the site and the slides.
Not used for: grading or feedback on your work.

title: Credits and licences
text:
What is ours, what is borrowed


Credits and licences

This site reuses other people’s data and other people’s charts. Attribution sits beside each one where it is used, and it is collected here too, so there is a single page to check.








THIS SITE

Course material, page design, and every chart built from the code shown on these pages: © Philipp K. Masur, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, released under CC BY 4.0. Reuse it, change it, teach with it; say where it came from.
That licence covers our work only. Third-party material keeps its own licence, listed below, and some of it is not free to reuse. That includes every data file the site serves: none of them is CC BY 4.0 because the site is, and charts drawn from the three share-alike datasets below carry their licence.



DATA

Every dataset is committed to the repository so the site builds offline. Each is used as published except for subsetting, reshaping and renaming; where more was done, the row says so. The files marked not served are drawn on at render time but not offered for download.

CONDITIONS THAT TRAVEL WITH THE DATA

Three datasets are share-alike, and the files and anything substantially derived from them keep that licence rather than this site’s: the HYG star catalogue and the V-Dem indices (CC BY-SA 4.0), and the CP 1919 profiles (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, which is also non-commercial: teaching qualifies, but it is a condition rather than a blanket permission). The van Langren digitisation is non-commercial at its source too.




REPRODUCED CHARTS

Each gallery exhibit that shows an original carries a full credit line directly under the image. Their status divides four ways:

Public domain: van Langren (1644), Playfair (1821, Charts No. 1 and No. 3), Minard (1869 and 1858), Nightingale (1858), Snow (1855), Mayr (1877), Sankey (1898), Du Bois and Atlanta University’s chart for the 1900 Paris Exposition (US public domain), and the National Center for Education Statistics’ PISA 2022 table (a US federal work). Credited anyway, because academic practice asks for it even where the law does not.
Freely licensed: Hawkins’s warming stripes, Tyler Vigen’s Spurious Correlations chart shown in week 2’s deck, and Rozado, Hughes & Halberstadt’s headline-sentiment figure from PLOS ONE (all CC BY 4.0); Powell’s Hertzsprung–Russell diagram and Drlovedrake’s vote-scaled election cartogram (CC BY-SA); the Reproducibility Project and Many Analysts figures, and Magog the Ogre’s county election map (CC0 1.0); and Gapminder World 2015 (CC BY 4.0; their licence names the wording to use, and the exhibit carries it verbatim: “Based on a free chart from www.gapminder.org”). Each keeps its own licence, not this site’s. Benkler, Faris & Roberts’s media ecosystem map is also openly licensed but more tightly: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, which is why it appears here unmodified and with its own caption. Wolfgang Viechtbauer’s forest plot from the metafor documentation is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, shown unmodified on this non-commercial site.
Copyrighted, quoted for criticism: Peter Saville’s Unknown Pleasures sleeve, Simon Scarr’s Iraq’s bloody toll, Autodesk Research’s Datasaurus figure, Chris Harrison and Christoph Römhild’s Bible Cross-References, and Orben & Przybylski’s specification curve (Nature Human Behaviour, 2019; shown from the author-deposited accepted manuscript at ORA). Reproduced at low resolution under the Dutch citation right (Auteurswet art. 15a), which permits quotation for criticism and review where the source is named and the extent is proportionate. Every exhibit page is a critique of the specific work it shows, which is what makes this available. These cannot be reused from here.
Reproduced by its own author: Figure 3 of Masur & Parry (2026), Technology, Mind, and Behavior. © American Psychological Association; shown here by one of the article’s authors under standard APA author reuse rights for teaching. Not reusable from here.


The full copyright position for every case, including the ones whose original is not shown and why, is in gallery/ORIGINALS.md in the repository.




SOFTWARE

Built with Quarto and R. Charts use ggplot2, with ggalluvial, ggraph, tidygraph, ggrepel, patchwork, ggridges, svglite and ragg. Type is Space Grotesk and IBM Plex Sans, both under the SIL Open Font License.
The design system is forked from the sibling course CADC, retuned to a green palette.



CORRECTIONS


If something here is misattributed, under-credited, or reproduced where it should not be, that is a mistake rather than a position. Say so and it will be fixed or removed. A course about honest charts should be easy to correct.

title: The gallery
text:
Cases first, principle second


The gallery

On this page, you’ll find real, published visualizations: some excellent, some bad, and a few that are both beautiful and dishonest. In every lecture, we discuss at least two of them. Here, you can explore the different examples and learn how published visualizations can be recreated with ggplot. Note: The gallery is a work in progress, and we will be adding more cases. It is our slightly “ambitious” attempt to show that everything can be done with ggplot.





GOOD AND BAD, NOT PRETTY AND UGLY


The question is always whether the chart’s claim survives scrutiny, and that does not line up with how it looks. The two most instructive cases are the ugly-but-honest chart, which reports exactly what it found in a badly typeset figure, and the beautiful-and-deceptive one, where good design is doing work the data does not support.




THE CASES

AllComparison & rankingDistribution & uncertaintyRelationships & structureChange over timeThe whole storySearch the galleryThe classicsMade before anyone called it data visualization.Distribution & uncertaintyVan Langren’s longitudesMichael Florent van Langren, 1644Twelve estimates of one distance on one line, usually called the first graph of statistical data. The spread shows at a glance; the bias cannot, until you draw the answer.The whole storyMinard’s march on MoscowCharles Joseph Minard, 1869Six variables and no chart type. The case for composing a figure rather than choosing one.The whole storyNightingale’s rose diagramFlorence Nightingale, 1858Polar area, and a real intervention: the graphic changed government policy. Also a lesson in what area does to a comparison.Comparison & rankingMayr’s radar chartGeorg Mayr, 1877The first radar chart came with a rule: only for a real cycle, where the last spoke belongs next to the first. Break it, and the order of the spokes decides which profile looks bigger.Relationships & structureSnow’s cholera mapJohn Snow, 1855Structure in space, before the vocabulary existed. Published after the pump handle came off: made to argue a conclusion he already held.Relationships & structureThe Hertzsprung–Russell diagramEjnar Hertzsprung 1911, Henry Norris Russell 1913A scatterplot that encodes an entire theory, and a reminder that a basic form can carry a great deal.Distribution & uncertaintyUnknown PleasuresPeter Saville 1979, after Harold Craft 1970A pulsar plot from a radio astronomy thesis, on an album cover. Ridgelines, and a hook that lands in about four seconds.Relationships & structureSankey and alluvial flowsafter Sankey, 1898Coalitions, energy budgets, funnels. Part to whole, over time, without pretending the parts are independent.Change over timePlayfair’s wheat and wagesWilliam Playfair, 1821The inventor of the line chart puts a price and a wage on one time axis, and the gap between them means nothing. Two pages later he draws the ratio, and the argument appears.Comparison & rankingDu Bois’s data portraitsW. E. B. Du Bois and Atlanta University, 1900Made to answer the racist science of 1900 with evidence: one generation after slavery, Black Americans’ illiteracy ranked among the nations of Europe. The comparison set is the argument, and it was a deliberate one.ModernNewsrooms, agencies and research groups, mostly this century.Change over timeWarming stripesEd Hawkins, 2018A century and a half of temperature with no axes at all. The cleanest demonstration that a chart is a claim and not a table.Relationships & structureCartograms and hexbin mapsMagog the Ogre & Drlovedrake, 2020Structure in space, normalised. Land does not vote, and a choropleth of counts quietly says it does.The whole storyWhy outbreaks spread exponentiallyHarry Stevens, Washington Post, 2020A simulation you watch rather than a chart you read, and the most read story in the paper’s history. Argument by letting the reader run it.Change over timePandemic trajectories on a log scaleJohn Burn-Murdoch, Financial Times, 2020Aligned by days since the tenth death rather than by calendar date, on a log axis. Both choices are arguable and both were argued about.Change over timeIraq’s bloody tollSimon Scarr, South China Morning Post, 2011An inverted axis so the bars hang down like blood. The encoding is unconventional, the reading is unambiguous, and it works.Change over timeGun deaths in FloridaChristine Chan, Reuters, 2014The same inverted axis as Scarr, on a rise that now reads as a fall. The article text said deaths went up. Pair it with the one above.Distribution & uncertaintyThe Datasaurus dozenMatejka & Fitzmaurice, Autodesk, 2017Thirteen datasets with identical means, variances and correlations, and nothing else in common. Anscombe’s point, made unignorable.Relationships & structureIncome and life expectancyHans Rosling, Gapminder, from 2006Four variables in a moving scatterplot, and a performance built around it. The case for animation, and the argument against it.Relationships & structureThe Bible’s cross-referencesChris Harrison & Christoph Römhild, 2007Sixty-three thousand arcs, made to be more beautiful than functional. An arc diagram that works because the chapters have an order, and a picture that answers almost nothing you could ask of it.Distribution & uncertaintyThe forest plotWolfgang Viechtbauer, metafor, from 2010Thirteen vaccine trials and one summary diamond. The standard figure of meta-analysis, and a lesson in what a pooled interval does not tell you.From the social sciencesFigures that carry an argument about people, and about method.The whole storyTwo centuries of extreme povertyOur World in Data, after Ravallion, 2019The count of the world’s poorest and the population they belong to, in one picture over two hundred years. Equally confident about the ten reconstructed estimates on its left as about the surveys on its right.Distribution & uncertaintyThe elephant curveLakner & Milanovic, World Bank, 2013Twenty years of income growth across the world’s distribution, read as who won and who lost from globalisation. It compares positions, not people, and the paper says so.Comparison & rankingThe PISA league tableNational Center for Education Statistics, 2023Eighty-one education systems in order, with significance marked against one country only. A printed rank that the data supports only as a range.Change over timeHeadlines turning negativeRozado, Hughes & Halberstadt, PLOS ONE, 2022Machine-coded sentiment of 23 million headlines, by year. A real trend, a percentage change on a scale with no zero, and an average over a growing room.Distribution & uncertaintyConditional effectsMasur & Parry, Technology, Mind, and Behavior, 2026A moderation from our own data, drawn both ways: pick-a-point and the Johnson–Neyman curve. One tells you how big, the other where it holds.Distribution & uncertaintyMany analysts, one datasetSilberzahn et al., 2018Twenty nine teams, one dataset, one question, and answers running from no effect to a large one. This course’s whole thesis, run as an experiment.Distribution & uncertaintyThe specification curveOrben & Przybylski, Nature Human Behaviour, 2019A specification curve over thousands of defensible analyses of the same survey data. The effect is there, and it is the size of eating potatoes.Relationships & structureOriginal against replicationOpen Science Collaboration, Science, 2015One hundred effect sizes, measured twice. A scatterplot where the interesting thing is how far the points sit from the diagonal.Relationships & structureThe asymmetric media ecosystemBenkler, Faris & Roberts, 2018Media Cloud link maps behind Network Propaganda. A network that is legible rather than a hairball, and what had to be decided to get there.Nothing matches that. Show everything

title: Cartograms and hexbin maps
text:
Gallery · Relationships & structure · back to the gallery


Cartograms and hexbin maps

A map is a chart whose areas were decided by geology. Colour those areas by something about people and the biggest, emptiest places shout loudest. Land does not vote, commit crimes or catch diseases, and the choropleth is the chart form that keeps forgetting it.








THE ORIGINAL



“2020 United States presidential election results map by county” by Magog the Ogre, via Wikimedia Commons, dedicated to the public domain under CC0 1.0.



“Results by county of the 2020 United States presidential election with counties scaled by number of votes cast” by Drlovedrake, via Wikimedia Commons, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. It keeps that licence here rather than the site’s.

The first is the map everyone sees on election night. Biden won this election by seven million votes, and you would not guess it from the ink. The second keeps every county and every county’s colour, and corrects only the areas: the result is a different country.
The problem is oldest and clearest in election maps, where an empty county can take hundreds of thousands of times as much ink per vote as a dense one. That ratio is measured further down this page.


How to read it


 A choropleth fills each region with a colour. The quantity is on colour; the area is geography and carries no information at all.


 But area is what the eye adds up. A reader sums coloured ink, so the map reports land area weighted by your variable, which is nobody’s question.


 A cartogram rescales the regions so that area encodes the thing that matters, usually population. Geography is sacrificed on purpose.


 A hex or tile map goes further: every region becomes an identical cell, so area carries nothing and only position hints at geography.





THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

Two maps of the same result. In the first, regions are filled with a colour and their outlines follow real borders, so a few enormous counties dominate the frame. In the second the outlines have been deformed until each county’s area matches its votes, and the familiar shape of the country is gone.



02 · Analyse

Two channels are in play and only one was chosen. Colour carries the variable and is a weak channel. Area carries nothing intentionally and is a strong one. The chart therefore has a loud, uncontrolled encoding sitting on top of a quiet, deliberate one.



03 · Interpret

Whatever the author meant, what a reader takes away is roughly “how much of the map is this colour”, which is a statement about territory. For anything measured on people, that is the wrong denominator before the colour scale is even chosen.



04 · Judge

Defensible only when the quantity really is about land, or when it has already been normalised and the reader is being asked where, not how much. Two fixes exist and they are different: normalising turns counts into rates and keeps the geography; a cartogram keeps the counts and throws the geography away. Choosing between them is choosing which question the map answers.





THE RECREATION

Both originals, from the same 3,152 county results and the same county outlines. Nothing changes between the two panels except what area means.


Show the R code
choropleth <- ggplot(county_xy, aes(long, lat, group = group, fill = margin)) +
  geom_polygon(linewidth = 0) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = vote_cols, limits = c(-1, 1),
                       na.value = "#eeece5",
                       labels = scales::label_percent(),
                       name = "Margin (Democratic − Republican)",
                       guide = guide_colourbar(title.position = "top",
                                               title.hjust = .5)) +
  labs(title = "As the originals draw it: one colour per county",
       subtitle = "Area is land. Biden won this election by 7.1 million votes") +
  theme_void(base_family = dsvar_font()) +
  theme(plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11, hjust = 0),
        plot.subtitle   = element_text(size = 9, colour = "#5a5a52", hjust = 0),
        legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.key.height = unit(6, "pt"), legend.key.width = unit(26, "pt"),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 8), legend.text = element_text(size = 7),
        plot.margin = margin(b = 14))

# The Dorling: every county becomes a circle at its centre, area = votes cast.
# A true contiguous cartogram deforms the borders instead; the circle version
# makes the same correction and is reachable with a geom you already know.
dorling <- ggplot(centroids, aes(long, lat)) +
  geom_polygon(data = states, aes(long, lat, group = group),
               fill = "#f2f0ea", colour = "white", linewidth = .2) +
  geom_point(aes(size = total_votes, fill = margin), shape = 21,
             colour = "white", stroke = .15) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 11, guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = vote_cols, limits = c(-1, 1),
                       na.value = "grey80", guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Area corrected to votes: a Dorling cartogram",
       subtitle = "Same counties, same colours. Only the areas were fixed") +
  theme_void(base_family = dsvar_font()) +
  theme(plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11, hjust = 0),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9, colour = "#5a5a52", hjust = 0))

choropleth / dorling










3,152 counties in the results file; 99.4% of the map’s polygon vertices join to one. The misses are the known awkward cases (independent cities, Alaska’s boroughs, counties renamed since the maps outlines were drawn), and they render grey. Alaska and Hawaii are absent from the outlines entirely.



A DORLING IS NOT THE SAME AS THE ORIGINAL CARTOGRAM

Drlovedrake’s map is contiguous: the county borders themselves are pushed and stretched until each area matches its votes, so the country stays joined up and stays recognisable. The Dorling here replaces each county with a circle instead. It makes the identical correction (area now means votes) and needs nothing beyond geom_point(), but it gives up the borders. Contiguous cartograms need an iterative algorithm over real polygons (the cartogram package, on sf geometry). The point being taught survives the substitution, which is why it is here.




THE MISMATCH, STATED DIRECTLY



Show the R code
# The two extremes of the map-ink-per-vote ratio, plus the two biggest counties
# by each of the axes.
big <- county_area |>
  slice_max(area, n = 2) |>
  bind_rows(slice_max(county_area, total_votes, n = 2),
            slice_max(county_area, area / total_votes, n = 1),
            slice_min(county_area, area / total_votes, n = 1)) |>
  mutate(label = paste0(str_remove(county_name, " County"), ", ",
                        state.abb[match(state_name, state.name)]))

ggplot(county_area, aes(area, total_votes)) +
  geom_point(colour = dsvar_accent(), size = .7, alpha = .25) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = big, aes(label = label), size = 2.8,
                           family = dsvar_font(), seed = 4, box.padding = .6,
                           segment.size = .2, bg.color = "#faf8f4", bg.r = .12) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title = sprintf("Land area tells you nothing about votes (r = %.2f)",
                       cor(log(county_area$area), log(county_area$total_votes))),
       subtitle = "US counties, 2020 presidential election. Both axes logarithmic",
       x = "Land area (square miles, log)", y = "Votes cast (log)",
       caption = sprintf("n = %s counties · area computed from the polygon outlines",
                         scales::comma(nrow(county_area))))










The correlation is -0.05: on logarithmic axes, across three thousand counties, land area and voters are unrelated. Loving County, Texas gets 9 square miles of map per vote. Manhattan gets one square mile for every 38,899 votes.


Every square mile gets an equal vote in the reader’s impression, and square miles are handed out almost independently of people.




COUNTS AND SHARES ARE DIFFERENT MAPS



Show the R code
county_map <- function(fill, title, sub, lab, labels) {
  ggplot(county_xy, aes(long, lat, group = group, fill = {{ fill }})) +
    geom_polygon(linewidth = 0) +
    coord_quickmap() +
    scale_fill_gradientn(colours = dsvar_ramp_light, name = lab,
                         labels = labels, na.value = "#eeece5") +
    labs(title = title, subtitle = sub) +
    theme_void(base_family = dsvar_font()) +
    theme(plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11, hjust = 0),
          plot.subtitle   = element_text(size = 9, colour = "#5a5a52", hjust = 0),
          legend.position = "bottom",
          legend.key.height = unit(6, "pt"), legend.key.width = unit(26, "pt"),
          legend.title = element_text(size = 8), legend.text = element_text(size = 7))
}

county_map(votes_dem, "Democratic votes, as a count",
           "Los Angeles sets the scale and flattens everything else", "Votes",
           scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale())) +
county_map(per_dem, "Democratic votes, as a share",
           "Normalised: a completely different map", "Share",
           scales::label_percent())










Same data, same outlines, same colour ramp. The left map is unreadable because one county (Los Angeles, with 3,028,885 Democratic votes) sets a scale nothing else can compete on. The right map is readable and answers a different question.



NORMALISING AND RESCALING ARE NOT THE SAME FIX

The share map and the cartogram both repair the count map, and they answer different questions. Normalising keeps real geography and tells you where support was strong, but it makes a county of 400 voters as visually important as one of two million, so a handful of ballots in an empty county shouts. A cartogram keeps the magnitudes and destroys the geography, so regional pattern becomes hard to read. The Dorling above does both at once (area for voters, colour for margin), which is usually the honest compromise and is also the least familiar to readers.




THE OPTION NOBODY OFFERS YOU



Show the R code
by_state <- elec |>
  summarise(dem = sum(votes_dem), gop = sum(votes_gop),
            votes = sum(total_votes), .by = state_name) |>
  mutate(margin = (dem - gop) / votes)

ggplot(by_state, aes(margin, fct_reorder(state_name, margin))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#a5a199", linewidth = .4) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = 0, yend = fct_reorder(state_name, margin)),
               colour = "#d8d3c7", linewidth = .3) +
  geom_point(aes(size = votes, fill = margin), shape = 21,
             colour = "#8a867e", stroke = .25) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 5.5, guide = "none") +
  # Squished at +/- 40 points: state margins never approach the +/- 100 the
  # county map needs, so the county scale would leave every state near-white.
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = vote_cols, limits = c(-.4, .4),
                       oob = scales::squish, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(title = "The same election, ranked instead of mapped",
       subtitle = "Dot size is votes cast. Precise, sortable, and not a map",
       x = "Margin (Democratic − Republican)", y = NULL,
       caption = sprintf("n = %d states and DC · county results summed",
                         nrow(by_state) - 1L)) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 6.5))










Before reaching for any map, ask whether the reader’s question is geographic. “Which states were closest?” is a ranking question and a sorted dot plot answers it better than every map on this page. A map earns its place when the answer is spatial: when neighbouring regions resembling each other is part of the finding. If you cannot say what the geography is contributing, you have drawn a very expensive bar chart.




SOURCES


The form: Dorling, D. (1996). Area Cartograms: Their Use and Creation. See also Mark Newman’s US election cartograms, personal.umich.edu/~mejn/election.
On maps that mislead: Monmonier, M. How to Lie with Maps. And Wilke, Fundamentals of Data Visualization, chapter on geospatial data.
Data: county results compiled by Tony McGovern scraped from Fox News, Politico and New York Times results pages, MIT licence. Vendored as data/raw/us-county-2020-president.csv. Outlines are ggplot2::map_data() and maps::county.fips, shipped with R.
Going further: the cartogram package builds true contiguous cartograms on sf geometry, and geofacet and statebins give the tile-map treatment this page describes but does not draw.
The modifiable areal unit problem: the companion issue this page does not cover: the boundaries you choose change the answer, and counties are an arbitrary unit.
Reproduce it: every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: The Datasaurus dozen
text:
Gallery · Distribution & uncertainty · back to the gallery


The Datasaurus dozen

Thirteen datasets with the same mean, the same standard deviation and the same correlation, to two decimal places. One of them is a dinosaur. It is the most efficient argument ever made for plotting your data before you summarise it.








THE ORIGINAL



“Same Stats, Different Graphs” by Justin Matejka and George Fitzmaurice, Autodesk Research, CHI ’17. Copyright Autodesk Research, reproduced for criticism and review under the Dutch citation right (Auteurswet art. 15a). The underlying data is separately MIT licensed, in the datasauRus R package.

This is the figure Justin Matejka and George Fitzmaurice use to set up their argument. On the left is Anscombe’s quartet (1973): four sets of eleven points with the same means, standard deviations, correlation and regression line, which look nothing alike. On the right are four datasets with matching statistics that look like nothing in particular. Their point is that Anscombe’s four are rare. Datasets with the same statistics are easy to make; datasets with the same statistics and clearly different shapes are not. The rest of their paper is a method for making them on demand, which is where the dinosaur comes from.


How to read it


 Each panel is a complete dataset. They are different datasets, not different views of one.


 Within each quartet the summary statistics match: the mean and standard deviation of x and of y, and the correlation between them.


 The grey line is the same in every panel: the least-squares fit, which the matching statistics fix in place.


 The ticks carry no numbers. Only the shapes are there to compare. The green tick and the red cross are the authors’ verdict: one quartet makes the point, the other does not.





THE RECREATION

The left half of the original, from datasets::anscombe, which ships with R. The axes are measured off the original: both run from 2, ticked every 2.


Show the R code
fit <- coef(lm(y ~ x, data = filter(quartet, set == "I")))   # the same for all four

ggplot(quartet, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = fit[1], slope = fit[2], colour = "grey78", linewidth = .6) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey15", size = 2.4) +
  geom_text(data = distinct(quartet, set), aes(label = set), x = 19.6, y = 2.6,
            hjust = 1, vjust = 0, family = "serif", fontface = "bold",
            size = 11, colour = "grey60") +
  facet_wrap(~set, ncol = 2, axes = "all") +   # every panel its own axes, as drawn
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2, 20, 2), limits = c(2, 20), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(2, 14, 2), limits = c(2, 14), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(title = "Anscombe's Quartet",
       subtitle = "Each dataset has the same summary statistics, and the datasets are clearly different") +
  theme_void(base_family = dsvar_font()) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, margin = margin(b = 4)),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10.5, margin = margin(b = 14)),
        axis.line = element_line(colour = "grey45", linewidth = .4),
        axis.ticks = element_line(colour = "grey45", linewidth = .4),
        axis.ticks.length = unit(4, "pt"),
        strip.text = element_blank(),
        panel.spacing = unit(18, "pt"),
        plot.margin = margin(12, 16, 12, 12))









Show the R code
q_stats <- quartet |>
  group_by(set) |>
  summarise(mx = mean(x), my = mean(y), sx = sd(x), sy = sd(y), r = cor(x, y))



n = 11 points per dataset. All four have a mean x of 9, a mean y of 7.5, a correlation of 0.82 and the same fitted line, y = 3 + 0.5x, computed here rather than quoted. Anscombe built them by hand. The right half of the original, the “unstructured” quartet, is not recreated: this page has the data for Anscombe’s four and for the dozen below, but not for those.




FROM FOUR TO THIRTEEN

Anscombe’s four took craft. Matejka and Fitzmaurice automated it, starting from Alberto Cairo’s “Datasaurus”, a scatterplot shaped like a dinosaur with unremarkable summary statistics. Their method is simulated annealing: nudge points at random, keep a nudge if it moves the shape towards a target while holding the statistics fixed, repeat. Twelve targets later, the dinosaur has a dozen siblings.


Show the R code
ggplot(dino, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(colour = dsvar_accent(), alpha = .65, size = .8) +
  facet_wrap(~dataset, ncol = 5) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Thirteen datasets. Same mean, same SD, same correlation.",
       subtitle = "Every panel: 142 points, identical summary statistics to two decimal places",
       x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = "n = 142 per dataset · Matejka & Fitzmaurice (2017), via datasauRus") +
  theme_dsvar(base_size = 9, grid = "none") +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank())












THE CLAIM, CHECKED

The page above asserts the statistics are identical. That is exactly the kind of claim this course says to verify rather than repeat, so here it is computed.


Show the R code
stats <- dino |>
  group_by(dataset) |>
  summarise(mean_x = mean(x), mean_y = mean(y),
            sd_x = sd(x), sd_y = sd(y), r = cor(x, y), .groups = "drop")

stats |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(v) round(v, 2))) |>
  knitr::kable()

identical_to_2dp <- rounded |> select(-dataset) |> distinct() |> nrow() == 1
spread <- stats |> summarise(across(where(is.numeric), \(v) max(v) - min(v)))


All thirteen agree to two decimal places: FALSE. At full precision they differ by at most 0.01 on any of the five statistics: the annealing gets close, not exact, and rounding does the rest.



WHAT A SUMMARY WOULD HAVE TOLD YOU



Show the R code
ggplot(dino, aes(dataset, y)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#dfe6e2", colour = "#5a5a52", linewidth = .35,
               outlier.size = .7) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "y",
       title = "The same thirteen datasets, as boxplots",
       subtitle = "A dinosaur, a star and a bullseye, rendered indistinguishable",
       caption = "n = 142 per dataset") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1, size = 7))










Boxplots are not the villain here: they do what they were designed to do, which is to throw away the shape and keep the quartiles. The mistake is asking a summary to tell you whether you need to look, because you cannot know a summary is sufficient without first looking at what it summarised.




SHOWING THE SHAPE INSTEAD



Show the R code
ggplot(dino, aes(y, after_stat(density))) +
  geom_density(fill = dsvar_accent(), colour = NA, alpha = .8, bw = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~dataset, ncol = 5, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "y", y = NULL,
       title = "The marginal distribution of y, per dataset",
       subtitle = "One number cannot say this, and one boxplot chose not to",
       caption = "n = 142 per dataset · bandwidth fixed at 3 so the panels are comparable") +
  theme_dsvar(base_size = 9, grid = "none") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())










Even the one-dimensional distribution separates them, once it is drawn rather than summarised. The bandwidth is fixed across panels on purpose: letting each panel pick its own would make them look more alike than they are.




SOURCES


Original: Matejka, J., & Fitzmaurice, G. (2017). Same stats, different graphs: Generating datasets with varied appearance and identical statistics through simulated annealing. Proceedings of the 2017 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, 1290–1294.
The ancestor: Anscombe, F. J. (1973). Graphs in statistical analysis. The American Statistician, 27(1), 17–21. And Alberto Cairo’s original Datasaurus.
Data: datasets::anscombe, shipped with R, for the quartet. datasaurus_dozen from the datasauRus package (MIT licence) for the thirteen, vendored here as data/raw/datasaurus.csv. Autodesk attaches no licence to the data and welcomed the package; MIT is the package’s.
Reproduce it: every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: The elephant curve
text:
Gallery · Distribution & uncertainty · back to the gallery


The elephant curve

Twenty years of income growth across the whole world’s distribution, in one line: big gains in the middle, big gains at the very top, almost nothing just below the top. It became the picture of who won and who lost from globalisation. It compares positions, not people, and its own authors say so.








THE ORIGINAL



Figure 1(a): Global growth incidence curve, 1988–2008, from Global Income Distribution: From the Fall of the Berlin Wall to the Great Recession by Christoph Lakner and Branko Milanovic, World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 6719, December 2013, doi:10.1596/1813-9450-6719. © World Bank, licensed CC BY 3.0 IGO (Open Knowledge Repository). Extracted from the PDF and reproduced unaltered; it keeps its own licence, not this site’s.

Christoph Lakner and Branko Milanovic, both at the World Bank, combined household surveys from more than a hundred countries into one distribution of the world’s income for 1988, 1993, 1998, 2003 and 2008. This is the first panel of their first figure. Its shape, a body, a dip, and a trunk raised at the right, later gave it its name, and Milanovic’s 2016 book Global Inequality made it famous. The journal version of the paper, in the World Bank Economic Review, carries a no-derivatives licence; this is the working paper’s figure, which does not.


How to read it


 Left to right is position in the world’s income distribution, poorest to richest. Each point is a group of the world’s population: twenty slices of 5%, except that the richest slice is split into the next 4% and the top 1%.


 Up is growth: how much the average income of that slice rose between 1988 and 2008, in per cent, after inflation and in prices comparable across countries.


 The dashed line is the world’s average: the mean income grew 24.34% over the twenty years, 1.1% a year. Above it, a slice gained more than the average.


 A slice is a position, not a set of people. The 80th percentile of 1988 and the 80th percentile of 2008 are whoever stood there in each year.





THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

One line through 21 markers on a percentile axis. It starts at 15% for the poorest 5%, climbs to 76% at the P50-P55 slice, drops to 1% at P75-P80, then rises steeply to 65% for the top 1%. A dashed red line marks the average, and a three-line note explains the axes. Stata’s default look.



02 · Analyse

Position in the distribution on x, relative growth on y, and a line joining groups that are categories rather than a continuous series. Every point is a percentage change, so a slice that started with $200 a year and one that started with $39,000 share one scale. The x axis is honest about widths: the top 1% sits one percentile from the P95–P99 point. But the line drawn to it turns a group of one person in a hundred into the tallest stroke on the chart.



03 · Interpret

The reading the chart became known for: globalisation’s winners were the middle of the world’s distribution, much of it in China and the rest of Asia, and the global top 1%; the people who gained almost nothing were around the 80th percentile, which in 1988 meant mostly the lower and middle classes of rich countries and Latin America. The trunk and the dip together became a picture of two kinds of people, a global elite and a squeezed Western middle.



04 · Judge

Accurate for what it measures, and easy to read as something else. It compares the income of whoever held a position in 1988 with whoever held it in 2008, and the people changed. The paper says so plainly: “It is these compositional changes which explain the shape of the global GIC.” Chinese households moved up into the 70th to 85th percentiles; compare their 2008 incomes with the Latin American incomes that sat there in 1988 and the growth looks small, “despite the fact that the top Chinese incomes have grown substantially faster than the global average.” The authors also show that following fixed country-deciles gives a similar shape. The chart is not wrong, but the sentence people put under it, about what happened to the people at the 80th percentile, is something it cannot show.





THE RECREATION

The 21 points, digitised from the figure (see below), drawn in Stata’s s2color look at the original’s proportions.


Show the R code
sans <- c(intersect(c("Arial", "Helvetica"), systemfonts::system_fonts()$family), "sans")[1]
navy  <- "#1a476f"   # Stata s2color's first line colour, sampled off the original
title <- "#1e2d53"
red   <- "#c71c47"
ground <- "#eaf2f3"

note <- paste(
  "Y-axis displays the growth rate of the fractile average income (in 2005 PPP USD). Weighted by population.",
  "Growth incidence evaluated at ventile groups (e.g. bottom 5%); top ventile is split into top 1% and 4% between P95 and P99.",
  sprintf("The horizontal line shows the growth rate in the mean of %.2f%% (1.1%% p.a.).", MEAN_GROWTH),
  sep = "\n")

recreation <- ggplot(gic, aes(x_plotted, growth_pct)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = MEAN_GROWTH, colour = red, linewidth = .75, linetype = "42") +
  geom_line(colour = navy, linewidth = .75) +
  geom_point(colour = navy, size = 2.6) +
  # Stata's axis: a tick at every fifth percentile and one more at 99, with
  # labels on some of them only
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(seq(5, 95, 5), 99),
                     labels = \(x) if_else(x %in% c(5, 10, seq(20, 90, 10), 95, 99), as.character(x), ""),
                     expand = expansion(add = c(1.8, 1.4))) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 80, 10), limits = c(-2.6, 82.4), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(title = "Figure 1(a): Global growth incidence curve, 1988-2008",
       x = "Percentiles of the global income distribution",
       y = "Cumulative growth rate %", caption = note) +
  theme_classic(base_family = sans, base_size = 15) +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = ground, colour = NA),
        panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_line(colour = "#eaf2f3", linewidth = .6),
        plot.title = element_text(colour = title, hjust = .5, size = 18.5,
                                  margin = margin(b = 6)),
        axis.text = element_text(colour = "black", size = 14),
        axis.text.y = element_text(hjust = 1),
        axis.ticks = element_line(colour = "black", linewidth = .5),
        axis.ticks.length = unit(5, "pt"),
        axis.title.x = element_text(size = 18, margin = margin(t = 4)),
        axis.title.y = element_text(size = 18, margin = margin(r = 8)),
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 10.4, lineheight = 1,
                                    margin = margin(t = 10)),
        plot.caption.position = "plot",
        plot.margin = margin(10, 22, 10, 10))

recreation










n = 21 fractile groups, digitised from the original. Drawn at its 1002 × 713 proportions in Stata’s colours, so the two can be compared directly.




Original · Lakner & Milanovic, 2013





Ours · ggplot















HOW WE KNOW

Why the points are digitised. The curve is computed from the authors’ World Panel Income Distribution, incomes by decile for each country and benchmark year. The World Bank’s download links for it return “Access Denied”, and no other copy states its terms of use, so it is not in this repository. The figure is CC BY 3.0 IGO. R/digitise-elephant.R reads the 21 markers off it: the line and the markers share one colour, and shrinking that colour’s pixels by four in each direction erases the thin line and leaves the centre of each round marker. The axis ticks turn pixels into percentiles and per cent.
Checked against the paper’s own numbers. Three of the 21 slices appear as single rows of the paper’s Table 3:


Show the R code
single <- tibble(
  check   = c("P90-P95", "P95-P99", "Top 1%"),
  printed = c(16.6, 26.9, 64.8),
  read    = gic$growth_pct[match(check, gic$group)]
) |> mutate(difference = round(read - printed, 2))
knitr::kable(single, col.names = c("Slice", "Table 3 (%)", "Read off the figure (%)", "Difference"))

Read to within 0.11 of a percentage point.
And two things that do not add up. Table 3 also prints five wider groups. A group made of two slices has to have grown at a rate between those of its two slices, because its income is their sum. Three of the five pass. Two do not:


Show the R code
pairs <- table3 |>
  filter(group %in% c("Bottom 10%", "P40-P50", "P50-P60", "P60-P70", "P80-P90")) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(slices = list(filter(gic, pop_from >= from, pop_to <= to)$growth_pct),
         low = min(slices), high = max(slices),
         from_incomes = round(100 * (inc_2008 / inc_1988 - 1), 1),
         verdict = if_else(growth_printed >= low & growth_printed <= high,
                           "between its slices", "outside")) |>
  ungroup() |>
  transmute(group, growth_printed, from_incomes,
            slices = sprintf("%.1f to %.1f", low, high), verdict)

The table is consistent with itself: its printed growth rates follow from its printed incomes. The figure has the P40–P50 slices at about 66 and 67 per cent where the table has the group at 70.6, and the P60–P70 slices a little above the table. The paper does not say why. The digitising is not the cause: it reproduces the three single-slice rows above to within a fifth of a point. The shape survives either way, but the exact height of the elephant’s back depends on which of the paper’s two presentations you read.



THE SAME TWENTY YEARS, OTHER CHOICES


Give each slice its width


Show the R code
ggplot(gic) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = pop_from, xmax = pop_to, ymin = 0, ymax = growth_pct),
            fill = dsvar_accent(), colour = p$paper, linewidth = .4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = MEAN_GROWTH, colour = p$ink_3, linewidth = .4, linetype = "22") +
  annotate("text", x = 75.6, y = MEAN_GROWTH + 2.5, hjust = 0, size = 3.1,
           family = dsvar_font(), colour = p$ink_3,
           label = sprintf("the world's mean: +%.1f%%", MEAN_GROWTH)) +
  annotate("text", x = 98.6, y = top1$growth_pct + 3, hjust = 1, size = 3.1,
           family = dsvar_font(), colour = p$ink_2, label = "top 1% →") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, 10), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = \(x) paste0(x, "%"), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .05))) +
  labs(title = "Drawn with its true width, the trunk is a sliver: one person in a hundred",
       subtitle = "Growth in average income by slice of the world's distribution, 1988–2008; each bar as wide as its share of people",
       x = "Percentile of the global income distribution", y = NULL,
       caption = "21 slices, digitised from Lakner & Milanovic (2013), Figure 1(a)") +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())










The line in the original is honest about where the top 1% sits on the axis, but a line has no width, so the eye weighs each point equally. Bars that are as wide as the share of people they stand for put the trunk in proportion. The body of the elephant, the slices from the 10th to the 70th percentile, is six people in ten, and the trunk is one in a hundred.



In dollars instead of per cent


Show the R code
gains <- table3 |>
  mutate(gain = inc_2008 - inc_1988,
         group = fct_reorder(group, from))
ratio <- with(gains, gain[group == "Top 1%"] / gain[group == "P50-P60"])

ggplot(gains, aes(gain, group)) +
  geom_col(fill = dsvar_accent(), width = .7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::dollar(gain)), hjust = -.12, size = 3.2,
            family = dsvar_font(), colour = p$ink_2) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .12))) +
  labs(title = sprintf("In dollars, the top 1%% gained %.0f times as much as the group at the peak of the elephant's back", ratio),
       subtitle = "Gain in average annual income per person, 1988 to 2008, 2005 PPP dollars",
       x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = "The eight groups printed in Lakner & Milanovic (2013), Table 3") +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = p$hairline))










The P50–P60 group grew by 72%, the top 1% by 65%, so in per cent they are neighbours; in dollars, one gained $568 a year and the other $25,249. The paper draws this too, as Figure 1(d), on a logarithmic axis. Which of the two is “growth” is a choice, and the elephant is the choice that makes the middle look like the winner.


A growth incidence curve answers “how did each position in the distribution change?”, and the sentence it is usually given is “how did these people fare?”. The two come apart whenever people move between positions, and over twenty years of the fastest catch-up in history, hundreds of millions did. The chart cannot warn you about that; only a sentence under it can, and in the paper there is one.





SOURCES


Original: Lakner, C., & Milanovic, B. (2013). Global income distribution: From the fall of the Berlin Wall to the Great Recession. Policy Research Working Paper 6719. World Bank. doi:10.1596/1813-9450-6719. CC BY 3.0 IGO, checked on the Open Knowledge Repository record, 9 October 2026.
Not reproduced: the journal version, Lakner & Milanovic (2016), World Bank Economic Review, is CC BY-NC-ND 3.0 IGO, which does not allow derivatives.
The book: Milanovic, B. (2016). Global Inequality: A New Approach for the Age of Globalization. Harvard University Press.
Data: the 21 points of Figure 1(a), digitised by R/digitise-elephant.R into data/raw/lakner-milanovic-gic-1988-2008.csv; the eight income groups typed in from the paper’s Table 3. The underlying World Panel Income Distribution (LM-WPID) is not included: its download links are dead and its terms could not be checked.
Reproduce it: every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: The forest plot
text:
Gallery · Distribution & uncertainty · back to the gallery


The forest plot

Thirteen trials of one vaccine, each drawn as an estimate and an interval, and a diamond underneath that says what they amount to together. It is the standard figure of evidence synthesis, so standard that it is easy to stop reading it. The diamond is the part everyone quotes, and it answers a narrower question than most readers think.








THE ORIGINAL



“Forest Plot” by Wolfgang Viechtbauer, The metafor Package plot gallery, page last modified 30 June 2026. Licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Reproduced unmodified; it keeps its own licence, not this site’s.

The figure the metafor documentation uses to show what forest() does, drawn from the BCG vaccine dataset that ships with the package (Colditz et al., 1994). Base R graphics, nine lines of code, published with that code beside it, which is what lets us check our recreation number by number.


How to read it


 Each row is one trial. The four counts are the 2 × 2 table it reported: people who did (TB+) and did not (TB−) develop tuberculosis, among the vaccinated and among the controls.


 The square is the trial’s risk ratio: the TB rate among the vaccinated divided by the rate among controls. Left of the dotted line at 1 means the vaccine helped. The square’s size says how much weight the trial gets in the pooled estimate.


 The line is its 95% confidence interval. An arrow means the interval runs off the edge of the axis.


 The axis is logarithmic. 0.25 and 4 are the same distance from 1 because halving and doubling a risk are symmetric changes.


 The diamond is the random-effects summary. Its centre is the pooled risk ratio and its tips are that estimate’s 95% interval. The text beside it reports how much the trials disagree (Q, I², τ²).





THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

A table and a chart fused into one figure. Thirteen rows of text and counts on the left, a dot-and-interval plot in the middle on a log axis with a reference line at no effect, the same estimates printed as numbers on the right, and a summary diamond under a rule at the bottom. Alternate rows are shaded. There is no colour.



02 · Analyse

Position on a common scale for the estimate, length for the uncertainty, area for the weight. The log axis is the right call for a ratio, and the dotted line at 1 does what the diagonal does in Original against replication: it turns every interval into a yes-or-no question you can answer by eye. The printed numbers duplicate the chart on purpose, because a meta-analysis is read by people who will want to cite them. The rows are in the dataset’s order, which is the order the trials were numbered in, not an order that means anything.



03 · Interpret

The claim is that BCG roughly halves the risk of tuberculosis: a pooled risk ratio of 0.49, with an interval well clear of 1. The figure makes that claim with the diamond. Everything above the bottom rule is the evidence; the diamond is the verdict.



04 · Judge

An honest and very well made figure that hands the reader a trap. The heterogeneity statistics are printed right beside the diamond (I² of 92%, meaning almost all the spread between trials is real rather than noise), but as text, while the diamond is drawn as a shape, and a reader looks at the shape. The diamond says how precisely we know the average effect; it says nothing about what the next trial will find, and with this much disagreement those are very different intervals.
