Two more things the figure cannot show: that the disagreement has a cause, and that the squares exaggerate the differences in weight. Both are below.





THE RECREATION

The original is base R graphics, and forest() gets its table-plus-chart layout from one trick: it draws everything, text columns included, in the coordinate system of the log risk ratio. The author names sit at an x of −16, the counts at −9.5 to −4.5, the risk ratios printed at +6. The recreation uses the same trick in ggplot: one panel, one coordinate system, every column a geom_text() at a fixed x.


Show the R code
alim  <- log(c(.05, 4))          # forest() sets the axis limits to range(at)
ticks <- log(c(.05, .25, 1, 4))
sw    <- sqrt(wt)

trials <- as_tibble(dat) |>
  mutate(row   = k:1,             # first trial at the top
         label = paste(author, year, sep = ", "),
         lo    = yi - qnorm(.975) * sqrt(vi),
         hi    = yi + qnorm(.975) * sqrt(vi),
         annot = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", exp(yi), exp(lo), exp(hi)),
         # forest()'s default point size: square root of the weight, rescaled
         # linearly onto 0.5 to 1.5. See "How we know" below.
         weight = wt,
         psize = .5 + (sw - min(sw)) / diff(range(sw)),
         shade = row %% 2 == 1)

counts <- trials |>
  select(row, tpos, tneg, cpos, cneg) |>
  pivot_longer(-row) |>
  mutate(x = c(tpos = -9.5, tneg = -8, cpos = -6, cneg = -4.5)[name])

diamond <- tibble(x = c(res$ci.lb, res$b[1], res$ci.ub, res$b[1]),
                  y = -1 + c(0, .17, 0, -.17))

# One interval runs past the axis limit; forest() clips it and draws an arrow.
arrows <- trials |>
  filter(hi > alim[2]) |>
  reframe(x = alim[2] - c(.23, 0, .23), y = row + c(-.12, 0, .12), row = row)

re_label <- sprintf(
  "plain('RE Model (Q = %.2f, df = %d, p < .001; ')*I^2*' = %.1f%%, '*tau^2*' = %.2f)'",
  res$QE, k - 1, res$I2, res$tau2)

# The original sits on a grey ground (#DDDDDD) with darker stripes (#CCCCCC),
# sampled off its pixels. The ground is not part of the chart's argument, so
# ours is white; the stripes stay, one step lighter, because they help the eye
# along a row.
ink <- "black"; ground <- "white"; zebra <- "#EEEEEE"
fs  <- 3.9  # text size, in mm

p_forest <- ggplot() +
  geom_rect(data = filter(trials, shade),
            aes(xmin = -16, xmax = 6, ymin = row - .5, ymax = row + .5),
            fill = zebra) +
  annotate("segment", x = -16, xend = 6, y = c(k + 1, 0), yend = c(k + 1, 0),
           linewidth = .45, colour = ink) +
  annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = 0, y = -1.5, yend = k + 1,
           linetype = "13", linewidth = .4, colour = ink) +
  # intervals, clipped to the axis, with end caps only where they are not
  geom_segment(data = trials,
               aes(x = pmax(lo, alim[1]), xend = pmin(hi, alim[2]), y = row, yend = row),
               linewidth = .35, colour = ink) +
  geom_segment(data = filter(trials, lo >= alim[1]),
               aes(x = lo, xend = lo, y = row - .14, yend = row + .14),
               linewidth = .35, colour = ink) +
  geom_segment(data = filter(trials, hi <= alim[2]),
               aes(x = hi, xend = hi, y = row - .14, yend = row + .14),
               linewidth = .35, colour = ink) +
  geom_polygon(data = arrows, aes(x, y, group = row), fill = ink) +
  geom_point(data = trials, aes(yi, row, size = psize * 2.49),
             shape = 15, stroke = 0, colour = ink) +
  geom_polygon(data = diamond, aes(x, y), fill = ink) +
  # the axis, drawn by hand: it spans the axis limits, not the panel
  annotate("segment", x = alim[1], xend = alim[2], y = -2.05, yend = -2.05,
           linewidth = .45, colour = ink) +
  annotate("segment", x = ticks, xend = ticks, y = -2.05, yend = -2.42,
           linewidth = .45, colour = ink) +
  annotate("text", x = ticks, y = -3.2, label = c("0.05", "0.25", "1", "4"),
           size = fs, colour = ink) +
  annotate("text", x = mean(alim), y = -4.3, label = "Risk Ratio (log scale)",
           size = fs, colour = ink) +
  # the table, in the same coordinates as the chart
  geom_text(data = trials, aes(-15.69, row, label = label),
            hjust = 0, size = fs, colour = ink) +
  geom_text(data = counts, aes(x, row - .05, label = value), size = fs, colour = ink) +
  geom_text(data = trials, aes(5.69, row, label = annot),
            hjust = 1, size = fs, colour = ink) +
  annotate("text", x = -15.69, y = k + 2, label = "Author(s) and Year",
           hjust = 0, size = fs, fontface = "bold", colour = ink) +
  annotate("text", x = 5.69, y = k + 2, label = "Risk Ratio [95% CI]",
           hjust = 1, size = fs, fontface = "bold", colour = ink) +
  annotate("text", x = c(-9.5, -8, -6, -4.5), y = k + 1.97,
           label = c("TB+", "TB-", "TB+", "TB-"),
           size = fs, fontface = "bold", colour = ink) +
  annotate("text", x = c(-8.75, -5.25), y = k + 2.8, label = c("Vaccinated", "Control"),
           size = fs, fontface = "bold", colour = ink) +
  annotate("text", x = -15.69, y = -1, hjust = 0, size = fs, colour = ink,
           parse = TRUE, label = re_label) +
  annotate("text", x = 5.69, y = -1, hjust = 1, size = fs, colour = ink,
           label = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", pi_$pred, pi_$ci.lb, pi_$ci.ub)) +
  scale_size_identity() +
  # The panel limits are the original's plot region plus its margins, measured
  # off the image: xlim = c(-16, 6) is forest()'s own, the rest is the margin.
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-16.62, 6.62), ylim = c(-5, 16.74), expand = FALSE) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = ground, colour = NA))

p_forest









Show the R code
# Checked, not asserted: the 14 intervals as printed on the original, typed in
# from the image, against what we compute.
printed <- c("0.41 [0.13, 1.26]", "0.20 [0.09, 0.49]", "0.26 [0.07, 0.92]",
             "0.24 [0.18, 0.31]", "0.80 [0.52, 1.25]", "0.46 [0.39, 0.54]",
             "0.20 [0.08, 0.50]", "1.01 [0.89, 1.14]", "0.63 [0.39, 1.00]",
             "0.25 [0.15, 0.43]", "0.71 [0.57, 0.89]", "1.56 [0.37, 6.53]",
             "0.98 [0.58, 1.66]", "0.49 [0.34, 0.70]")
ours <- c(trials$annot, sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", pi_$pred, pi_$ci.lb, pi_$ci.ub))
n_match <- sum(printed == ours)



n = 13 trials, 357,347 participants. Random-effects model, REML, fitted with metafor::rma() exactly as the original’s code does. 14 of the 14 printed intervals match the original to the second decimal. Rendered at the original’s 9 × 7 proportions so the two can be compared directly. Data: Colditz et al. (1994), via the metadat package (GPL).




Original · metafor





Ours · ggplot













Side by side, at the same size. The remaining differences are the typeface (the original’s PNG device used Arial, ours Helvetica) and sub-pixel placement of the text.




HOW WE KNOW THE SQUARES ARE THAT SIZE

The original’s code does not set the size of the squares, so forest() falls back on a default, and the documentation describes it only loosely. The rule, read out of the function’s source: take the square root of each trial’s weight, then stretch those values linearly so the smallest becomes 0.5 and the largest 1.5, and use that as the symbol size. The colours are not documented at all; sampled off the original’s pixels, the ground is #DDDDDD and the stripes #CCCCCC. Our version keeps the stripes, lighter, and drops the grey ground.
A square’s side is set by the rescaled value, so its area goes with the square of it, and the 0.5 floor means the smallest trial always gets exactly a ninth of the largest one’s ink, however close their weights actually are.


Show the R code
ink_share <- trials |>
  mutate(area   = 100 * psize^2 / sum(psize^2),
         label  = fct_reorder(label, weight)) |>
  select(label, weight, area) |>
  pivot_longer(-label) |>
  mutate(name = factor(name, c("weight", "area"),
                       c("Share of the pooled estimate", "Share of the squares' ink")))

ggplot(ink_share, aes(value, label)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = label), colour = dsvar_light$hairline, linewidth = 1.6) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = name), size = 2.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(dsvar_cat[2], dsvar_cat[3]), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1),
                     limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .05))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "The squares stretch the differences between trials",
       subtitle = sprintf(
         "Weights run from %.1f%% to %.1f%%, a ratio of %.1f. The squares' areas run at a ratio of 9, by construction.",
         min(wt), max(wt), max(wt) / min(wt)),
       caption = "n = 13 trials · random-effects weights from metafor::weights() · areas from forest()'s default sizing") +
  theme_dsvar(base_size = 11, grid = "x") +
  theme(legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "left")











WHY THE WEIGHTS ARE SO EVEN TO BEGIN WITH

TPT Madras enrolled 176,782 people, 49% of everyone in all thirteen trials, and gets 10.2% of the weight. Under a random-effects model each trial’s weight is 1 / (its own variance + τ²), and when trials disagree as much as these do, τ² swamps the sampling variance and every trial’s weight heads towards equal. That is the model doing what it was asked: it treats the trials as a sample of settings, and a huge trial in one setting is still one setting. It is also the opposite of what the eye expects from “bigger study, bigger square”.




THE SAME DATA, DIFFERENT CHOICES

Two things the original leaves out, both available in the same dataset. One is the prediction interval: where the effect of a new trial, in a new setting, would be expected to fall. The other is an order that means something: the trials were run at very different distances from the equator, and the dataset records it.


Show the R code
rows <- trials |>
  arrange(ablat, year) |>
  mutate(label = sprintf("%s  ·  %d°", label, ablat),
         y     = row_number() + 2)

pooled <- tibble(
  y   = c(1, 0),
  lab = c("Pooled estimate (95% CI)", "Prediction interval for a new trial"),
  lo  = c(pi_$ci.lb, pi_$pi.lb), hi = c(pi_$ci.ub, pi_$pi.ub))

ggplot(rows, aes(y = y)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = dsvar_light$muted, linewidth = .4, linetype = "22") +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = exp(lo), xmax = exp(hi)), colour = dsvar_light$ink_3,
                 linewidth = .5) +
  geom_point(aes(x = exp(yi), size = weight), shape = 15, colour = dsvar_accent()) +
  geom_linerange(data = pooled, aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi, y = y, colour = lab),
                 linewidth = c(3.2, 1.2)) +
  annotate("point", x = pi_$pred, y = c(1, 0), shape = 18, size = 4,
           colour = dsvar_light$ink) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(.05, .1, .25, .5, 1, 2, 4), labels = c(.05, .1, .25, .5, 1, 2, 4)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(rows$y, pooled$y), labels = c(rows$label, pooled$lab),
                     expand = expansion(add = .6)) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 4, guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(dsvar_light$ink, dsvar_cat[3]), guide = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(.05, 7)) +
  labs(x = "Risk ratio, vaccinated against control (log scale)", y = NULL,
       title = "Sorted by latitude, the disagreement turns into a gradient",
       subtitle = sprintf(
         "The pooled interval runs %.2f to %.2f. A new trial could land anywhere from %.2f to %.2f.",
         pi_$ci.lb, pi_$ci.ub, pi_$pi.lb, pi_$pi.ub),
       caption = "n = 13 trials · square area proportional to random-effects weight · latitude = absolute degrees from the equator") +
  theme_dsvar(base_size = 11, grid = "x")











Show the R code
mreg <- rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ ablat, data = dat)
grid <- tibble(ablat = seq(10, 57, by = .5))
fit  <- predict(mreg, newmods = grid$ablat, transf = exp) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  bind_cols(grid)
per10 <- 1 - exp(10 * coef(mreg)[["ablat"]])

ggplot(trials, aes(ablat, exp(yi))) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = dsvar_light$muted, linewidth = .4, linetype = "22") +
  geom_ribbon(data = fit, aes(ablat, ymin = ci.lb, ymax = ci.ub), inherit.aes = FALSE,
              fill = dsvar_accent(), alpha = .14) +
  geom_line(data = fit, aes(ablat, pred), colour = dsvar_accent(), linewidth = .9) +
  geom_point(aes(size = weights(mreg)), shape = 21, fill = dsvar_accent(),
             colour = "white", alpha = .85, stroke = .4) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(.1, .25, .5, 1, 2), labels = c(.1, .25, .5, 1, 2)) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 9, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Absolute latitude of the trial (degrees from the equator)",
       y = "Risk ratio (log scale)",
       title = sprintf("Every 10° further from the equator, the risk ratio falls by another %.0f%%", 100 * per10),
       subtitle = sprintf(
         "Latitude accounts for %.0f%% of the between-trial heterogeneity (meta-regression, QM = %.1f, p < .001)",
         mreg$R2, mreg$QM),
       caption = "n = 13 trials · bubble area proportional to meta-regression weight · band is the 95% CI of the fitted line") +
  theme_dsvar(base_size = 11)










The original is not wrong about anything. It reports I² and τ², it draws every interval, it is reproducible to the decimal. But it presents thirteen trials in the order they were numbered and sums them into one diamond, and the diamond invites the sentence “BCG halves the risk of TB”. The latitude plot invites a different one, “BCG works far better far from the equator”, which is closer to what the trials actually say and was the finding of the meta-analysis these data come from. One leading explanation is exposure to environmental mycobacteria in warmer climates, which gives some protection already and leaves less for the vaccine to add. Order is an argument too, and sorting by the dataset’s row number is a choice not to make one.




SOURCES


Original: Viechtbauer, W. Forest Plot. The metafor Package plot gallery, metafor-project.org/doku.php/plots:forest_plot. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
Software: Viechtbauer, W. (2010). Conducting meta-analyses in R with the metafor package. Journal of Statistical Software, 36(3), 1–48. doi:10.18637/jss.v036.i03.
Data: Colditz, G. A., Brewer, T. F., Berkey, C. S., Wilson, M. E., Burdick, E., Fineberg, H. V., & Mosteller, F. (1994). Efficacy of BCG vaccine in the prevention of tuberculosis: Meta-analysis of the published literature. JAMA, 271(9), 698–702. As dat.bcg in the metadat package (GPL ≥ 2), vendored as data/raw/bcg-trials.csv.
The related cases: Original against replication for a reference line doing the arguing, and The specification curve for another way of drawing many estimates of one effect.
Reproduce it: every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: Gun deaths in Florida
text:
Gallery · Change over time · back to the gallery


Gun deaths in Florida

The same inverted axis as Iraq’s bloody toll, by a designer who cited it as the inspiration. This time the chart reads as saying the opposite of what its own article said. Read the two pages together.








THE ORIGINAL



“Gun deaths in Florida” by Christine Chan, Reuters, 16 February 2014. Copyright Reuters, reproduced at reduced resolution for criticism and review under the Dutch citation right (Auteurswet art. 15a). Not a free licence: it cannot be reused from here. Reuters no longer serves the graphic; this copy is the one carried in LiveScience’s contemporary write-up, and retains Chan’s byline and the Reuters mark.

Christine Chan’s graphic for Reuters (February 2014), accompanying an article on Florida’s Stand Your Ground law.


How to read it


 The horizontal axis is years, 1990 to 2012, with the 2005 Stand Your Ground law marked.


 The vertical axis is firearm murders, and it is inverted. Zero is at the top; the numbers increase as you go down.


 The area under the line is filled red, so it reads as a pool rather than a trend.


 Therefore: where the line appears to fall, deaths rose. After 2005 the shape plunges downward: that is the increase.





THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

A filled line chart, red, with years across the bottom and a labelled vertical axis whose values increase downward. A marker indicates 2005. The filled shape is deepest at the far left, narrows through the 1990s to its thinnest around 1999, then deepens sharply after 2005 and stays deep.



02 · Analyse

Quantity is on position and the axis is labelled correctly, so nothing here is factually wrong. But the filled line chart is one of the most conventional forms there is, and its convention is that up means more. Inverting the axis leaves that expectation in place, and now it produces a false answer.



03 · Interpret

What the chart is meant to say is that firearm homicides rose after Stand Your Ground. What a fluent chart reader takes from a glance is that they fell. The article’s own text says they rose, so the graphic and its caption are arguing with each other.



04 · Judge

It fails the test the Iraq chart passes: there is a plausible wrong reading, and it is the one most readers will reach. The inversion was borrowed for the metaphor without the condition that made the metaphor safe: Scarr’s bars cannot be misread as “fewer”, and a descending line can. The chart is not a lie, but it is not defensible either.





THE RECREATION, BOTH WAYS UP



Show the R code
blood <- "#8C1C13"

p_data <- bind_rows(mutate(fl, how = "As published: axis inverted"),
                    mutate(fl, how = "Conventional axis")) |>
  mutate(how = factor(how, levels = c("As published: axis inverted", "Conventional axis")))

base_layers <- list(
  geom_area(fill = blood, alpha = .9),
  geom_vline(xintercept = syg, colour = "#3a3a34", linewidth = .4, linetype = "22"),
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Murders committed with a firearm")
)

# The label is placed at an explicit y per panel rather than at Inf: under
# scale_y_reverse, Inf is the BOTTOM of the frame, so an Inf-anchored
# annotation silently vanished off the top of the inverted plot.
top_of <- max(fl$firearm_murders)
lab <- function(y) annotate("text", x = syg + .4, y = y,
                            label = "Stand Your Ground, 2005", hjust = 0,
                            size = 2.8, colour = "#3a3a34", family = dsvar_font())

# Two different y transforms cannot live on one facetted plot, so these are
# two plots placed side by side. patchwork's guide collection and `&` are
# broken against ggplot2 4.x, so each is themed on its own. See the README.
p1 <- ggplot(fl, aes(year, firearm_murders)) + base_layers + lab(60) +
  scale_y_reverse(expand = expansion(mult = c(.08, 0))) +
  labs(title = "As published: axis inverted",
       subtitle = "The shape plunges after 2005: that is the increase")

p2 <- ggplot(fl, aes(year, firearm_murders)) + base_layers + lab(top_of * .97) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .08))) +
  labs(title = "Conventional axis",
       subtitle = "The same numbers, reading the way readers expect")

library(patchwork)
p1 + p2










n = 23 years. Murders committed with a firearm in Florida, 1990–2012. Source: Florida Department of Law Enforcement, Florida Statewide Murder by Firearm, 1971–2020, the same series Chan used.




WHAT THE NUMBERS ACTUALLY DO



Show the R code
tibble(
  Period = c("1999–2004 (before)", "2006–2012 (after)"),
  `Mean firearm murders per year` = round(c(pre, post)),
  Change = c("—", sprintf("+%.0f%%", 100 * (post - pre) / pre))
) |> knitr::kable()





Period
Mean firearm murders per year
Change




1999–2004 (before)
526
—


2006–2012 (after)
732
+39%





Firearm murders in Florida averaged about 526 a year in the six years before the law and about 732 a year in the seven years after, a rise of roughly 39%. The published chart shows that rise as a downward plunge.


WHAT THIS PAGE IS NOT CLAIMING

That Stand Your Ground caused the increase. A before-and-after difference on one state with no control group cannot establish that, and this page is about an encoding, not a causal question. Researchers who have taken the causal question seriously do report increases (see RAND’s review), but the chart here is not the evidence for it, and neither is the table above.




A CHART THAT SHOWS IT BETTER

Turning the axis the right way up fixes the direction, but the chart still counts murders in a state that grew by 5,900,000 people over these years. Per 100,000 residents, and with the murders that were not committed with a gun drawn beside the ones that were, the picture is sharper than either version above.


Show the R code
rates <- fl |>
  mutate(Firearm = firearm_murders / population * 1e5,
         `Other means` = (total_murders - firearm_murders) / population * 1e5) |>
  pivot_longer(c(Firearm, `Other means`), names_to = "means", values_to = "rate")

# The averages the table above compares, as segments over the years they cover
periods <- rates |>
  mutate(period = case_when(year %in% 1999:2004 ~ "before",
                            year %in% 2006:2012 ~ "after")) |>
  filter(!is.na(period)) |>
  summarise(rate = mean(rate), from = min(year), to = max(year), .by = c(means, period))
change <- periods |>
  select(means, period, rate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = period, values_from = rate) |>
  mutate(pct = 100 * (after - before) / before)
gun_up   <- change$pct[change$means == "Firearm"]
other_dn <- -change$pct[change$means == "Other means"]

cols <- c(Firearm = dsvar_accent(), `Other means` = "grey55")

ggplot(rates, aes(year, rate, colour = means)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = syg, colour = "#3a3a34", linewidth = .4, linetype = "22") +
  annotate("text", x = syg + .25, y = 8.2, label = "Stand Your Ground, 2005",
           hjust = 0, size = 3, colour = "#3a3a34", family = dsvar_font()) +
  geom_segment(data = periods, aes(x = from - .4, xend = to + .4, y = rate, yend = rate),
               linewidth = 2.4, alpha = .25, lineend = "butt") +
  geom_line(linewidth = .9) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  # Labelled at the line ends, so there is no legend to decode
  geom_text(data = filter(rates, year == max(year)),
            aes(label = means), hjust = 0, nudge_x = .35, size = 3.4,
            family = dsvar_font(), fontface = "bold") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cols, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1990, 2010, 5), expand = expansion(add = c(.5, 3))) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .05))) +
  labs(title = sprintf("After 2005, more of Florida's murders were committed with guns: the firearm rate rose %.0f%%, other murders fell %.0f%%",
                       gun_up, other_dn),
       subtitle = "Murders per 100,000 residents. Shaded bars: averages for 1999–2004 and 2006–2012",
       x = NULL, y = "Murders per 100,000 residents",
       caption = sprintf("n = %d years · Florida Department of Law Enforcement, UCR; population from the same series · a before-and-after comparison, not a causal estimate",
                         nrow(fl)))










Three changes from the original, each of which the original’s question needed: the axis is upright and starts at zero; the counts are rates, so population growth is not mistaken for a trend; and the murders committed without a gun are on the same chart, which is the comparison that shows the change was in the weapon more than in the number of killings. The note above still applies: this is a description of what happened after 2005, not evidence about why.




THE MOST USEFUL THING ABOUT THIS CASE


Chan was not hiding anything. The axis was labelled, the article said deaths rose, and she explained afterwards that she preferred to show deaths as descending and had taken the idea from Scarr’s Iraq graphic. Everything about the intent was honest, and the chart still misleads, because a reader spends about four seconds on a graphic and spends them on the shape, not the axis labels. That is why “but it is technically accurate” is not a defence, and why the useful question is never “is this true?” but “what will this be read to say?”




SOURCES


Original: Chan, C. (2014). Gun deaths in Florida. Reuters. Copyright Reuters; shown above at reduced resolution as a quotation for criticism and review.
Data: Florida Department of Law Enforcement, Florida Statewide Murder by Firearm, 1971–2020, Uniform Crime Reports. Vendored as data/raw/florida-firearm-murders.csv.
The pair: Iraq’s bloody toll, Simon Scarr, South China Morning Post (2011), which Chan named as the inspiration.
On the causal question: RAND Corporation, The Effects of Stand-Your-Ground Laws on Violent Crime. Not settled by either chart.
Reproduce it: every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram
text:
Gallery · Relationships & structure · back to the gallery


The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram

A plain scatterplot of two measurements that turned out to contain an entire theory of how stars live and die. It also runs its brightness axis backwards: the third axis-inversion case in this gallery, and the one where the inversion is least controversial.








THE ORIGINAL






Figure from “Relations between the spectra and other characteristics of the stars” by Henry Norris Russell, Nature 93, 252 (1914). Scan via Michael Richmond’s lecture notes, RIT. Public domain in the US; in copyright in the EU until the end of 2027 (Russell died in 1957). Shown at reduced size under the Dutch citation right (Auteurswet art. 15a), for the critique on this page.






“The Hertzsprung Russell Diagram” by Richard Powell, via Wikimedia Commons, licensed CC BY-SA 2.5.




Independently arrived at by Ejnar Hertzsprung (1911) and Henry Norris Russell (1913): plot a star’s colour against its intrinsic brightness and the points do not scatter. They fall into a diagonal band with distinct clumps off it. Russell’s plate, on the left, shows a few hundred stars with measured distances; the modern rendering beside it shows many thousands and names the regions Russell left unlabelled. The plate already has the essentials, including the brightness axis that runs backwards. Because spectral class was a category, the plate’s stars stand in vertical columns, one per class. The modern version uses a continuous colour index instead, so the columns melt into a cloud. And the two straight lines Russell ruled along the edges of the band are the first luminosity-class lines: the pink curves on the right, and in the recreation below, are their descendants.


How to read it


 Each point is a star. Nothing else is encoded: no size, no time, no groups.


 Left to right is colour, and therefore temperature: blue-hot on the left, red-cool on the right. Classic versions put temperature here and reverse it; plotting colour index instead gets the same order without reversing anything.


 Up is brighter. The axis is absolute magnitude, a scale on which smaller numbers mean brighter stars, so it is plotted inverted, and the numbers count down as you go up.


 The diagonal band is the main sequence: stars steadily fusing hydrogen, which is most of them, for most of their lives.


 The clump above and right are giants: cool but enormous, so bright anyway. The faint hot points at lower left are white dwarfs, dead cores.





THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

A scatterplot of many thousands of points, with the vertical axis numbered in decreasing order. The points are not uniformly spread: a dense diagonal band runs across it, with a separate cluster up and to the right and a sparse group at lower left.



02 · Analyse

Two quantitative variables, both on position, the most accurate channel there is, and nothing else: no colour scale, no size, no annotation layer. The content is where the points are and, more importantly, where they are not.



03 · Interpret

The claim is that stars are not free to be any combination of temperature and brightness. The empty regions are the finding: they say that certain states are unstable or short-lived, which is why the diagram became a theory of stellar evolution rather than a summary of a catalogue.



04 · Judge

It holds completely. Its inverted brightness axis is not a problem, though the Florida chart’s is: the reversal here is universal in the field, inherited from a magnitude scale that predates the plot by two thousand years, and taught to every reader of the diagram. A convention the whole audience shares is not a trick; one that only the author holds is.





THE RECREATION



Show the R code
# The original's pink lines are the luminosity classes. They are not traced
# from it: each star's spectral type carries its class (G2V is a main-sequence
# star, K0III a giant, DA a white dwarf), so every line here is the median
# brightness of the stars that say they belong to it, in bins of 0.1 in colour.
#
# Two rules decide where a line is drawn, and both are the data's, not taste:
#   - a bin needs 30 stars (5 for the white dwarfs, of which there are 153);
#   - a giant or subgiant bin must sit at least one magnitude above the main
#     sequence in the same bin. Among hot stars it does not: this catalogue's
#     A and F "giants" are as faint as its dwarfs, and a line there would only
#     draw the classification noise.
# Class II and the supergiants fail the first rule within 250 parsecs (II also
# sits on top of III), so they are left out rather than borrowed from elsewhere.
PINK <- "#ff4fd8"
binned <- stars |>
  mutate(lc = if_else(str_detect(spect, "^D"), "WD",
                      str_extract(spect, "Iab|Ia|Ib|III|II|IV|V")),
         bin = round(ci, 1)) |>
  filter(lc %in% c("V", "IV", "III", "WD")) |>
  group_by(lc, bin) |>
  summarise(absmag = median(absmag), n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n >= if_else(lc == "WD", 5, 30))
main_seq <- binned |> filter(lc == "V") |> select(bin, ms = absmag)
lum_bins <- binned |>
  left_join(main_seq, by = "bin") |>
  filter(lc %in% c("V", "WD") | is.na(ms) | absmag <= ms - 1) |>
  # and, for the giants and subgiants, only the longest unbroken run of bins,
  # so a class the rule above cuts into pieces is still drawn as one line
  group_by(lc) |>
  mutate(run = cumsum(c(TRUE, diff(bin) > .15))) |>
  group_by(lc, run) |> mutate(len = n()) |>
  group_by(lc) |> filter(lc %in% c("V", "WD") | len == max(len)) |>
  ungroup()

# One gentle smoothing pass, so the lines read as loci rather than staircases
lum_lines <- lum_bins |>
  group_by(lc) |>
  reframe({
    sp <- smooth.spline(bin, absmag, df = min(5, n() - 1))
    tibble(ci = seq(min(bin), max(bin), by = .02),
           absmag = predict(sp, ci)$y)
  })

# Labels as the original sets them: beside each line's cool end
lum_labels <- lum_lines |>
  group_by(lc) |>
  slice_max(ci, n = 1) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(x = ci + .04, y = absmag,
         label = c(III = "III  Giants", IV = "IV  Subgiants",
                   V = "V  Main sequence", WD = "White dwarfs")[lc])

ggplot(stars, aes(ci, absmag)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = ci), size = .28, alpha = .4) +
  geom_path(data = lum_lines, aes(group = lc), colour = PINK, linewidth = .55) +
  # ggrepel only for its halo; force = 0 keeps every label where it was put
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = lum_labels,
                           aes(x, y, label = label), hjust = 0,
                           colour = PINK, bg.color = SKY, bg.r = .15,
                           force = 0, force_pull = 0, min.segment.length = Inf,
                           family = dsvar_font(), size = 3) +
  geom_point(data = named, shape = 21, colour = "white", fill = SKY,
             size = 1.8, stroke = .7) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = named, aes(label = proper),
                           size = 2.9, family = dsvar_font(), seed = 5,
                           colour = "white", box.padding = .5,
                           segment.size = .2, segment.colour = "grey70",
                           bg.color = SKY, bg.r = .12) +
  scale_star() +
  # ONE axis is reversed, not two. Magnitude runs backwards (smaller number =
  # brighter star), so scale_y_reverse puts bright at the top. Colour index is
  # already ordered the right way: low B-V is blue and hot, so plotted normally
  # it lands on the left, which is where the convention wants it. Reversing x
  # as well — the first version of this chunk did — puts the blue stars on the
  # right and quietly breaks the diagram.
  scale_y_reverse() +
  labs(title = "Stars are not free to be any brightness at any temperature",
       subtitle = "Absolute magnitude against colour index, 67,000 stars within 250 parsecs",
       x = "← hotter (blue)    colour index B−V    cooler (red) →",
       y = "← fainter    absolute magnitude    brighter →",
       caption = sprintf("n = %s stars · HYG database v4.1, compiled from Hipparcos, Yale and Gliese catalogues · CC BY-SA 4.0",
                         format(nrow(stars), big.mark = ","))) +
  theme_sky(grid = "none")










The pink lines are the original’s luminosity classes, computed rather than traced: each is the median brightness of the stars whose spectral type names that class. Two of the original’s lines are missing. Within 250 parsecs this catalogue holds 68 supergiants, too few to draw, and its bright giants (class II) sit on top of the giants. That is the selection effect below, at work on the diagram itself.
Nothing forbids a star from sitting in the gap between the main sequence and the giants; stars just do not stay there long enough to be caught.




WHAT THE SELECTION IS DOING

The diagram above is a picture of the stars we can see, which is not the same as a picture of the universe.


Show the R code
sel <- bind_rows(
  stars |> slice_min(dist, n = 3000) |> mutate(pick = "The 3,000 nearest stars"),
  stars |> slice_min(mag,  n = 3000) |> mutate(pick = "The 3,000 brightest in our sky")
) |> mutate(pick = factor(pick, levels = c("The 3,000 nearest stars",
                                           "The 3,000 brightest in our sky")))

ggplot(sel, aes(ci, absmag, colour = ci)) +
  geom_point(size = .5, alpha = .6) +
  facet_wrap(~pick) +
  scale_star() +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  labs(x = "← hotter (blue)    colour index B−V    cooler (red) →",
       y = "brighter ↑    absolute magnitude",
       title = "Same axes, two ways of choosing which stars to plot",
       subtitle = "Nearest is roughly a fair sample. Brightest-in-our-sky is not a sample of anything",
       caption = "n = 3,000 per panel, drawn from the same catalogue") +
  theme_sky(grid = "none")










This is the selection-effect lesson the course teaches in week 4, and stars are the cleanest case of it anywhere. Pick the brightest objects in your sky and you will conclude that the universe is full of giants, because the faint majority cannot be seen far away. The shape of your scatter is the shape of your sampling, and no amount of care with the encoding will tell you that; only knowing how the rows got into the table will.




THE SAME STARS, ANOTHER QUESTION

The diagram asks where stars can sit. Cut it into strips by spectral class instead, and ask how bright the stars of one colour are, and a different finding comes forward: at the same colour there are two kinds of star.


Show the R code
CLASSES <- c("B", "A", "F", "G", "K", "M")
by_class <- stars |>
  mutate(cls = str_sub(spect, 1, 1)) |>
  filter(cls %in% CLASSES) |>
  mutate(cls = factor(cls, levels = rev(CLASSES))) |>
  group_by(cls) |>
  mutate(n = n(), typical_ci = median(ci)) |>
  ungroup()

# Where the two kinds of K star peak, read off the data rather than typed in:
# the densest magnitude on each side of the dip between them.
peak <- function(x) { d <- density(x); d$x[which.max(d$y)] }
k <- filter(by_class, cls == "K")$absmag
k_giant <- peak(k[k < 3.5])
k_dwarf <- peak(k[k >= 3.5])
times   <- 10^(.4 * (k_dwarf - k_giant))   # five magnitudes = 100 times

# The M row, for the caption: how far away its dwarfs and its giants are.
m <- filter(by_class, cls == "M") |> mutate(giant = absmag < 3.5)
m_dist <- m |> group_by(giant) |> summarise(d = median(dist)) |> deframe()

labels_n <- by_class |> distinct(cls, n) |>
  mutate(lab = sprintf("%s  ·  %s", cls, format(n, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)))

ggplot(by_class, aes(absmag, cls, fill = typical_ci)) +
  ggridges::geom_density_ridges(scale = 1.25, rel_min_height = .004,
                                colour = SKY, linewidth = .5, alpha = .95) +
  # Written inside the K row's two humps, on the fill, so they cannot collide
  # with the row above
  annotate("text", x = c(k_giant, k_dwarf), y = 2.07, vjust = 0,
           label = c("giants", "dwarfs"), colour = SKY, fontface = "bold",
           family = dsvar_font(), size = 3.1) +
  scale_star("fill") +
  # Brighter to the right, the way a reader expects "more" to go. The H-R
  # diagram puts it up; this chart has no up to spare.
  scale_x_reverse(breaks = seq(15, -5, -5)) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = setNames(labels_n$lab, labels_n$cls),
                   expand = expansion(add = c(.2, 1.35))) +
  labs(title = sprintf("At the same colour, two kinds of star: K giants are about %s times brighter than K dwarfs",
                       format(signif(times, 1), big.mark = ",")),
       subtitle = "Absolute magnitude within each spectral class, hot at the top to cool at the bottom",
       x = "← fainter    absolute magnitude    brighter →", y = NULL,
       caption = sprintf("n = %s stars with a spectral class B to M, out of %s · each ridge is scaled to its own class · HYG database v4.1, CC BY-SA 4.0",
                         format(nrow(by_class), big.mark = ","),
                         format(nrow(stars), big.mark = ","))) +
  theme_sky(grid = "x") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(hjust = 0, vjust = 0, colour = "grey85",
                                   size = rel(.95)))










This is the split Hertzsprung noticed before the diagram had a name: cool stars come either faint or very bright, with little in between, and he called them dwarfs and giants. The scatterplot shows it as two separate regions. The ridges show it as two humps in one row, which is easier to see and easier to measure. The M row splits the same way, and carries the selection effect from above: its dwarfs sit a median 22 parsecs away and its giants 198, because an M dwarf any further out is too faint to have made it into these catalogues.

The ridges give up what the diagram is for. Colour is now six categories, not a continuous axis, so the main sequence is no longer a line you can see bend. And each ridge is scaled to its own class, so a row of 1,806 M stars looks as big as a row of 20,824 F stars. Ridgelines compare shapes, not counts, which is why the count is printed on every row.



SOURCES


The finding: Hertzsprung, E. (1911). Publikationen des Astrophysikalischen Observatoriums zu Potsdam; Russell, H. N. (1914). Relations between the spectra and other characteristics of the stars. Nature, 93, and Popular Astronomy, 22.
The 1914 plate: Russell (1914), Nature 93, 252. Scan via Michael Richmond, RIT. Public domain in the US. In the EU it stays in copyright until the end of 2027, seventy years after Russell’s death, so it is shown here under the citation right (Auteurswet art. 15a), at reduced size, for the critique on this page.
The diagram shown: “The Hertzsprung Russell Diagram” by Richard Powell, atlasoftheuniverse.com/hr.html, via Wikimedia Commons, licensed CC BY-SA 2.5. A modern rendering, reproduced under that licence.
Data: the HYG database v4.1 (Hipparcos, Yale Bright Star and Gliese catalogues), astronexus/HYG-Database, CC BY-SA 4.0. Subset to stars within 250 parsecs with a measured colour index, vendored as data/raw/hyg-stars.csv. Share-alike: that file and the charts on this page drawn from it are CC BY-SA 4.0, not the site’s CC BY.
The other inversions: Iraq’s bloody toll and Gun deaths in Florida, where the same move is defensible once and not the other time.
Reproduce it: every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: Many analysts, one dataset
text:
Gallery · Distribution & uncertainty · back to the gallery


Many analysts, one dataset

Twenty-nine teams were given the same data and the same question, and they did not get the same answer. This is the closest thing the social sciences have to a controlled experiment on the course’s central claim: that a dataset supports more than one defensible story. It is the reason this gallery exists.








THE ORIGINAL



“Results summary” from the Many Analysts, One Data Set project materials by Raphael Silberzahn, Eric L. Uhlmann, Daniel P. Martin et al., via osf.io/gvm2z, dedicated to the public domain under CC0 1.0. The authors’ own figure, not the journal’s typeset version, which is SAGE copyright.

Twenty-nine teams, 61 analysts, one dataset of football referee decisions, and one question: are referees more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players than to light-skinned players? Every team chose its own analytic approach. The results were then collected and plotted together. All 29 sit on one odds-ratio axis, which means four have been converted from a Cohen’s d or a correlation, and the figure does not say which four. The asterisks against teams 21 and 27 mark something else: those two intervals run off the right edge, which is cut at 5.


How to read it


 Each row is one analysis team, sorted by the size of the effect they found, not by team number, so the ordering is a finding rather than an index.


 The dot is that team’s estimate and the line through it is their confidence interval.


 The vertical reference line is “no effect”: an odds ratio of 1. A team whose interval crosses it did not find a significant effect.


 The spread across rows is what matters. It comes from the analytic choices, not sampling error: every team had the identical data.





THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

A forest plot: one row per team, a point estimate with a horizontal interval, sorted ascending, with a vertical line at the null value. Some intervals cross the line and most do not. The x axis is an odds ratio.



02 · Analyse

The design decision that makes this work is sorting by estimate rather than by team. Sorted by team number it is noise; sorted by size it becomes a distribution you can see the shape of. The reference line does the same job as the diagonal on the replication page: it converts position into a judgement.



03 · Interpret

The claim is that analytic flexibility is a source of variation on the scale of the effect being studied. Note what it is not claiming: the teams mostly agree on direction. The disagreement is about magnitude and significance, which is precisely the range over which papers get published or not.



04 · Judge

It holds, and it is honest about a subtlety the headline usually loses: this is not a demonstration that the answer is unknowable. Most teams found a positive effect. What the figure shows is that the published answer would have depended on which team happened to write the paper.





THE RECREATION



Show the R code
tip <- arrow(length = unit(.055, "in"), type = "closed")

ggplot(plotted, aes(est, rank, colour = sig)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "#5a5a52", linewidth = .5, linetype = "22") +
  # Each interval is drawn as two segments out from the estimate, so the ends
  # that run off the axis can carry an arrowhead and the ends that do not can't.
  geom_segment(data = ~ filter(.x, !clip_lo), aes(xend = lo_draw, yend = rank), linewidth = .6) +
  geom_segment(data = ~ filter(.x, !clip_hi), aes(xend = hi_draw, yend = rank), linewidth = .6) +
  geom_segment(data = ~ filter(.x,  clip_lo), aes(xend = lo_draw, yend = rank), linewidth = .6, arrow = tip) +
  geom_segment(data = ~ filter(.x,  clip_hi), aes(xend = hi_draw, yend = rank), linewidth = .6, arrow = tip) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = source), size = 2, stroke = .9, fill = NA) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Interval excludes 1" = "#1e7c50",
                                 "Interval includes 1" = "#a5a199"),
                      name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Reported as a ratio" = 16, "Converted from d or r" = 1),
                     name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = plotted$rank, labels = paste("Team", plotted$team),
                     expand = expansion(add = .8)) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = XLIM) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(order = 1), shape = guide_legend(order = 2)) +
  labs(title = "Same data, same question, 29 answers",
       subtitle = "Odds ratio for a dark-skinned player receiving a red card, by analysis team",
       x = "Odds ratio (log scale). 1 = no effect", y = NULL,
       caption = sprintf("n = %d teams, %d of them converted to an odds ratio from a d or an r. Arrowheads mark intervals that continue past the axis · Silberzahn et al. (2018)",
                         nrow(plotted), sum(plotted$derived))) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 7.5), legend.position = "bottom")










20 of 29 intervals exclude 1. Estimates run from 0.89 to 2.93, from slightly protective to nearly three times the odds. The four hollow points are the teams that reported a Cohen’s d or a correlation; we converted them, as the original does, and the values match the published figure to two decimals. Because the conversion is monotone and sends 0 to 1, it cannot move a team across the reference line: it changes where they sit, never which side they are on.




THE PROBLEM BEFORE THE PLOT



Show the R code
teams |>
  count(units, name = "teams") |>
  mutate(`Effect size reported` = recode(units,
                                         OR  = "Odds ratio",
                                         IRR = "Incidence rate ratio",
                                         D   = "Cohen's d",
                                         R   = "Correlation r"),
         `No effect means` = if_else(units %in% c("OR", "IRR"), "1", "0"),
         `To get onto the odds-ratio axis` =
           if_else(units %in% c("OR", "IRR"),
                   "nothing: already a ratio with a null of 1",
                   if_else(units == "D", "OR = exp(d · π / √3)",
                           "r → d, then OR = exp(d · π / √3)"))) |>
  select(`Effect size reported`, teams, `No effect means`,
         `To get onto the odds-ratio axis`) |>
  knitr::kable()











Effect size reported
teams
No effect means
To get onto the odds-ratio axis




Cohen’s d
2
0
OR = exp(d · π / √3)


Incidence rate ratio
5
1
nothing: already a ratio with a null of 1


Odds ratio
20
1
nothing: already a ratio with a null of 1


Correlation r
2
0
r → d, then OR = exp(d · π / √3)







EVEN ASSEMBLING THE CHART REQUIRED A CHOICE

The teams did not report on a common scale. Twenty-five gave ratios, on which 1 means no effect; four gave a Cohen’s d or a correlation, on which 0 does. Putting all 29 on one chart means converting those four, and the formulas rest on an assumption the original teams never made: that behind the binary outcome there is a continuous, logistically distributed propensity to be shown a card. That is what lets a d become an odds ratio at all.
So the chart above cannot be assembled without an analytic choice, in a paper about analytic choices. We make the same choice the original makes, and get the same numbers. What we add is a visible seam (the converted teams are drawn hollow), so the reader can tell the authors’ reported values from arithmetic performed on their behalf. The alternative, plotting only the 25 and dropping four teams from a study whose entire subject is the variation across teams, is defensible too, and worse.




WHAT THE SORT IS DOING



Show the R code
both <- bind_rows(
  plotted |> mutate(pos = team, how = "Ordered by team number"),
  plotted |> mutate(pos = rank, how = "Ordered by estimate")
) |> mutate(how = factor(how, c("Ordered by team number", "Ordered by estimate")))

ggplot(both, aes(est, pos)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "#5a5a52", linewidth = .4, linetype = "22") +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = lo_draw, xmax = hi_draw), colour = "#c2cdc7", linewidth = .5) +
  geom_point(colour = dsvar_accent(), size = 1.5) +
  facet_wrap(~how) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = XLIM) +
  labs(x = "Odds ratio (log scale)", y = NULL,
       title = "Identical estimates. One decision about row order.",
       caption = "n = 29 teams") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())










On the left the teams look like noise around a value; on the right you can see the shape of the disagreement, read off how many cross the line, and spot that the spread is asymmetric. Week 2 makes this point about bar charts. Here the sort is the difference between a table with dots on it and a finding.




WHAT WOULD HAVE BEEN PUBLISHED



Show the R code
LV <- c("Significant positive", "No significant effect", "Significant negative")

verdicts <- effects |>
  mutate(verdict = factor(case_when(lo > 1 ~ LV[1], hi < 1 ~ LV[3], TRUE ~ LV[2]), LV),
         label = as.character(team),
         # The same order as the forest plot, folded into a grid that reads
         # left to right, top to bottom, smallest effect first. Keeping the
         # order means the grid can show *where* the nulls are, not just how
         # many — a grouped unit chart would throw that away.
         col =  (rank - 1) %%  10 + 1,
         row = -((rank - 1) %/% 10))

# ggplot 4 only draws a legend key for a level it has data for, so an empty
# category would silently vanish from the legend — which is the opposite of
# what this chart is for. One off-panel square gives the key something to draw
# and the coord clips it away.
ghost <- tibble(col = 99, row = 99, label = "", verdict = factor(LV[3], LV))

ggplot(bind_rows(verdicts, ghost), aes(col, row, fill = verdict)) +
  # No tile border: the gap is made by shrinking the tile, so it stays
  # transparent and the grid works on both the light and the dark site.
  geom_tile(width = .88, height = .88, colour = NA) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label, colour = verdict), show.legend = FALSE,
            size = 3.2, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = setNames(c("#1e7c50", "#a5a199", "#8c3a2b"), LV),
                    drop = FALSE, name = NULL) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = setNames(c("#ffffff", "#3a3a34", "#ffffff"), LV),
                      guide = "none") +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0.4, 10.6), ylim = c(-2.6, 0.6), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "The same study, written up 29 times",
       subtitle = "What each team would have reported, in the order they appear above, smallest effect first",
       caption = sprintf("%d of %d teams would have published a significant effect. None would have published the opposite · Silberzahn et al. (2018)",
                         sum(verdicts$verdict == LV[1]), nrow(verdicts))) +
  theme_dsvar(base_size = 11, grid = "none") +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.title = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(), axis.line.x = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom")










The forest plot answers how big. This chart answers what would have been concluded, which is the question the literature runs on, and it needs a different form because the outcome is a category and not a quantity. Two thirds of these parallel papers report an effect, one third report a null, and none report the reverse. The third key in the legend has nothing behind it on purpose: the absence of a category is a finding, and a chart that silently drops an empty category lets you assume the teams disagreed about direction. They never did; the argument was only ever about magnitude.


Keeping the estimate order pays off here. The nulls are not scattered: eight of the nine sit in the smallest third, and the ninth is team 27 at the far end, whose interval was so wide it could not rule out anything: a null for the opposite reason. Look too at what interrupts the run at the start. Teams 10, 4 and 11 are significant while their neighbours are not, and all three are converted teams whose reported intervals are extraordinarily narrow: team 4’s d ran from 0.1026 to 0.1031. Grouping the squares by verdict would have given the same 20 : 9 split and hidden every one of these.




SOURCES


Original: Silberzahn, R., Uhlmann, E. L., Martin, D. P., et al. (2018). Many analysts, one data set: Making transparent how variations in analytic choices affect results. Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 337–356.
Data: the project’s reported effects file, osf.io/gvm2z. Vendored as data/raw/silberzahn-effects.csv.
The companion: The specification curve: one analyst, many specifications, rather than many analysts.
The related case: Original against replication, where the same design is repeated rather than the same data reanalysed.
Reproduce it: every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: The asymmetric media ecosystem
text:
Gallery · Relationships & structure · back to the gallery


The asymmetric media ecosystem

Network maps of who links to whom have become the standard picture of political polarisation. They are also the chart form where the layout algorithm does more of the arguing than the data does, and the reader has no way to tell.








THE ORIGINAL



Figure 2.1, “Network map of election media sources based on media inlinks”, from Benkler, Y., Faris, R., & Roberts, H. (2018). Network Propaganda: Manipulation, Disinformation, and Radicalization in American Politics. Oxford University Press. © Yochai Benkler, Robert Faris and Hal Roberts 2018, published open access under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Reproduced unmodified, with its caption, from the OAPEN edition. Maps generated with Media Cloud.

Yochai Benkler and colleagues mapped the US media ecosystem by who links to whom, and found the two sides were not mirror images. The left runs continuously into the centre, all of it orbiting the Washington Post, the New York Times, CNN and Politico. The right is anchored by Breitbart and Fox News, has almost no overlap with the centre, and has barely a centre-right at all. That asymmetry was the finding: asymmetric polarisation, not just polarisation. It is a claim about shape rather than about any number.


How to read it


 Each circle is a news source, sized by how many other sources link to it. The Washington Post is the biggest because 5,100 distinct outlets cite it.


 A line means one outlet linked to the other, and the more they link, the closer the layout pulls them. The whole dataset is links; everything else on the chart is inferred from them.


     The colour is not the side the outlet takes: it is who shared it. Dark blue means at least 4:1 of the people tweeting its stories also retweeted Clinton; light blue 3:2; green roughly even; pink 3:2 Trump; red 4:1 Trump.


 So position and colour come from different datasets. Where a node sits comes from hyperlinks between publishers; its colour comes from Twitter sharing by readers. Nothing on the figure says so.


 Position is not data. A force-directed layout puts connected nodes near each other and pushes unconnected ones apart. There are no axes, and absolute position means nothing.


 What is real is the clustering (who ends up next to whom) and the density of each group. Distance between two specific dots is not.





THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

A cloud of coloured points joined by many thin lines, with no axes, no scale and no gridlines. Some regions are dense to the point of being solid; others are sparse. Point size varies with how much each node is linked to.



02 · Analyse

The only data channel is topology: who connects to whom. The layout algorithm converts that into two spatial dimensions, and it is a choice: different algorithms, or the same one with a different random seed, give visibly different pictures of the same graph. Colour carries the group label, which is external to the network.



03 · Interpret

The claim is about structure: the communities are real, they are unequally dense, and one is more insulated than the other. Those are properties of the graph, which is why they survive the layout, but the picture makes them feel more precise than they are.



04 · Judge

Defensible when the claims stay topological and are backed by numbers, which Benkler’s are. Indefensible when a hairball is presented as evidence on its own. The honest test: could you state your finding as a statistic? If yes, show the statistic and the map. If no, the map is probably not showing it either.





THE RECREATION

Media Cloud’s link data is not openly downloadable, so this uses the dataset Benkler’s work descends from: Adamic and Glance’s 2005 map of US political blogs during the 2004 election. It is the original polarised-blogosphere network, and it is openly available.


Show the R code
set.seed(3)
ggraph(g, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(alpha = .04, colour = "#3a3a34",
                 edge_width = .2, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = side, size = deg), alpha = .8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal, name = NULL) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(.4, 4), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "US political blogs, 2004",
       subtitle = "Force-directed layout. Two communities, few links across",
       caption = sprintf("n = %s blogs, %s links · Adamic & Glance (2005)",
                         format(gorder(g), big.mark = ","),
                         format(gsize(g), big.mark = ","))) +
  theme_void(base_family = dsvar_font()) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12, hjust = 0),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9.5, colour = "#5a5a52", hjust = 0),
        plot.caption = element_text(size = 7.5, colour = "#7a7a70", hjust = 0),
        legend.position = "bottom")










1,222 blogs and 19,089 links: the largest weakly-connected component of the Adamic–Glance network, which is the part their paper analyses. Colour is the side each blog was coded to; node size is degree. Layout is Fruchterman–Reingold with a fixed seed.



TWO NODES DECIDED WHAT THIS FIGURE LOOKED LIKE

The file holds 1,224 linked blogs, and two of them (digital-democrat.blogspot.com and thelonedem.com) link to each other and to nothing else in the dataset. A force-directed layout has no attractive force between disconnected components, only repulsion, so that pair drifts until it hits the edge of the canvas and the other 1,222 blogs collapse into a blob in the opposite corner. The first version of this page shipped exactly that: one stray dot top-left, the entire argument squeezed into a fifth of the frame.
Nothing was wrong with the data and nothing errored. The fix is one line (keep the giant component), but notice what the line is: a decision about which nodes exist, taken because of how the drawing came out. That is a defensible choice here, and it is the same kind of choice as dropping an inconvenient case. The difference is only that this one is in the code above and in this box.




THE LAYOUT IS NOT THE DATA



Show the R code
set.seed(9)
make <- function(lay, lab) {
  ggraph(g, layout = lay) +
    geom_edge_link(alpha = .03, colour = "#3a3a34", edge_width = .15) +
    geom_node_point(aes(colour = side), size = .5, alpha = .8, show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = pal) +
    labs(title = lab) +
    theme_void(base_family = dsvar_font()) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 9.5, hjust = .5, colour = "#3a3a34"))
}
library(patchwork)
make("fr", "Fruchterman–Reingold") + make("kk", "Kamada–Kawai") + make("drl", "DrL")











SAME GRAPH, THREE PICTURES

Identical nodes, identical edges, three algorithms. The clusters survive, which is reassuring and is why the topological claim holds. But the shapes, the apparent distance between the groups, and how dramatic the separation looks all change completely. A reader shown only one of these has no way to know which features are the data and which are the optimiser. Reporting the layout algorithm matters as much as reporting your axis limits.




SAY IT WITH A NUMBER INSTEAD



Show the R code
cross <- g |>
  activate(edges) |>
  mutate(same = .N()$side[from] == .N()$side[to]) |>
  as_tibble()

within <- g |> activate(nodes) |> as_tibble() |> count(side, name = "blogs")

tibble(
  Measure = c("Links within the same side", "Links across sides",
              "Share of links crossing"),
  Value = c(format(sum(cross$same), big.mark = ","),
            format(sum(!cross$same), big.mark = ","),
            sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mean(!cross$same)))
) |> knitr::kable()





Measure
Value




Links within the same side
17,401


Links across sides
1,688


Share of links crossing
8.8%





Show the R code
within |> knitr::kable(col.names = c("Side", "Blogs"))





Side
Blogs




Liberal
586


Conservative
636







Show the R code
asym <- g |>
  activate(edges) |>
  mutate(from_side = .N()$side[from], same = .N()$side[from] == .N()$side[to]) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  summarise(inward = mean(same), n = n(), .by = from_side)

ggplot(asym, aes(inward, fct_rev(from_side), colour = from_side)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = .5, yend = fct_rev(from_side)), linewidth = .5) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = .5, colour = "#a5a199", linewidth = .4, linetype = "22") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(), limits = c(.5, 1)) +
  # Computed, not asserted: on the 2004 blogs the two sides are about equally
  # sealed. (An earlier title said "not equally sealed", which is Benkler's
  # finding on his own Media Cloud data, not this file's.)
  labs(title = sprintf("Each side keeps about %.0f%% of its links to itself",
                       100 * mean(asym$inward)),
       subtitle = "Share of each side's links that stay within its own side",
       x = "Links staying in-group", y = NULL,
       caption = sprintf("n = %s links · Adamic & Glance (2005). The dashed line is 50%%, i.e. no preference.",
                         format(gsize(g), big.mark = ",")))










The chart above states the whole argument as two numbers, in one sentence. The network map is still worth drawing: it shows shape and the outliers, and it persuades in a way a percentage cannot. But it should never be the only evidence, because a hairball is compatible with almost any claim, and the reader cannot check it. Draw the map to communicate; compute the statistic to know.




SOURCES


Original: Benkler, Y., Faris, R., & Roberts, H. (2018). Network Propaganda: Manipulation, Disinformation, and Radicalization in American Politics. Oxford University Press. doi:10.1093/oso/9780190923624.001.0001. Open access under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; the full PDF is at OAPEN and the book is readable at Oxford Academic. Figure 2.1 is on p. 48; the methods behind the maps are in ch. 2 and the online appendix.
Data used here: Adamic, L. A., & Glance, N. (2005). The political blogosphere and the 2004 US election. Proceedings of the 3rd International Workshop on Link Discovery. Network via Mark Newman’s network data collection. No formal licence: Newman lists it as free for scientific use, posted with Adamic’s permission. Vendored as data/raw/polblogs-*.csv.
Drawing it: the tidygraph and ggraph packages.
Reproduce it: every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: Nightingale’s rose diagram
text:
Gallery · The whole story · back to the gallery


Nightingale’s rose diagram

A chart made to change a government’s mind, and it did. It is also built on an encoding the course spends a week warning you about, which makes it worth an hour rather than a slide.








THE ORIGINAL



Diagram of the Causes of Mortality in the Army in the East by Florence Nightingale, 1858, in Notes on Matters Affecting the Health, Efficiency and Hospital Administration of the British Army. Public domain (author died 1910); scan via Wikimedia Commons.

Florence Nightingale’s Diagram of the Causes of Mortality in the Army in the East, drawn in 1858 for a royal commission on the health of the British army. Two roses, one per year of the Crimean War, each divided into twelve months running clockwise.


How to read it


 Each wedge is one month, twelve to a circle, going clockwise. The right-hand rose is the first year of the war, the left-hand one the second.


 Blue is death from preventable disease: cholera, typhus, dysentery. It is almost all of the area.


 Red is death from wounds. Being shot at was a small part of what killed the army.


 Black is everything else.


 The wedges radiate from a common centre, so the quantity is the area of the wedge, not its radius. Most recreations get this wrong (below).





THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

Two circular diagrams, each cut into twelve wedges of equal angle. Each wedge is filled in up to a different radius, in three colours layered from the centre. A block of hand-set text explains the construction, because without it the reader cannot know what the radius means.



02 · Analyse

Time is on angle, which is a poor channel for order: you cannot see at a glance which month came first. Quantity is on area, which Cleveland and McGill rank near the bottom for accuracy. Almost every encoding choice here is one the course would talk you out of, and the chart still works.



03 · Interpret

The claim is not “disease was seasonal” but “disease killed far more of this army than the enemy did, and it fell when we cleaned the hospitals.” For that claim you do not need to read a value. You need to see one colour swamp the others, and then shrink.



04 · Judge

It survives, because the claim it makes is one that area can carry: a ratio so large that even an inaccurate channel cannot blur it. Copy the form for a comparison of similar-sized quantities and it collapses immediately. An encoding is only as bad as the claim it is asked to support.





THE RECREATION



Show the R code
# Nightingale's colours, sampled from the lithograph rather than invented.
causes <- c("Preventable disease" = "#7FA8C9",
            "Wounds"              = "#B0413E",
            "Other causes"        = "#3a3a34")

ggplot(long, aes(Month, rate, fill = cause)) +
  # position = "identity" matters: the three causes are drawn OVER one another
  # from the centre, exactly as Nightingale drew them, not stacked.
  geom_col(width = 1, position = "identity", alpha = .85,
           colour = "white", linewidth = .2) +
  coord_polar(start = 0) +
  facet_wrap(~period) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = causes, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "Disease killed far more of the army than wounds did",
       subtitle = "Annual death rate per 1,000, by month and cause, Crimean War",
       caption = "n = 24 months · Nightingale (1858), via HistData") +
  theme_dsvar(base_size = 10, grid = "none") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom")










This recreation is less faithful than it looks: geom_col in polar coordinates maps the value to radius, whereas Nightingale mapped it to area. The next section is about that difference.




THE TRAP EVERY RECREATION FALLS INTO



RADIUS IS NOT AREA

A wedge’s area grows with the square of its radius. Nightingale knew this and scaled her wedges so that area was proportional to deaths; she says so in the note on the plate. coord_polar() does not: it maps your value straight onto radius, so a month with four times the deaths is drawn with four times the radius and sixteen times the area. Every quick ggplot recreation of this chart, including the one above, exaggerates the peaks. The fix is one line.



Show the R code
# Facets sort alphabetically unless told otherwise, which silently put "area"
# on the left and made the caption below wrong the first time this rendered.
hows <- c("Value on radius\n(ggplot's default)", "Value on area\n(what Nightingale drew)")
compare <- bind_rows(
  long |> filter(cause == "Preventable disease") |> mutate(r = rate,       how = hows[1]),
  long |> filter(cause == "Preventable disease") |> mutate(r = sqrt(rate), how = hows[2])
) |>
  mutate(how = factor(how, levels = hows)) |>
  # Each panel is scaled to its own maximum. facet_grid shares one radial
  # scale, and sqrt(1023) is 32, so the area version rendered as a dot. What is
  # being compared here is the SHAPE — how the months relate to each other —
  # not the absolute size, and the caption says so.
  mutate(r = r / max(r), .by = c(period, how))

ggplot(compare, aes(Month, r)) +
  geom_col(width = 1, fill = causes[["Preventable disease"]], alpha = .85,
           colour = "white", linewidth = .2) +
  coord_polar() +
  facet_grid(period ~ how, switch = "y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "The same deaths, drawn two ways",
       subtitle = "Preventable disease only, both years",
       caption = "Taking the square root before plotting puts the quantity back on area, where Nightingale had it.") +
  theme_dsvar(base_size = 9, grid = "none") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 90, size = 7.5),
        strip.text.x = element_text(size = 8.5))










Left: what you get by default. Right: the same numbers with sqrt() applied, so area carries the quantity. Each panel is scaled to its own maximum, so compare the shapes rather than the sizes: January’s wedge dominates its neighbours far more on the left than it should. Absolute magnitudes across the two years are in the chart above and the one below.




THE SAME DATA, UNROLLED



Show the R code
ggplot(long, aes(Date, rate, fill = cause)) +
  geom_area(alpha = .9) +
  annotate("segment", x = as.Date("1855-03-01"), xend = as.Date("1855-03-01"),
           y = 0, yend = 1100, colour = "#5a5a52", linewidth = .4, linetype = "22") +
  annotate("text", x = as.Date("1855-03-20"), y = 1050, hjust = 0, size = 3,
           colour = "#3a3a34", family = dsvar_font(),
           label = "Sanitary Commission arrives") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = causes, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Deaths per 1,000 per year",
       title = "The same 24 months on a time axis",
       subtitle = "Readable, orderable, and much easier to argue with",
       caption = "n = 24 months · Nightingale (1858), via HistData") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")










This version is better on every measure the course usually cares about: time on position, quantity on length, the turning point annotated. It is also the version that would not have been printed, passed around a commission, or remembered for 160 years. Nightingale was not choosing between accurate and beautiful but between a chart that was read and one that was not.




SOURCES


Original: Nightingale, F. (1858). Diagram of the causes of mortality in the army in the East. Public domain.
Data: Nightingale in Friendly, M., HistData, digitised from the 1858 plate. Nightingale’s figures are public domain; HistData is GPL. Vendored here as data/raw/nightingale.csv.
On the area question: Cleveland, W. S., & McGill, R. (1984). Graphical perception. JASA, 79(387), 531–554.
Reproduce it: every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: Pandemic trajectories on a log scale
text:
Gallery · Change over time · back to the gallery


Pandemic trajectories on a log scale

Two decisions, both arguable, both argued about at the time: put deaths on a log axis, and start every country’s clock at its own tenth death rather than on a shared calendar date. Together they turned an unreadable tangle into the chart a lot of people used to think about 2020.








THE ORIGINAL



“Coronavirus deaths in Italy, Spain and the US are increasing more rapidly than they did in China”. FT graphic by John Burn-Murdoch, Financial Times, data updated 26 March 2020. © The Financial Times Limited. The FT made its coronavirus charts free to read throughout the pandemic; the graphics remain FT copyright. Reproduced here at reduced resolution as a quotation for criticism and review — see ORIGINALS.md.

John Burn-Murdoch’s trajectory charts ran daily in the Financial Times through 2020 and were among the most widely reproduced graphics of the pandemic.


How to read it


 Each line is one country, and the vertical axis is cumulative deaths: a running total, so it can only go up.


 The horizontal axis is not calendar time. Day 0 is the day that country passed its tenth death, so outbreaks that began months apart can be laid on top of each other.


 The vertical axis is logarithmic. Equal vertical steps are equal multiplications: 10 to 100 is the same distance as 100 to 1,000.


 So a straight line means constant doubling, and the slope is the growth rate. Flattening means the rate is falling, not that deaths have stopped.





THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

A line chart of a few dozen series, each labelled at its end rather than in a legend. The vertical axis is unevenly spaced and labelled in powers of ten. Faint straight guide lines run diagonally across the plot, annotated with doubling times.



02 · Analyse

Two transformations do the work. The log axis turns exponential growth, which is unreadable on a linear scale, into slope, which people read well. The alignment removes the biggest confound: countries were at different points in their outbreak. Direct labels instead of a legend keep forty series legible.



03 · Interpret

The claim is about rate, not level: given a comparable starting point, some countries bent their curve and others did not. That is a much narrower claim than “country A did worse than country B”, and the chart is careful not to make the wider one.



04 · Judge

It holds, and the criticism it attracted was fair anyway. On a log axis a catastrophe and a disaster look similar, and “flattening” reads as good news when deaths are still climbing. The FT’s answer was to label the axis loudly, draw the doubling guides, and keep publishing linear versions alongside. A transform with this much effect has to be taught on the chart itself.





THE RECREATION



Show the R code
# The doubling guides: on a log axis constant doubling is a straight line, so
# these are the reference the eye actually measures slope against.
guides <- expand_grid(days = c(2, 3, 7), day = 0:120) |>
  mutate(total_deaths = 10 * 2^(day / days),
         label = paste0("doubles every ", days, " days")) |>
  filter(total_deaths <= 1e5)

ends <- aligned |> slice_max(day, n = 1, by = country)

ggplot(aligned, aes(day, total_deaths, group = country)) +
  geom_line(data = guides, aes(group = label), colour = "#c9c4b8",
            linewidth = .35, linetype = "22") +
  geom_line(aes(colour = country %in% focus), linewidth = .7, alpha = .9) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = filter(ends, country %in% focus),
                           aes(label = country), size = 2.8, hjust = 0,
                           family = dsvar_font(), seed = 2, direction = "y",
                           nudge_x = 3, segment.size = .2,
                           bg.color = "#faf8f4", bg.r = .12) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = dsvar_accent(), `FALSE` = "#c2cdc7"),
                      guide = "none") +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 135), ylim = c(10, 1e5)) +
  labs(title = "Same starting point, very different slopes",
       subtitle = "Cumulative deaths on a log axis, aligned at each country's 10th death",
       x = "Days since the 10th death", y = "Cumulative deaths (log scale)",
       caption = sprintf("n = %d countries, 2020 · WHO via Our World in Data (CC BY 4.0)",
                         length(unique(aligned$country))))












THE TWO DECISIONS, TAKEN APART

Each panel changes exactly one thing from the chart above.


Show the R code
cal <- cov |> filter(!is.na(total_deaths), total_deaths >= 10) |>
  mutate(day = as.numeric(date - as.Date("2020-01-01")))

grid4 <- bind_rows(
  cal     |> mutate(t = "Calendar date", s = "Linear"),
  cal     |> mutate(t = "Calendar date", s = "Log"),
  aligned |> mutate(t = "Aligned at 10th death", s = "Linear"),
  aligned |> mutate(t = "Aligned at 10th death", s = "Log")
) |>
  mutate(t = factor(t, c("Calendar date", "Aligned at 10th death")),
         s = factor(s, c("Linear", "Log")))

# One plot per y-transform, because a single facetted plot cannot carry two
# different scales — the mistake that produced two identical panels on the
# Gapminder page.
mk <- function(scale_lab) {
  g <- ggplot(filter(grid4, s == scale_lab), aes(day, total_deaths, group = country)) +
    geom_line(colour = dsvar_accent(), alpha = .55, linewidth = .5) +
    facet_wrap(~t, scales = "free_x") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = paste0("Cumulative deaths (", tolower(scale_lab), ")"),
         title = paste(scale_lab, "vertical axis"))
  if (scale_lab == "Log") g + scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) else
    g + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma())
}

library(patchwork)
mk("Linear") / mk("Log")










The bottom-right panel is the only one you can read, and it took both decisions to get there. The chart everyone remembers is not a neutral view of the numbers: it is two strong transformations, chosen because the raw version says nothing. Every one of those choices was available to someone who wanted a different answer.




WHAT THE LOG AXIS COSTS



Show the R code
three <- aligned |> filter(country %in% c("United States", "Germany", "South Korea"))

lin <- ggplot(three, aes(day, total_deaths, colour = country)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = dsvar_cat[1:3], name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "Days since 10th death", y = NULL, title = "Linear") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

lg <- lin + scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "Log")

lin + lg










Same three countries, same 120 days. On the right the three lines look like variations on a theme. On the left one of them is an order of magnitude above the others. Both are true; only one of them feels like 300,000 people.




SOURCES


Original: Burn-Murdoch, J. (2020). Coronavirus tracked: the latest figures as countries fight the Covid-19 resurgence. Financial Times. FT copyright.
Data: World Health Organization COVID-19 deaths, via Our World in Data’s COVID-19 dataset, ourworldindata.org/coronavirus, CC BY 4.0 (OWID replaced its earlier Johns Hopkins CSSE series, also CC BY 4.0, with WHO’s). Subset to 13 countries through 2020 and vendored as data/raw/owid-covid-deaths-2020.csv.
Reproduce it: every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: Playfair’s wheat and wages
text:
Gallery · Change over time · back to the gallery


Playfair’s wheat and wages

Two and a half centuries of the price of wheat and the wage of a skilled workman, on one page, by the man who invented the line chart and the bar chart. The chart is famous, but the argument it was drawn for is about how many weeks of work a quarter of wheat cost, and that is the one thing it does not show. In the same pamphlet, Playfair drew the chart that does.








THE ORIGINAL



Chart, Shewing at One View the Price of the Quarter of Wheat, & Wages of Labour by the Week, from the Year 1565 to 1821, Chart No. 1 in William Playfair, A Letter on Our Agricultural Distresses, Their Causes and Remedies (London: William Sams, 1821). Public domain (author died 1823); scan via Wikimedia Commons.

William Playfair invented the line chart and the bar chart in 1786 and the pie chart in 1801. This chart comes late in his career, from a pamphlet addressed to the Lords and Commons on the distress of English agriculture. Its point, in the words of the R package that carries its data, was that working men had never been as well off in what their wages would buy as they had become toward the end of the period.


How to read it
