 Across: time, 1565 to 1821, in five-year steps, with the reigning monarch in a band along the top and the centuries above that.


 Each dark bar is the price of a quarter of wheat, eight bushels, in shillings, averaged over five years.


 The red line over the pale blue area is a week’s wage of “a good mechanic”, a skilled workman, also in shillings.


 One scale serves both, shillings from 0 to 100 on either side. A price per quarter and a wage per week share the unit and nothing else.





THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

A grid in five-year and five-shilling steps from 1565 to 1821. Dark bars, one per five years, hover between 25 and 65 shillings for two centuries and then jump to 99 in 1810. Beneath them a red line over a pale blue area climbs slowly from 5 to 30 shillings and stops in 1810. Reigns along the top, centuries above them, a cartouche with the title in the upper middle. No legend: the line is labelled along its length.



02 · Analyse

Time on the horizontal axis, and two quantities on one vertical scale in the same unit: a price per quarter of wheat as bars, a wage per week as a line with an area under it. The two encodings fit what each series is, a level held over five years and a wage that accumulates. The reigns are a categorical annotation of time, the first of their kind. What the shared scale invites is a comparison of heights, and the two heights do not measure the same thing.



03 · Interpret

The claim is that wages had caught up with the price of bread: the gap between the bars and the line narrows from Elizabeth to George III, so a week’s work bought more wheat at the end than at the start. The reader is asked to see the two series move toward each other.



04 · Judge

A claim about a ratio, drawn as a gap. The vertical distance between a price per quarter and a wage per week has no meaning, so the eye is measuring the wrong thing, and the steep last bars say the opposite of the claim: wheat was dearer than ever. The ratio is in the data but not on the chart, and Playfair knew it: Chart No. 3 of the same pamphlet, below, draws the price of the quarter in days of a mechanic’s wages, and there the argument is visible at a glance. The famous chart is the weaker one.





THE RECREATION

The data is HistData’s digitisation of the chart. Bars are drawn the way the engraver shaded them, darkest at the top; the wage line and its area, the reigns and the cartouche are placed where the plate has them.


Show the R code
serif <- c(intersect(c("Hoefler Text", "Baskerville", "Georgia"),
                     systemfonts::system_fonts()$family), "serif")[1]
paper <- "#ece6d4"; ink <- "#2e2a27"; red <- "#c8343a"; blue <- "#a9c8cd"

bars <- wheat |>
  mutate(xmin = Year, xmax = lead(Year, default = 1821.6))
cart <- tibble(t = seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 200),
               x = 1637 + 29 * cos(t), y = 66 + 12.5 * sin(t))
reigns <- monarchs |>
  mutate(level = rep(c(0, 1), length.out = n()),
         ymin = 95.6 - level * 1.8, ymax = ymin + 1.2,
         mid = (start + end) / 2,
         label = recode(name, "W&M" = "William\nand Mary"))

recreation <- ggplot() +
  # the grid, heavier at the centuries
  geom_vline(xintercept = seq(1565, 1825, 5), colour = "#b9b1a0", linewidth = .2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(1600, 1700, 1800), colour = ink, linewidth = .6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = seq(0, 100, 5), colour = "#b9b1a0", linewidth = .2) +
  # wages: a pale area under a red line
  geom_area(data = both, aes(Year, Wages), fill = blue, alpha = .9) +
  geom_line(data = both, aes(Year, Wages), colour = red, linewidth = 1.1) +
  # wheat: the bar, then its dark top, as the engraver shaded it
  geom_rect(data = bars, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = pmax(Wheat - 22, 0), ymax = Wheat),
            fill = ink, alpha = .35) +
  geom_rect(data = bars, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = pmax(Wheat - 9, 0), ymax = Wheat),
            fill = ink, alpha = .85) +
  # the reigns
  geom_rect(data = reigns, aes(xmin = start, xmax = end, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax), fill = ink) +
  geom_text(data = reigns, aes(mid, ymin - 1.9, label = label), family = serif,
            fontface = "italic", size = 2.4, colour = ink, vjust = 1, lineheight = .85) +
  annotate("text", x = c(1582, 1650, 1750, 1810), y = 102.5,
           label = c("16th Century", "17th Century", "18th Century", "19th Century"),
           family = serif, fontface = "bold", size = 3.3, colour = ink) +
  # the cartouche
  geom_polygon(data = cart, aes(x, y), fill = "#f4efe2", colour = ink, linewidth = .6) +
  annotate("text", x = 1637, y = c(74.5, 69.5, 65, 61, 57.5), family = serif, colour = ink,
           label = c("CHART,", "Shewing at One View", "The Price of The Quarter of Wheat,",
                     "& Wages of Labour by the Week, from 1565 to 1821,", "by WILLIAM PLAYFAIR."),
           size = c(5.2, 3.2, 3.2, 2.7, 2.6), fontface = c("bold", "italic", "italic", "plain", "bold")) +
  annotate("text", x = 1662, y = 9.6, label = "Weekly Wages of a Good Mechanic", angle = 3,
           family = serif, fontface = "italic", size = 2.6, colour = ink) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1570, 1820, 10), expand = c(0, 0),
                     labels = function(x) if_else(x %% 100 == 0, as.character(x), substr(x, 3, 4))) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, 10), expand = c(0, 0),
                     sec.axis = dup_axis(name = "Price of the Quarter of Wheat in Shillings")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(1565, 1825), ylim = c(0, 100), clip = "off") +
  labs(x = "5 Years each division", y = NULL) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = paper, colour = NA),
        panel.background = element_rect(fill = paper, colour = ink, linewidth = .8),
        axis.text = element_text(family = serif, size = 8, colour = ink),
        axis.text.x = element_text(margin = margin(t = 3)),
        axis.title.x = element_text(family = serif, face = "italic", size = 8.5, colour = ink,
                                    margin = margin(t = 4)),
        axis.title.y.right = element_text(family = serif, face = "italic", size = 8.5,
                                          colour = ink, angle = 90, margin = margin(l = 6)),
        plot.margin = margin(30, 12, 8, 10))

recreation










n = 53 five-yearly prices, 50 of them with a wage, as digitised in HistData::Wheat. Drawn at the scan’s proportions, 1109 × 586. The grid, the scale and the order of layers follow the plate; the shading of the bars and the lettering are approximations of an engraving.




Original · Playfair, 1821





Ours · ggplot













Side by side, at the same size. The bar heights and the wage line are the data. The shading, the lettering and the arcs over the centuries are the engraver’s, and ours are only an imitation.




HOW WE KNOW

The values. Playfair published a table with the pamphlet, but the numbers used here were read off Chart No. 1 itself: digitised for Michael Friendly’s gallery of historical graphics, carried into the Protovis examples, and shipped in the HistData package as Wheat and Wheat.monarchs. The comparison above is the check: a misread value would show as a bar out of place.
The unit. A quarter of wheat is eight bushels. HistData’s help page calls it a “quarter bushel”, which is not what Playfair measured; at 47 shillings a quarter in the 1560s, a quarter bushel would have cost more than a week’s wage several times over.
Chart No. 3 against the data. The prices on No. 3, averaged over quarter-centuries, match the digitised bars to within about two shillings in every period. Its days’ wages do not match a simple division of the digitised weekly wage: for 1565 to 1599 the plate shows about 73 days, while dividing the data, at a six-day week, gives 55; for 1800 to 1821 it shows about 14, while the data give 18, partly because the digitised wages end in 1810, the year of the dearest wheat. Playfair’s table must have used wages other than the line on No. 1, or another working week. The ratio drawn below is the division of the numbers we have. It agrees with No. 3 on the direction and on when the fall happened, not on the day counts.



THE SAME NUMBERS, DIFFERENT CHOICES


His own answer: Chart No. 3


Chart Shewing the Value of the Quarter of Wheat in Shillings & in Days Wages of a Good Mechanic from 1565 to 1821, Chart No. 3 in Playfair (1821). Copperplate with added colour, 13.5 × 28.7 cm. Public domain; scan via Wikimedia Commons, from the copy at Princeton, reduced to 1400 pixels wide.


One quarter-century per block, and two prices for the same quarter of wheat: in shillings, and in days of work. Green while the price in days stood above the price in shillings, pink once it fell below. The shillings rise at the end; the days fall all the way. The same pamphlet, two pages on, makes the argument Chart No. 1 only gestures at.



The same numbers, divided


Show the R code
ggplot(both, aes(Year, weeks)) +
  geom_segment(data = periods, aes(x = start, xend = end, y = weeks, yend = weeks),
               colour = dsvar_accent(), linewidth = 2.2, alpha = .45) +
  geom_step(colour = p$ink, linewidth = .7, direction = "hv") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .05))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1575, 1800, 25)) +
  labs(title = sprintf("A quarter of wheat cost %.1f weeks of a mechanic's wage in 1565 to 1599, and %.1f in 1800 to 1810",
                       first_p$weeks, last_p$weeks),
       subtitle = "Weeks of wages per quarter, every five years; the bars are averages over Playfair's quarter-centuries",
       x = NULL, y = "weeks of wages",
       caption = sprintf("Price per quarter ÷ weekly wage, from HistData::Wheat. n = %d five-yearly values. Cheapest: %.1f weeks in %d.",
                         nrow(both), cheapest$weeks, cheapest$Year)) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = p$hairline, linewidth = .3))










One line where the original had two, and the claim can be read off it. The fall happens between the late seventeenth century and the middle of the eighteenth, and the dear years after 1795 push it back up only a little. A week’s wage bought more wheat at the end than at the start, which is what Playfair argued and what Chart No. 1 cannot show.



Two scales, any story


Show the R code
dual <- function(meet) {
  # Rescale wages onto the price axis so the two series touch at `meet`, with
  # the ranges matched: the second axis is a and b, chosen.
  b <- diff(range(both$Wheat)) / diff(range(both$Wages))
  a <- both$Wheat[both$Year == meet] - b * both$Wages[both$Year == meet]
  ggplot(both, aes(Year)) +
    geom_col(aes(y = Wheat), fill = p$muted, width = 4.2) +
    geom_line(aes(y = a + b * Wages), colour = dsvar_accent(), linewidth = 1.1) +
    scale_y_continuous(name = "price, shillings a quarter",
                       sec.axis = sec_axis(~ (. - a) / b, name = "wage, shillings a week")) +
    labs(title = sprintf("Wages catch up with wheat in %d", meet), x = NULL) +
    theme(axis.title.y.right = element_text(colour = dsvar_accent()),
          axis.text.y.right = element_text(colour = dsvar_accent()))
}
dual(1700) | dual(1800)










Playfair kept one scale, the honest choice. Give the wage its own axis, as two series in different units usually get, and where the line meets the bars is set by two numbers somebody chose: the offset and the stretch of the second axis. Both panels are the same 50 pairs of values. Neither crossing means anything.


Two series on one time axis invite the reader to read the gap between them, and the gap between a price and a wage measures nothing. When the claim is about how one quantity stands against another, divide them and draw the result. Playfair, who invented the form that made the first chart possible, drew the second chart himself, two pages later.





SOURCES


Original: Playfair, W. (1821). A Letter on Our Agricultural Distresses, Their Causes and Remedies; Accompanied with Tables and Copper-plate Charts, Shewing and Comparing the Prices of Wheat, Bread, and Labour, from 1565 to 1821. London: William Sams. Charts No. 1 and No. 3. Public domain; scans via Wikimedia Commons.
Data: Wheat and Wheat.monarchs from the HistData package (version 1.1.1), digitised from Chart No. 1. GPL in HistData; the chart itself is public domain. Vendored here as data/raw/playfair-wheat.csv and data/raw/playfair-monarchs.csv.
History: Friendly, M., & Denis, D. (2005). The early origins and development of the scatterplot. Journal of the History of the Behavioral Sciences, 41(2), 103–130.
Reproduce it: every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: Sankey and alluvial flows
text:
Gallery · Relationships & structure · back to the gallery


Sankey and alluvial flows

A form for showing where a quantity went: how a whole divides, recombines and loses some of itself along the way. It is the only chart type in this gallery that a reader can follow with a finger, which is what it is for.








THE ORIGINAL



Diagram of the thermal efficiency of steam engines by Matthew H. P. R. Sankey, 1898, from Minutes of Proceedings of the Institution of Civil Engineers. Public domain; scan via Wikimedia Commons.

Matthew Henry Phineas Riall Sankey drew this in 1898 to show where the energy in a steam engine actually goes. The answer, visible without reading a number, is: mostly not into work.


How to read it


 Follow the flow from one side to the other. The whole quantity enters as a single band and is progressively divided.


 The width of every band is the amount flowing through it, and widths are conserved: what leaves a junction equals what entered it.


 Branches that peel off are losses. Their width is how much was lost, and where they leave is where in the process it happened.


 The narrow band at the end is the useful output. Its thinness relative to the input is the argument.





THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

Bands of varying width running left to right, splitting at junctions. Every band is labelled with what it carries. There are no axes and no gridlines, and the only quantitative channel is thickness.



02 · Analyse

Quantity is on width, which is a length and therefore reasonably accurate, but most of the work is done by conservation. Because widths must sum at every junction, the reader can check the diagram against itself. Very few chart types let you do that, and it is why a Sankey feels trustworthy in a way a pie chart does not.



03 · Interpret

The claim is that the losses are the story: the useful output is a thin remnant of what went in, and you can see exactly where the rest went.



04 · Judge

Excellent for a conserved quantity moving through stages, and badly overused for anything else. The form silently promises that the thing being tracked is the same thing throughout and that nothing appears from outside. Point it at categories that merely co-occur and it will still draw a confident picture of a process that does not exist.





THE SAME FORM, DIFFERENT DATA

Unlike most exhibits in this gallery, this section does not redraw the original. Sankey’s engine is a single process measured once; what the form looks like in ggplot is easier to see on data you can load yourself. So this is the same form applied to datasets::Titanic, which ships with R: 2,201 people, by class, sex and survival. It is the categorical version of Sankey’s diagram, usually called an alluvial diagram, and the rule is the same: every band’s width is an amount, and the amounts add up at every step.


Show the R code
ggplot(titanic, aes(y = Freq, axis1 = Class, axis2 = Sex, axis3 = Survived)) +
  geom_alluvium(aes(fill = Survived), width = .28, alpha = .78, knot.pos = .3) +
  geom_stratum(width = .28, fill = "#f2f0ea", colour = "#d8d3c7", linewidth = .3) +
  geom_text(stat = "stratum", aes(label = after_stat(stratum)),
            size = 2.9, family = dsvar_font()) +
  scale_x_discrete(limits = c("Class", "Sex", "Outcome"), expand = c(.08, .08)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Died = "#a5a199", Survived = dsvar_accent()),
                    name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Where 2,201 people went",
       subtitle = "Every band's width is a number of people, and widths are conserved at each step",
       y = "People", x = NULL,
       caption = "n = 2,201 · datasets::Titanic, shipped with R") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")










Read a single band with your finger: third class → male → died is the widest path on the chart. First class → female → survived is almost undiminished.




WHAT A STACKED BAR LOSES



Show the R code
titanic |>
  summarise(n = sum(Freq), .by = c(Class, Survived)) |>
  ggplot(aes(Class, n, fill = Survived)) +
  geom_col(width = .7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Died = "#a5a199", Survived = dsvar_accent()),
                    name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "The same people, summarised by class alone",
       subtitle = "Correct, readable, and the interaction with sex has vanished",
       x = NULL, y = "People",
       caption = "n = 2,201 · datasets::Titanic") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")










Nothing here is wrong, and for the single question “did class matter?” it is the better chart: shorter, easier, no bands to trace. What it cannot show is that third-class women survived at a higher rate than second-class men, because once you collapse to one variable the joint structure is gone. The alluvial answers a question this chart cannot be asked.




THE FORM’S OWN TRAP



Show the R code
set.seed(11)
fake <- expand_grid(Breakfast = c("Coffee", "Tea"),
                    Commute   = c("Bike", "Tram", "Car"),
                    Weather   = c("Rain", "Dry")) |>
  mutate(Freq = sample(40:400, n()))

ggplot(fake, aes(y = Freq, axis1 = Breakfast, axis2 = Commute, axis3 = Weather)) +
  geom_alluvium(aes(fill = Weather), width = .28, alpha = .7, knot.pos = .3) +
  geom_stratum(width = .28, fill = "#f2f0ea", colour = "#d8d3c7", linewidth = .3) +
  geom_text(stat = "stratum", aes(label = after_stat(stratum)),
            size = 2.9, family = dsvar_font()) +
  scale_x_discrete(limits = c("Breakfast", "Commute", "Weather"), expand = c(.08, .08)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Rain = "#a5a199", Dry = dsvar_accent()), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Nothing flows from your breakfast to the weather",
       subtitle = "Random numbers, three unrelated variables, and a diagram that looks like a process",
       y = NULL, x = NULL,
       caption = "Simulated data. The chart cannot tell, and neither can the reader.")











THE LEFT-TO-RIGHT READS AS CAUSATION

An alluvial diagram of three arbitrary categorical variables is visually indistinguishable from one tracking a real process. The form supplies a direction, a sense of stages, and an implication that what happens later depends on what happened earlier. None of that is in the data. Before drawing one, check that your quantity really is conserved and really does move through those stages in that order. If it does not, you have drawn a claim you cannot support.




SOURCES


Original: Sankey, M. H. P. R. (1898). Introductory note on the thermal efficiency of steam engines. Minutes of Proceedings of the Institution of Civil Engineers, 134. Public domain.
Data: datasets::Titanic, shipped with R: 2,201 people by class, sex, age and survival.
Drawing it: the ggalluvial package, which supplies geom_alluvium() and geom_stratum().
Reproduce it: every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: The specification curve
text:
Gallery · Distribution & uncertainty · back to the gallery


The specification curve

Every defensible analysis at once. Where many analysts hands a dataset to twenty-nine teams, this form does the same job with one team and a loop. This is the closest a chart gets to showing you the space of answers a paper could have reported.








THE ORIGINAL



Figure 1 from Orben, A., & Przybylski, A. K. (2019). The association between adolescent well-being and digital technology use. Nature Human Behaviour, 3, 173–182. Accepted-manuscript version, deposited by the authors at the Oxford University Research Archive. © Orben & Przybylski 2019; the article itself is not open access. Reproduced here at reduced resolution as a quotation for criticism and review — see ORIGINALS.md.

Amy Orben and Andrew Przybylski ran the screen-time-and-wellbeing question across every defensible analysis of the same survey data, and plotted every result. The famous conclusion, that the association is about the size of the association with eating potatoes, only means anything because the whole distribution is on the page. This is the Youth Risk and Behaviour Survey panel; two more, on 40,000 and 20,000 specifications, follow it in the paper.


How to read it


 The upper panel is every result, one per analysis, sorted from most negative to most positive. It is a distribution of answers, not a time series.


 Each point is one complete analysis: a particular well-being measure, technology measure and set of controls, run to completion. Black is significant, red is not.


 The dashed horizontal line is the median of the whole curve: β = −.035 here. It is the paper’s headline number, and it is a summary of the distribution rather than a result of any one analysis.


 The lower panel is the recipe. Read straight down from any point and the marked rows tell you exactly which choices produced it.


 Vertical bands of marks are the finding. TV Use is marked under the whole right-hand end and nowhere else: the choice of technology measure is doing most of the work.





THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

Two stacked panels sharing a horizontal axis. Above: a dense line or cloud of point estimates, ordered by size, usually with intervals. Below: a grid of small marks, one row per analytic option, aligned to the panel above.



02 · Analyse

The horizontal axis is rank, not a variable: it exists only to order the results. That is unusual and it is the trick: it turns a set of unrelated analyses into a distribution you can read the shape of. The lower panel is a lookup table pretending to be a chart, and the alignment between the two is the entire mechanism.



03 · Interpret

The claim is about the robustness of a result rather than its value. A curve that sits entirely on one side of zero says something a single estimate cannot; one that crosses zero says the headline depended on choices the reader never saw.



04 · Judge

It works, with one limit: the curve contains only the specifications its author thought to include, so it looks exhaustive and is not. A specification curve is a much better summary than one regression, and it is still a set of choices about which choices to vary.





THE RECREATION

The survey data behind the original is registration-gated, so this runs the same question on a synthetic stand-in for one wave of pairfam: does adolescent media use go with worse well-being? The specifications are built with specr, which turns the choices into a factorial design and fits every cell: three lines of set-up in place of a hand-written loop.


Show the R code
# Every combination of these is one defensible analysis. specr expands the
# controls into all four subsets (none, each, both) on its own, and `subsets`
# additionally runs each specification on girls, on boys, and on everyone.
specs <- setup(
  data     = d,
  x        = c("tv_use", "sns_use", "internet_use"),
  y        = c("self_esteem", "depression", "depression_p1", "life_satisfaction_r"),
  model    = "lm",
  controls = c("friend_satisfaction", "age"),
  subsets  = list(gender = c("female", "male"))
)

results <- specr(specs)


specr() fits all of them and returns one row per analysis. The package’s own plot() turns that into a specification curve in a single line, with no ggplot written at all:


Show the R code
plot(results)










The package default, straight out of plot(results): every estimate ranked by size above, the dashboard of choices below. Fine for looking at your own results. Not yet a figure for a reader: the labels are column names, there is no median, and a model row is shown even though only one model was fitted.

That is not where specr stops, because results$data is an ordinary tibble: one row per specification, with the estimate, its interval, its p-value and the choices that produced it as columns, and anything ggplot can draw can be drawn from it. Here is the same curve built by hand, with plain labels, a median line, the dashboard grouped by kind of choice, and the site’s colours.


Show the R code
# results$data is a plain tibble, so from here on this is ordinary ggplot:
# every choice below is one plot() makes for you and you can make differently.
r <- as_tibble(results$data) |>
  mutate(subsets = replace_na(as.character(subsets), "all")) |>
  arrange(estimate) |>
  mutate(rank = row_number(),
         sig  = factor(if_else(p.value < .05, "p < .05", "not significant"),
                       levels = c("p < .05", "not significant")))

pal  <- c("p < .05" = dsvar_cat[1], "not significant" = "#a5a199")
med  <- median(r$estimate)

curve <- ggplot(r, aes(rank, estimate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = .5, colour = dsvar_light$ink_3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = med, linetype = "22", linewidth = .4,
             colour = dsvar_light$muted) +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high, colour = sig),
                 linewidth = .5, alpha = .55) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = sig), size = 1.1) +
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = med, hjust = 0, vjust = -0.7, size = 3.1,
           colour = dsvar_light$muted,
           label = sprintf("median β = %.3f", med)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal, name = NULL) +
  labs(y = "Standardised β", x = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), legend.position = "top")

# The dashboard. One row per option, a mark wherever that option was used —
# and the marks carry the same colour as the estimate above them, so a band of
# grey in one row is visible as "this choice is where the effect disappears".
nice <- c(tv_use = "TV use", sns_use = "social media use",
          internet_use = "internet use",
          self_esteem = "self-esteem", depression = "depression",
          depression_p1 = "depression (subscale)",
          life_satisfaction_r = "life satisfaction",
          "no covariates" = "no controls",
          friend_satisfaction = "+ friend satisfaction", age = "+ age",
          "friend_satisfaction + age" = "+ both",
          all = "everyone", female = "girls only", male = "boys only")

choices <- r |>
  select(rank, sig, x, y, controls, subsets) |>
  pivot_longer(c(x, y, controls, subsets), names_to = "block", values_to = "choice") |>
  mutate(block  = factor(block, levels = c("x", "y", "controls", "subsets"),
                         labels = c("Predictor", "Outcome", "Controls", "Sample")),
         choice = factor(nice[choice], levels = rev(nice)))

dash <- ggplot(choices, aes(rank, choice, colour = sig)) +
  geom_point(size = .9, shape = 15) +
  facet_grid(block ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y", switch = "y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Specifications, ranked by effect size", y = NULL) +
  theme_dsvar(base_size = 9, grid = "none") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
        strip.placement  = "outside",
        strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0, face = "bold"),
        panel.spacing.y  = unit(4, "pt"))

# cowplot rather than patchwork: the two panels have different y-label widths,
# and align = "v", axis = "lr" is the reliable way to make the ranks line up.
plot_grid(curve, dash, ncol = 1, align = "v", axis = "lr",
          rel_heights = c(1.4, 2))










144 specifications on n = 3,130 cases. Estimates run from -0.072 to 0.184, median 0.070; 104 of 144 reach p < .05. All variables standardised, so β is comparable across specifications. The four well-being indicators are positively inter-correlated in this file (r = .40 to .92), so they point the same way and a positive β means more media use goes with higher scores on all four. Synthetic pairfam data from Masur’s specification curve tutorial.



WHAT SPECR DOES AND WHAT IT DOES NOT

setup() builds the factorial design and specr() fits it. plot() is the quick look; because the results are a tibble, the figure a reader sees can be whatever you build from it. The package removes the bookkeeping, not the thinking: the list of choices passed to setup() is still the whole argument, and it is the part no function can check for you.




WHICH CHOICE MOVES THE RESULT

The curve tells you how robust the effect is. The dashboard tells you which choice moves it, and the eye is bad at reading that off a grid of marks. Fitting a mixed model to the 144 estimates, with a random intercept per kind of choice, answers it directly.


Show the R code
vc <- lme4::lmer(estimate ~ 1 + (1 | x) + (1 | y) + (1 | controls) + (1 | subsets),
                 data = r) |>
  lme4::VarCorr() |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  transmute(choice = recode(grp, x = "Which media measure", y = "Which well-being measure",
                            controls = "Which controls", subsets = "Which sample",
                            Residual = "Everything else (residual)"),
            percent = 100 * vcov / sum(vcov))

ggplot(vc, aes(percent, fct_reorder(choice, percent))) +
  geom_col(fill = dsvar_accent(), width = .62) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.0f%%", percent)), hjust = -0.25,
            size = 3.2, colour = dsvar_light$ink_3) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .12))) +
  labs(title = "The predictor and the sample do the work. The controls do nothing.",
       subtitle = "Share of variance in the 144 estimates attributable to each kind of choice",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())










Any single one of these 144 analyses could have been written up as the result, with a perfectly honest methods section, and the number in the abstract would have run anywhere from -0.072 to 0.184 depending on which one the author ran first. The curve cannot remove that problem, but it makes it visible, which is the most a chart can do.




THE SAME 144, WITHOUT THE RANK AXIS

The critique says the curve’s horizontal axis is rank rather than a variable, and that this is the trick. It is also the cost: sorting by effect size throws the design away, and the dashboard underneath is there to put it back one row at a time. These 144 analyses are a complete 3 × 4 × 4 × 3 factorial, so they do not need reconstructing: they can be laid out on their own axes, every cell filled exactly once. This is close to the grid Steegen and colleagues drew for the multiverse analysis four years before the curve became the standard form, and it answers a different question.


Show the R code
# The four choices become two nested axes and two facets. Nothing is sorted, so
# every position on this page means something.
pred_lab <- c(tv_use = "TV use", sns_use = "social media use",
              internet_use = "internet use")
samp_lab <- c(all = "everyone", female = "girls only", male = "boys only")
out_lab  <- c(self_esteem = "self-esteem", depression = "depression",
              depression_p1 = "depression (sub)",
              life_satisfaction_r = "life satisfaction")
ctrl_lab <- c("no covariates" = "none", friend_satisfaction = "+ friends",
              age = "+ age", "friend_satisfaction + age" = "+ both")

# Brown-to-teal rather than red-to-green: the sign is the whole point of this
# scale, so it has to survive red-green colour vision deficiency. Neutral at
# zero, and the limits are symmetric so equal-and-opposite betas read as equal.
div <- c("#8c5109", "#cf9a4a", "#e9e4d8", "#5ab4ac", "#01665e")
lim <- max(abs(r$estimate))

# The number inside a cell sits on a fill that runs from near-white to near-
# black, so the label colour is computed from the tile rather than guessed from
# a cut-off on beta: take the actual hex, then whichever of ink and paper wins
# on WCAG contrast.
relative_luminance <- function(hex) {
  ch <- t(grDevices::col2rgb(hex)) / 255
  ch <- ifelse(ch <= .03928, ch / 12.92, ((ch + .055) / 1.055)^2.4)
  as.numeric(ch %*% c(.2126, .7152, .0722))
}
contrast_ratio <- function(a, b) {
  (pmax(relative_luminance(a), relative_luminance(b)) + .05) /
  (pmin(relative_luminance(a), relative_luminance(b)) + .05)
}

g <- r |>
  transmute(
    estimate, sig = p.value < .05,
    predictor = factor(pred_lab[x], levels = pred_lab),
    sample    = factor(samp_lab[subsets], levels = samp_lab),
    outcome   = factor(out_lab[y],  levels = rev(out_lab)),
    controls  = factor(ctrl_lab[controls], levels = ctrl_lab)) |>
  mutate(tile  = scales::gradient_n_pal(div)((estimate + lim) / (2 * lim)),
         label = if_else(contrast_ratio(tile, dsvar_light$ink) >=
                         contrast_ratio(tile, "#ffffff"),
                         dsvar_light$ink, "#ffffff"))

ggplot(g, aes(controls, outcome)) +
  # No tile border, and the gap made by shrinking the tile, so the page's paper
  # shows through rather than a drawn line — the same move as the unit chart in
  # the many-analysts exhibit.
  geom_tile(aes(fill = estimate), width = .94, height = .94, colour = NA) +
  # Significance cannot ride on the fill, which is already carrying magnitude.
  # Outlining only the nulls keeps the extra ink on the minority of cells.
  geom_tile(data = filter(g, !sig), fill = NA, colour = dsvar_light$ink,
            linewidth = .45, linetype = "22", width = .94, height = .94) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", sprintf("%.2f", estimate)),
                colour = I(label)), size = 2.5) +
  facet_grid(sample ~ predictor) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = div, limits = c(-lim, lim),
                       name = "Standardised β",
                       guide = guide_colourbar(title.position = "top",
                                               title.hjust = .5)) +
  coord_fixed(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "All 144 specifications, with the analytic choices as the axes",
       subtitle = "One cell per analysis. Dashed outline: not significant at p < .05",
       x = "Controls", y = "Well-being outcome") +
  theme_dsvar(base_size = 10, grid = "none") +
  theme(axis.text  = element_text(size = 8),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 8.5, colour = dsvar_light$ink_3),
        axis.line.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9),
        panel.spacing = unit(5, "pt"),
        legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.key.height = unit(6, "pt"), legend.key.width = unit(40, "pt"))










The same 144 numbers as the curve, and the same significance test. Positive still means more media use goes with higher scores on all four well-being indicators. Read the bar chart above straight off this picture: the four columns inside every panel are the four control sets and they are the same colour, which is the 0% for controls; the panels deepen from left to right, which is the 38% for the predictor; and they deepen from top to bottom, which is the 34% for the sample. Nothing here is sorted, so every position on the page means something.


Neither the curve nor the bar chart can show this: TV use among girls is the one block on this page that runs the other way, with mean β = −.031 across its 16 cells against +.093 for the same measure among boys. A ranked list has nowhere to put an interaction, and the mixed model above cannot report one either, because it fits main effects only. Add a predictor × sample term to it and 16% of the variance moves out of the residual, which falls from 29% to 22%. The grid did not test for that; it put the cells where an interaction would be visible if there were one, which is what a layout is for.



WHY THIS IS NOT THE DEFAULT

The grid works here because the design is small and completely crossed. Drop one cell and it has a hole; add a choice with twenty levels and it has no shape; and at Orben and Przybylski’s 40,000 specifications there is no grid at all: 144 cells fit on a page and 40,000 do not. It also drops the intervals. The curve draws a confidence interval for every specification; this has room for a point estimate and a significance flag and nothing more. Most of all, it cannot be read as a distribution: the median, the share that crosses zero and the shape of the space of answers, which are the curve’s entire argument, are not in this picture. The curve asks how much the answer moves; the grid asks where the movement comes from.




THE LIMIT OF THE FORM



IT LOOKS EXHAUSTIVE AND IT IS NOT

144 is not every analysis of this data; it is every analysis we thought to list. We varied the predictor, the outcome, two controls and the sample. We did not vary how the scales were built, whether to model the items rather than their mean, how to handle missing data, whether to log the heavily skewed use variables, or whether to fit a multilevel model, and every one of those is defensible. Orben and Przybylski’s curve has the same limit at a much larger scale: forty thousand specifications is still a list somebody wrote. The honest caption states which choices were varied, not just how many analyses were run.



AND THE COUNT ITSELF IS FRAGILE

Two rows of this file have no recorded gender. Passing subsets = list(gender = unique(d$gender)), the obvious thing to write, makes NA a third subset level, and specr then emits the pooled “everyone” specification twice: 192 rows instead of 144, with 48 of them exact duplicates. Nothing errors, the curve looks the same, and the median barely moves. A number in an abstract that says “we ran 192 specifications” can be wrong in a way no plot will show you, which is a good reason to print the design and read it before fitting anything.




SOURCES


Original: Orben, A., & Przybylski, A. K. (2019). The association between adolescent well-being and digital technology use. Nature Human Behaviour, 3, 173–182. doi:10.1038/s41562-018-0506-1. Figure 1 shown above from the author-deposited accepted manuscript at ORA.
The method: Simonsohn, U., Simmons, J. P., & Nelson, L. D. (2020). Specification curve analysis. Nature Human Behaviour, 4, 1208–1214. Earlier and still worth reading: Steegen, S., Tuerlinckx, F., Gelman, A., & Vanpaemel, W. (2016). Increasing transparency through a multiverse analysis. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 11, 702–712.
The package: Masur, P. K., & Scharkow, M. specr: Conducting and visualizing specification curve analyses. masurp.github.io/specr.
The tutorial this recreation follows: Specification curve analysis, CCS Amsterdam R course material, which is also where the synthetic pairfam data comes from (CC BY 4.0). The data are synthetic, not pairfam survey data; this site replaces the file’s id column with the row number.
The companion: Many analysts, one dataset.
Reproduce it: Rscript R/fetch-gallery-data.R pulls the data; every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: Van Langren’s longitudes
text:
Gallery · Distribution & uncertainty · back to the gallery


Van Langren’s longitudes

Twelve estimates of how far Rome lies east of Toledo, on a single line. This graph is often called the first graph of statistical data, and it was drawn to win a royal grant. It works the way a strip plot still works: you see at once how far the estimates disagree. What it does not show is that every one of them is wrong.








THE ORIGINAL



Grados de la Longitud, from La Verdadera Longitud por Mar y Tierra by Michael Florent van Langren, Antwerp, 1644. Public domain (author died 1675); scan via Wikimedia Commons.

Finding longitude was the great unsolved problem of seventeenth-century navigation. Latitude you can read off the sun; longitude needs the time at a reference place, and there was no clock that kept it at sea. Van Langren, royal cosmographer to Philip IV of Spain, believed he had a method, using the way light falls on the mountains and craters of the Moon, and he spent more than twenty years asking the Spanish crown to pay for it. This graph is the case for paying. The book’s title is the argument: The true longitude, by sea and land.


How to read it


 Toledo is zero. The scale is degrees of longitude east of Toledo, from 0 to 30, ticked every degree.


 Each ring is one authority’s answer to the question “how far east is Rome?” Their name is written straight up above it, in Latin form: Iansonius is Jan Jansson, Ptolomeus is Ptolemy.


 There are twelve answers, from 17.7° to 30.1°.


 ROMA labels the cluster, not a value. It is set in a convenient gap and is neither an average nor van Langren’s own answer. See below.


 The right answer is not on the graph. Nobody had it in 1644. Today’s figure is 16.5°, to the left of every ring.





THE CRITIQUE




01 · Describe

One horizontal scale from 0 to 30 degrees, with TOLEDO written up the left edge at zero. Twelve small markers sit on the scale between about 18 and 30, each with a name written vertically above it. The word ROMA is set in the gap between two clusters of markers. The title fills the empty left half. Nothing else: no second axis, no legend, no list of sources.



02 · Analyse

One continuous variable on one common scale, so position carries every value, and position is the channel people read most accurately. In today’s vocabulary it is a strip plot. The labels keep who said what, so it needs no table beside it. The scale starts at Toledo, a true zero for a distance, which makes the empty left half information rather than waste: every authority puts Rome at least 17 degrees away. The markers fall into two clusters, between 18 and 21 degrees and between 25 and 30.



03 · Interpret

The claim is that the experts disagree, by 12.4 degrees, about the distance between two of the best-known cities in Europe. At Toledo’s latitude that is about 1,060 km. The audience was a royal patron, and the unstated next step is the point: if Toledo to Rome is this uncertain, a ship’s position in the Atlantic is worse, and van Langren knew how to fix it.



04 · Judge

For its claim, close to perfect. A table makes the reader find the spread by subtracting; the line shows it before anyone reads a name. Its limit is the more useful lesson now. It shows variability and cannot show bias. Every estimate is too large, by 1.2 to 13.6 degrees, and the graph cannot say so, because a chart can only show error against a reference that is not on it.





THE RECREATION

The data is HistData’s digitisation of the graph. The marks are drawn the way the engraver drew them: a ring on the scale, with a smaller ring on top.


Show the R code
ink <- p$ink

# The original is set in an old-style serif. Use the closest one installed.
serif <- c(intersect(c("Hoefler Text", "Baskerville", "Georgia"),
                     systemfonts::system_fonts()$family), "serif")[1]

# Names on neighbouring marks would print on top of each other, so nudge them
# apart until no two are closer than `gap` degrees, keeping each crowded run
# centred on the marks it labels. The engraver did the same by hand.
spread_out <- function(x, gap) {
  o <- order(x); y <- x[o]
  repeat {
    moved <- FALSE
    runs  <- cumsum(c(TRUE, diff(y) >= gap - 1e-9))
    for (r in unique(runs)) {
      i <- which(runs == r)
      if (length(i) < 2) next
      want <- mean(x[o][i]) + (seq_along(i) - (length(i) + 1) / 2) * gap
      if (any(abs(want - y[i]) > 1e-9)) { y[i] <- want; moved <- TRUE }
    }
    if (!moved) break
  }
  replace(x, o, y)
}

ticks  <- tibble(x = 0:30, len = if_else(x %% 5 == 0, .11, .07))
marks  <- tibble(x = c(0, langren$Longitude))      # Toledo gets a mark too
labels <- langren |> mutate(at = spread_out(Longitude, .5))

recreation <- ggplot() +
  annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = 30, y = 0, yend = 0, colour = ink, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_segment(data = ticks, aes(x = x, xend = x, y = 0, yend = -len),
               colour = ink, linewidth = .9) +
  annotate("text", x = c(10, 20, 30) - .35, y = -.16, label = c(10, 20, 30),
           family = serif, size = 5.4, colour = ink) +
  # each mark is a ring on the scale with a smaller ring on top, as engraved
  geom_point(data = marks, aes(x, .045), shape = 1, size = 3.4, stroke = 1.5, colour = ink) +
  geom_point(data = marks, aes(x, .115), shape = 1, size = 2.2, stroke = 1.3, colour = ink) +
  geom_text(data = labels, aes(at, .165, label = paste0(Name, ".")),
            angle = 90, hjust = 0, family = serif, fontface = "bold.italic",
            size = 5, colour = ink) +
  annotate("text", x = .05, y = .17, label = "TOLEDO.", angle = 90, hjust = 0,
           family = serif, size = 8.2, colour = ink) +
  annotate("text", x = 23.35, y = .075, label = "ROMA", family = serif,
           size = 8.4, colour = ink) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.6, y = .5, label = "GRADOS DE LA LONGITUD.", hjust = 0,
           family = serif, size = 9.6, colour = ink) +
  # The limits put 0 and 30 where the engraving has them, measured off the scan
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-.6, 32.06), ylim = c(-.4, 1), expand = FALSE) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = p$paper, colour = NA))

recreation










n = 12 determinations, as digitised in HistData::Langren1644. Drawn at the scan’s proportions, 595 × 151, with 0 and 30 where the engraving puts them, so the two can be compared directly. Names are spelled as HistData transcribes them (Jansonius where the engraver set Iansonius), and the title is in capitals where the engraver used small capitals.



HOW WE KNOW

The values. Nobody typed these in from a table, because van Langren never published one. Friendly, Valero-Mora and Ibáñez Ulargui digitised them from the graph itself for their 2010 paper, and they ship with the HistData package. The comparison above is the check: a misread value would show as a ring out of place.
What ROMA means. The word is easy to read as van Langren’s best estimate, set in the middle of the range. It is not. Friendly and colleagues found earlier versions of the graph, the oldest in a letter to the Archduchess Isabella from before March 1628, where ROMA is written in front of each authority’s name: every marker is “Rome, according to this person”. Combining several observations into one average was not yet an idea anyone had published. They date its first statement to 1635, seven years after that letter.
The right answer. Taking Toledo at 4.03° W and Rome at 12.5° E, the difference is 16.53°. That figure took more than a century after this graph to pin down, and it is the one number the critique needs that van Langren could not have had.



THE SAME TWELVE NUMBERS, DIFFERENT CHOICES


The table he could have sent


Show the R code
langren |>
  transmute(authority = Longname, `worked in` = City,
            `degrees east of Toledo` = Longitude) |>
  arrange(authority) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)





authority
worked in
degrees east of Toledo




Andrea Argoli
Padua
28.2


Christoph Clavius
Rome
26.3


Claudius Ptolemaeus
Alexandria
27.8


David Origanus
Frankfurt
30.1


Gerardus Mercator
Leuven
19.9


Giovanni Antonio Magini
Bologna
29.8


Jan Jansson
Amsterdam
17.7


Johann Muller
Nuremberg
25.6


Johann Schoner
Bamberg
20.6


Oronce Fine
Paris
26.0


Phillip van Lansberge
Middelburg
21.1


Tycho Brahe
Hven
21.4






Sorted by name, as a list of authorities would be. Every number is here, and the 12-degree spread is not: finding it means reading all twelve rows and subtracting. Twelve rows are not too many for a table, and the graph still wins.



With the answer we have now


Show the R code
langren |>
  ggplot(aes(Longitude, fct_reorder(Longname, Longitude))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = TRUE_LONG, colour = p$ink_3, linewidth = .6) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = TRUE_LONG, xend = Longitude, yend = Longname),
               colour = dsvar_accent(), alpha = .45, linewidth = .8) +
  geom_point(colour = dsvar_accent(), size = 2.8) +
  annotate("text", x = TRUE_LONG - .25, y = 12.6, hjust = 1, size = 3.2,
           label = sprintf("the true distance, %.1f°", TRUE_LONG),
           family = dsvar_font(), colour = p$ink_3) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(12, 31), breaks = seq(15, 30, 5),
                     labels = \(x) paste0(x, "°")) +
  scale_y_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(.6, 1.3))) +
  labs(title = sprintf("All twelve overshoot: the nearest by %.1f°, the farthest by %.1f°",
                       min(err), max(err)),
       subtitle = "Each line runs from the true distance to one authority's estimate",
       x = "Degrees of longitude east of Toledo", y = NULL,
       caption = sprintf("True distance from Toledo %.2f° W and Rome %.2f° E. n = %d.",
                         abs(TOLEDO[["lon"]]), ROME[["lon"]], nrow(langren))) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = p$hairline, linewidth = .35))










One added line turns a picture of disagreement into a picture of bias. Van Langren’s graph shows the estimates are spread out. This one shows they are spread out on the wrong side.



On a map


Show the R code
romes <- langren |>
  mutate(lon = TOLEDO[["lon"]] + Longitude, lat = ROME[["lat"]],
         where = maps::map.where("world", lon, lat))
n_italy   <- sum(romes$where == "Italy", na.rm = TRUE)
n_sea     <- sum(is.na(romes$where))
n_balkans <- sum(romes$where %in% c("North Macedonia", "Bulgaria"))
stopifnot(n_italy + n_sea + n_balkans == nrow(romes))

cities <- tibble(name = c("Toledo", "Rome"),
                 lon = c(TOLEDO[["lon"]], ROME[["lon"]]),
                 lat = c(TOLEDO[["lat"]], ROME[["lat"]]))

# Names written straight up, as van Langren set them, nudged apart where two
# estimates sit closer than a line of type (spread_out() is from the
# recreation above). No name moves more than a tenth of a degree.
named <- romes |> mutate(at = spread_out(lon, .5))

# Each arrow stops a little short of its dot, so the head is not hidden under
# it. "Short" has to be measured along the direction the curve arrives from,
# not the straight line from Toledo: a curve of curvature k arrives turned by
# about 2·atan(k) from its chord. Worked on the drawn map, where a degree of
# longitude is cos(latitude) as wide as a degree of latitude.
CURVE <- .25
squash <- cos(mean(c(35.5, 46.5)) * pi / 180)
trips <- romes |>
  mutate(chord = atan2(lat - TOLEDO[["lat"]], (lon - TOLEDO[["lon"]]) * squash),
         arrive = chord + 2 * atan(CURVE),
         xend = lon - .24 * cos(arrive) / squash,
         yend = lat - .24 * sin(arrive))

ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = map_data("world"), aes(long, lat, group = group),
               fill = "#ece8de", colour = "#d6d0c2", linewidth = .2) +
  # One trip per estimate, as on a flow map: Toledo is where every one starts
  geom_curve(data = trips, aes(x = TOLEDO[["lon"]], y = TOLEDO[["lat"]],
                               xend = xend, yend = yend),
             curvature = CURVE, colour = dsvar_accent(), alpha = .35, linewidth = .3,
             arrow = arrow(length = unit(1.4, "mm"), type = "closed")) +
  geom_text(data = named, aes(at, lat + .4, label = Name), angle = 90, hjust = 0,
            family = dsvar_font(), size = 2.5, colour = p$ink_3) +
  geom_point(data = romes, aes(lon, lat), colour = dsvar_accent(), size = 2.6) +
  geom_point(data = cities, aes(lon, lat), colour = p$ink, size = 2.6, shape = 15) +
  geom_text(data = cities, aes(lon, lat, label = name), vjust = 1.9,
            family = dsvar_font(), fontface = "bold", size = 3.4, colour = p$ink) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(-9.5, 29), ylim = c(35.5, 46.5), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = sprintf("Twelve Romes: %d in Italy, %d in the Adriatic, %d in the Balkans",
                       n_italy, n_sea, n_balkans),
       subtitle = "Each estimate measured east from Toledo and placed on Rome's latitude",
       x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = "Coastlines: the maps package.") +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
        axis.line.x = element_blank(),
        panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#e3edf0", colour = NA))










The same numbers as distances on the ground, which is what they were for. Christoph Clavius taught in Rome, at the Collegio Romano, and his figure puts the city in North Macedonia.


A graph of many estimates of one quantity shows how much they disagree. It cannot show whether they are right, because the right answer is not one of the marks. That is still true: when 29 research teams analysed one dataset, the chart of their answers made the same argument van Langren’s did, and had the same missing line. See Many analysts, one dataset. Spread is visible; bias needs a reference, so if you have one, draw it.





SOURCES


Original: van Langren, M. F. (1644). La Verdadera Longitud por Mar y Tierra. Antwerp. Public domain; scan via Wikimedia Commons.
History, and the earlier versions: Friendly, M., Valero-Mora, P., & Ibáñez Ulargui, J. (2010). The first (known) statistical graph: Michael Florent van Langren and the “secret” of longitude. The American Statistician, 64(2), 174–184. doi:10.1198/tast.2010.09154
Data: Langren1644 from the HistData package (version 1.1.1), the digitisation from that paper. The 1644 graph is public domain; the digitisation is Friendly et al.’s, CC BY-NC 3.0 at datavis.ca and GPL in HistData. Vendored here as data/raw/langren-1644.csv.
Map: country outlines from the maps package.
Reproduce it: every figure on this page is built by the code shown above it.

title: Data Science: Visualisation and Analytics in R
text:
MA · Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam


Data Science: Visualisation and Analytics in R

Welcome to “Data Science: Visualisation and Analytics in R”! The key idea behind this course is that any visualization tries to make an argument, but most datasets can support more than one. The eight-week course is about the choices that decide which argument a chart makes, and the rules that guide those choices. The course is built around the R programming language, and the ggplot2 package in particular, but it is not about programming: it is about using programming to make better charts.

Start with Week 1 




OVERVIEW: AN EIGHT-WEEK COURSE

The argument in the graphWEEK 1 · the thesisComparison & rankingWEEK 2 · categorical × continuous · opens laterDistribution & uncertaintyWEEK 3 · one continuous · opens laterRelationships & structureWEEK 4 · two continuous · opens laterChange over timeWEEK 5 · continuous × time · opens laterStructure in space and textWEEK 6 · space, graph, text · opens laterThe whole storyWEEK 7 · your data · opens laterThe take-homeWEEK 8 · no sessions · opens later

Each week is about a different job a visualization is asked to do. Read the small print across the two rows: each week adds one variable, or one new kind of variable. By the way, every thumbnail here is a real ggplot figure, built from data that comes with R. All the graphs and figures on this site are made with the same tools you will learn in the course.




BUILDING A FIGURE: THE SAME SEQUENCE, EVERY WEEK


01QuestionWhat are you asking of the data02ClaimThe sentence the chart has to earn03EvidenceWhat the data can actually support04EncodingThe choice that does the arguing05AnnotationWhere the honesty lives


One chart in five states, with the same data throughout. The only thing that changes is what its author has decided to show. Step five adds an annotation or highlight, the step that most often gets skipped: a chart without annotation has drawn its data but has not made its claim. Every week we go through the same steps and ask the same questions; what changes is the data and the claim the chart is asked to support.

title: First steps in R, and the grammar in ggplot
text:
02 CLAIM Work group 1 · First steps in R, and the grammar in ggplot Thursday 13:30 · 105 min
Today is about getting started with R and in RStudio. You learn enough R to read a file and look at it, then the handful of functions that get a table into shape for a chart, and then you build one chart, one grammar slot at a time, using the same eight settings you saw in Tuesday’s lecture. Important: Nothing is handed in this week. Yet, whatever you do not finish in the room, finish at home: week 2 assumes that you understood all of it.

title: First steps in R, and the grammar in ggplot
text:
1 · Setup
Run these in the console, the pane at the bottom left of RStudio. Each line prints something; none should give an error.

library(tidyverse)          # loads ggplot2, dplyr, tidyr, readr and a few more
packageVersion("ggplot2")   # 3.5 or higher; the course is written on 4.0
R.version.string            # 4.4 or higher

Then, in the Terminal tab (not the console), type quarto check. It should end with Checking Knitr engine render… OK.

This week’s folder
Every work group comes with a folder: the data, the course theme, and a Quarto file to work in.
Download the week 1 folder

Unzip it into your dsvar folder. On Windows that is right-click → Extract All. Working inside the zip without extracting it is the most common reason R cannot find a file.
Double-click dsvar-week-01.Rproj. RStudio opens with this folder as its working directory, which is why "data/…" below needs no full path. Every week, start here.
Open workgroup-01.qmd and press Render. If a page appears, R, Quarto, the theme and the data all work.








workgroup-01.qmd
Today’s working file. This page’s headings, an empty chunk under each. Not handed in


theme-dsvar.R
The course theme


data/
Today’s file, exactly as the KNMI publishes it





Console or file
There are two places to type R.

The console runs a line the moment you press Enter, and forgets it. Use it to try things out.
A chunk in workgroup-01.qmd (the grey box that starts with ```{r}) keeps your code. Put the cursor on a line and press Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on a Mac) to run it, or the green arrow to run the whole chunk.

Anything you want to keep goes in the file. From section 2 on, type into the chunk under each heading.

title: First steps in R, and the grammar in ggplot
text:
2 · R basics

2.1 · R as a calculator

144 / 10                   # tenths of a degree, into degrees
(17.2 + 18.9 + 19.4) / 3

The [1] in front of each answer is R numbering its output. You can ignore it.
Everything after a # is a comment. R skips it; it is there for whoever reads the code next, which is usually you. The code on this site uses comments to say what a line does.


2.2 · Objects
<- stores a value under a name. Read it out loud as “gets”: july gets 18.1.

july <- 18.1
july * 2

Nothing prints when you store something. Type the name on its own to see it, or look in the Environment pane at the top right, which lists every object you have made. Names are case sensitive, so July is a different object, and one that does not exist yet. Try it in the console and read the error: object ‘July’ not found is the error you will see most often this term, and it nearly always means a typo.


RED TEXT IS NOT ALWAYS AN ERROR

R prints three kinds of red text, and only one means it failed. An error starts with Error and stops: nothing was made, and an error in a chunk stops Render too. A warning starts with Warning: it ran, but check the result. A message is information: the lines library(tidyverse) printed in section 1 were messages.



2.3 · Vectors
c() combines several values into one vector. These are De Bilt’s summer means for 2022 to 2025, in °C. Arithmetic on a vector happens to every value at once.

summers <- c(18.6, 18.4, 17.7, 18.5)
summers - 17
length(summers)



PREDICT, THEN RUN

If you run summers * 10, how many numbers will be printed?

Every column of a table is a vector, which 2.8 comes back to.


2.4 · Kinds of value
Numbers are one kind of value. Two more are important to know:

"JUL"                # text, always in quotes
summers > 18         # a comparison: TRUE or FALSE, once for every value
class(summers)
class("JUL")
class(summers > 18)

class() shows the kind. R calls numbers numeric, text character, and TRUE or FALSE logical. glimpse() in section 3 writes the same kinds as short tags: <dbl> for numbers, <chr> for text, <lgl> for TRUE or FALSE.
A comparison is all filter() in 4.2 needs: it keeps the rows where the condition is TRUE.


PREDICT, THEN RUN

What does "18.1" * 2 give?

In quotes, 18.1 is text, and R does no arithmetic on text. When a column of numbers arrives as <chr>, there is nearly always a letter or a symbol hiding in it somewhere.


2.5 · Functions
A function takes values in and gives a value back. The values inside the brackets are its arguments, and they can have names.

mean(summers)
round(18.36, digits = 1)
seq(1901, 2021, by = 30)

One more thing to know from the first day: missing values, which are written as NA.

mean(c(17.2, NA, 19.4))
mean(c(17.2, NA, 19.4), na.rm = TRUE)

One missing value makes the whole mean missing, unless you tell R how to handle it. R is being careful here, not difficult: an average of the values you happen to have is a different number, and R wants you to choose it on purpose. Today’s data set has missing values in it.


2.6 · Help
? and a function’s name, typed in the console, open its help page in the Help pane, bottom right. So does F1, with the cursor on the name.

?mean

Every help page has the same parts:



Description
what the function does, in a sentence or two


Usage
how to call it: every argument, and its default


Arguments
what each argument means


Value
what it gives back


Examples
code that runs, at the bottom. Try one in the console



Under Usage, ?mean shows mean(x, trim = 0, na.rm = FALSE, ...). An argument written with = has a default, and R uses it whenever you leave the argument out. na.rm = FALSE is why 2.5 gave NA: unless you say otherwise, R keeps the missing values in. A default is still a choice; someone else made it.
Help pages are written for people who already know R, so do not expect to understand all parts immediately. Usage and Examples are enough to start.


2.7 · Packages
A package is a set of functions someone else wrote. You install it once per computer and load it once per session.

install.packages("tidyverse")   # once. You did this before Thursday
library(tidyverse)              # every session, at the top of every file

ggplot2, which draws every chart in this course, is one of the packages in the tidyverse.


2.8 · Tables
A table in R is a data frame: vectors of the same length, side by side, one per column. tibble(), from the tidyverse, makes one from vectors you name. 2022:2025 is every whole number from 2022 to 2025.

recent <- tibble(year = 2022:2025, summer = summers)
recent
recent$summer        # $ takes one column back out, as a vector

Every column holds one kind of value, and the tags under the names say which; <int> is a whole number. A tibble is the tidyverse’s own data frame, and it prints more tidily. Help pages and AI answers say data frame; in this course the two mean the same thing.
Every table in this course is a data frame like this one, read from a file instead of typed in. That is next.

title: First steps in R, and the grammar in ggplot
text:
3 · Meet the data
The Royal Netherlands Meteorological Institute (KNMI) publishes monthly mean temperatures for its weather stations. This is De Bilt, the reference station, and this is what the file looks like when it arrives:


Deze gegevens mogen vrij worden gebruikt mits de volgende bronvermelding wordt gegeven:
KONINKLIJK NEDERLANDS METEOROLOGISCH INSTITUUT (KNMI)

These data can be used freely provided that the following source is acknowledged:
ROYAL NETHERLANDS METEOROLOGICAL INSTITUTE

MAAND- en JAARGEMIDDELDE TEMPERATUREN (0.1 graden Celsius)
MONTHLY AND YEARLY MEAN TEMPERATURES (0.1 degrees Celsius)

STN = stationsnummer / WMO-number = 06... (235=De Kooy,240=Schiphol,260=De Bilt,270=Leeuwarden,280=Eelde,
      290=Twenthe,310=Vlissingen,344=Rotterdam,370=Eindhoven,380=Maastricht)


STN,YYYY,   JAN,   FEB,   MAR,   APR,   MAY,   JUN,   JUL,   AUG,   SEP,   OCT,   NOV,   DEC,  YEAR

260,1901,    -3,   -10,    35,    89,   120,   144,   184,   164,   144,   102,    52,    29,    88
260,1902,    45,    -4,    52,    84,    92,   155,   153,   146,   129,    85,    37,     8,    82
260,1903,    29,    56,    70,    55,   126,   140,   153,   150,   141,   110,    56,     7,    91


Two things to notice before reading it in. Thirteen lines of notes come before the header, and R has to be told to skip them. And the unit is “0.1 degrees Celsius”, so 144 means 14.4 °C. Nothing in the numbers tells you that; only the notes do.

bilt <- read_csv("data/knmi-de-bilt-monthly.txt", skip = 13)
glimpse(bilt)

glimpse() lists every column, its kind and its first values. Every column of bilt is <dbl>: the file holds no text at all. Four more ways to look:

View(bilt)       # the table in a spreadsheet-style tab. Look, do not edit
nrow(bilt)       # how many rows
bilt$JUL         # one column, as a vector. $ picks a column by name
summary(bilt)    # six numbers for every column, and how many are missing

summary() works on one column too, and it is worth running on every new file:

summary(bilt$JUL)
summary(bilt$YEAR)

The six numbers are the smallest and the largest, the mean, the median in the middle, and the two quartiles, a quarter of the way in from each end. Two things in them should stop you. The warmest July reads 223, which is no temperature in degrees: that is the unit from the notes, showing in the numbers. And YEAR has one NA, a year with no annual mean.
What is one row? One year. The twelve months sit side by side as columns, and YEAR is KNMI’s own annual mean. It is blank for 2026, which is not over yet.







Column
What it is




STN
Station number. 260 is De Bilt. The same in every row


YYYY
The year


JAN … DEC
Monthly mean temperature, tenths of °C


YEAR
KNMI’s annual mean, tenths of °C. Blank for the current year



Source, for every caption you write today: KNMI, De Bilt monthly means.

Type the columns
Every week starts the same way: go down the columns and explain each one. Four words cover almost everything this course will meet:







identifier
names a row; you never compare by it


categorical
sorts rows into groups: nominal with no order, ordinal with one


continuous
a measured quantity, where differences mean something


date
a point in time, ordered by nature



These words are about what a column means. The tags from 2.4 are about how R stores it, and the two do not always match. STN is an identifier. YYYY is a date, stored as a plain number. JAN to DEC and YEAR are continuous. Week 2 is built on the categorical kind.

title: First steps in R, and the grammar in ggplot
text:
4 · Wrangling with the pipe
A chart can only show the table or data set it is given. Most of the work before a chart is getting the table into the right shape: the right rows, the right columns, the right units, one row per thing you want to draw. The tidyverse does this with a handful of functions, often called verbs. Each one takes a table and gives back a table, which is why they chain.

4.1 · The pipe
|> passes what is on its left into the function on its right, as the first argument. Read it out loud as “and then”. These two lines do exactly the same:

glimpse(bilt)
bilt |> glimpse()

The pipe earns its place once there are several steps. Inside out, you read the last step first:

head(filter(bilt, YYYY >= 2016), 3)

With the pipe, you read the steps in the order they happen: take bilt, and then keep the years from 2016, and then show the first three rows.

bilt |>
  filter(YYYY >= 2016) |>
  head(3)



NOTHING IS SAVED UNTIL YOU SAY SO

A verb returns a new table and leaves bilt as it was. To keep the result, give it a name with <-. Running bilt |> filter(YYYY >= 2016) and then nrow(bilt) still gives 126.



4.2 · filter() keeps rows
filter() keeps the rows for which a condition is true. Everything else is dropped.


bilt |> filter(YYYY >= 2016)                  # from 2016 on
bilt |> filter(YYYY >= 1991, YYYY <= 2020)    # a comma means "and"
bilt |> filter(!is.na(YEAR))                  # ! means "not"




==
equal to. Two signs: one = sets an argument, == compares


!=
not equal to


>, <, >=, <=
greater, smaller, or equal


%in%
one of: month %in% c("JUN", "JUL", "AUG")


is.na()
missing





PREDICT, THEN RUN

How many rows does the second line keep? Then add |> nrow() to the end of it and check.



4.3 · select() keeps columns
select() keeps the columns you name, in the order you name them. A minus sign drops one, and new = old renames it on the way.


bilt |> select(YYYY, JAN, JUL)        # three columns
bilt |> select(-STN)                  # every column except STN
bilt |> select(year = YYYY, YEAR)     # keep two, and rename one
bilt |> select(YYYY, JAN:DEC)         # a colon means "from ... to"



4.4 · mutate() makes a column
mutate() adds a column, or replaces one, by computing it row by row. The arithmetic is the vector arithmetic from 2.3, done to a whole column at once.


bilt |> mutate(temp = YEAR / 10)                    # tenths of a degree, into degrees
bilt |> mutate(summer = (JUN + JUL + AUG) / 30)     # summer mean, in degrees

The second line divides by 30: three months added up, divided by three for the mean and by ten for the unit. For 2022 to 2025 it gives the four summers you typed in 2.3.


4.5 · arrange() sorts rows

bilt |>
  mutate(temp = YEAR / 10) |>
  arrange(desc(temp)) |>        # desc(): largest first
  head(5)



PREDICT, THEN RUN

The five warmest years at De Bilt since 1901: from which decades do you expect them to come?



4.6 · group_by() and summarise(): one row per group
summarise() collapses many rows into one. After group_by(), it does that once per group. Here the groups are decades: floor(year / 10) * 10 turns 1987 into 1980.


bilt |>
  filter(!is.na(YEAR)) |>
  mutate(temp = YEAR / 10, decade = floor(YYYY / 10) * 10) |>
  group_by(decade) |>
  summarise(temp = mean(temp), n = n())

Always ask for n = n(). It says how many rows each summary stands for, and here it shows something the means hide: the first decade has nine years (the record starts in 1901) and the last has six. count(decade) is a shortcut for group_by(decade) |> summarise(n = n()).


4.7 · Wide and long: pivot_longer() and pivot_wider()
A table is tidy when every variable is a column and every row is one observation. bilt is not quite tidy: month is a variable, but its twelve values, JAN to DEC, are the column names. That shape is called wide. It is good for reading, and bad for ggplot, which can only map a column: there is no column called month to put on an axis or split into panels.
pivot_longer() turns the columns you name into two new columns: one for the old names, one for the values.


long <- bilt |>
  select(YYYY, JAN:DEC) |>
  pivot_longer(JAN:DEC, names_to = "month", values_to = "temp")



PREDICT, THEN RUN

bilt has 126 rows. How many will long have? Then run nrow(long).

pivot_wider() is the way back. It takes the names for the new columns from one column and their values from another.


long |> pivot_wider(names_from = month, values_from = temp)

Neither shape is wrong. Wide is for people reading a table; long is what ggplot and group_by() need. You will pivot in both directions this term.


4.8 · The whole pipeline
Everything at once: the table the grammar section uses, made in one pipe.


annual <- bilt |>
  filter(!is.na(YEAR)) |>      # keep the rows where YEAR is not missing
  mutate(temp = YEAR / 10) |>  # a new column: tenths of a degree, into degrees
  select(year = YYYY, temp)    # keep two columns, and rename one



PREDICT, THEN RUN

bilt has 126 rows. How many will annual have, and why? Then run nrow(annual).

125 complete years, 1901 to 2025. That number is the n on the chart you are about to build.

title: First steps in R, and the grammar in ggplot
text:
5 · The grammar in ggplot
Tuesday’s lecture described every chart with the same eight slots or lines. In ggplot each slot is a piece of code, and you add the pieces with +. Most slots have a default, so a chart can be very short and still have all eight.








Slot
What it decides
In ggplot




data
which table
ggplot(annual, ...)


mapping
which column goes to which channel
aes(x = year, y = temp)


geom
the mark
geom_point(), geom_line()


stat
anything computed before drawing
geom_smooth()


scale
how a value becomes a position or a colour
scale_y_continuous()


coord
the space the marks are drawn in
coord_cartesian()


facet
splitting into small panels
facet_wrap()


theme
everything that is not data
theme_minimal(), labs()



Add one slot, run it, and look at what changed before you add the next.

5.1 · Data and mapping


PREDICT

What appears when there is data and a mapping but no geom?


ggplot(annual, aes(x = year, y = temp))

Axes with the right ranges and nothing on them. The mapping is set; no marks have been drawn yet.


5.2 · Geom
One mark per year:

ggplot(annual, aes(x = year, y = temp)) +
  geom_point()

Same mapping, another geom:

ggplot(annual, aes(x = year, y = temp)) +
  geom_line()

A line says the years are connected, that the temperature existed between two measurements and moved from one to the next. For a temperature that is true. For two separate surveys it would not be.


5.3 · Stat
Some layers draw something that is computed from the rows rather than the rows themselves. geom_smooth() fits a curve through the points and draws that, with a band around it.

ggplot(annual, aes(x = year, y = temp)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_smooth()

The message R prints says what it computed. Nothing on the chart says so, which is why a chart with a smooth needs a caption.


5.4 · Scale
The scale decides how a value becomes a position. Here the y axis is made to run from 0 to 20 °C:

ggplot(annual, aes(x = year, y = temp)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 20))



LOOK AGAIN

Same data, same geom, and the warming has almost disappeared. Only the scale changed. Which version is right is week 2’s question. For now, notice how much one line can change.



5.5 · Coord
The coord is the space the marks are drawn in. coord_cartesian() zooms in on part of it without dropping any data:

ggplot(annual, aes(x = year, y = temp)) +
  geom_line() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(1990, 2025))



5.6 · Facet
A facet splits one chart into small panels, one per group. It needs a column that says which group each row is in, and annual has none. The months are the obvious groups, but in bilt they are column names. This is where 4.7 pays off: pivot_longer() moves them into a column of their own.

seasons <- bilt |>
  filter(!is.na(DEC)) |>                      # complete years only
  select(year = YYYY, JAN, APR, JUL, OCT) |>  # one month from each season
  pivot_longer(JAN:OCT, names_to = "month", values_to = "temp") |>
  mutate(temp = temp / 10)

seasons

Four rows per year now, one per month. ggplot can only map a column, so the shape of the table decides which charts are one line away.

ggplot(seasons, aes(x = year, y = temp)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ month)

The panels are in alphabetical order, April first. That is R’s default for text, and week 2 is about why it is rarely the order you want.


5.7 · Theme and labels
labs() writes the words, and the title is the most-read line on a chart. Tuesday’s lecture argued that a chart is a claim, so the title states the claim instead of naming the variables. The caption carries the n, the source and what the chart cannot tell you.

ggplot(annual, aes(x = year, y = temp)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title    = "De Bilt is about two degrees warmer than a century ago",
       subtitle = "Annual mean temperature at De Bilt, °C",
       caption  = "n = 125 complete years, 1901 to 2025 · KNMI, De Bilt monthly means · one station, raw record",
       x = NULL, y = "°C")

Every chart on this page has used the course theme, which the setup chunk of workgroup-01.qmd switched on with theme_set(theme_dsvar()). A theme added to one chart overrides it for that chart only:

... + theme_minimal()

What is inside a theme, and how to write your own, is week 7.


5.8 · Your turn
Change slots, not data. Start this in the room if there is time; otherwise it is homework. Starting from the chart in 5.7:

Draw July only, with points instead of a line. (Which table has July in it, and which function keeps some rows?)
Add a smooth.
Write a title that says what the chart shows, in one sentence with a verb.
